Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapter

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:29:32 GMT

With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.

And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.

Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.

Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.

He made his closing pitch on Monday in front of the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".

But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.

His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.

"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.

"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.

At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."

Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?

The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.

Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.

Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.

"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."

Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.

There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.

"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.

"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."

"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.

When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.

"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."

"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.

"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."

That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.

But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.

Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.

In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.

Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.

"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.

"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."

The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative values.

"One dollar more on gas is not going to change what we believe in," Tim McKinnon told me.

If Democrats do win a large swathe of seats on Tuesday night, it won't necessarily be because voters love them – they just hate them a little less.

The party, however, is already looking ahead to a 2028 presidential election in which they will have to unite behind a single candidate. That is easier said than done given their clear fractures - some of which spilled out publicly during this election cycle, including in Michigan over the weekend.

Democrats will be closely watching these results for lessons ahead of 2028. Can they really win in Texas? Can they tempt rural voters in deep Republican strongholds? And will some of their rising stars, such as Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas, live up to the hype?

If the answer to some of these questions is no, there will be much to ponder for the party over the next year. And the post-mortem may not be pretty.

"This represents an opportunity, really, for Democrats to expand a lot of their influence, not just in terms of numbers, but in terms of perception of where they can compete," Hawkins, from the pollster More in Common, said.

Republican attempts, including from Trump himself, to paint the Democrats as dangerous communists have not landed with all voters.

In Detroit, Michigan, Nicole Williams - who owns her own hairdressing salon - summed up the view of many people I spoke to. "Anything is better than what we have now," she said. "Socialist? Socialised? It don't matter to me. Lower my cost of living."

"People are just tired of the disrespect to Americans, because he is an American," Gwen Jackson, another Michigan voter, said, referring to the state's left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed who Trump has repeatedly attacked.

"People are just tired," she said. "They're ready to see a change."

Even when a sitting president is more popular than Trump, their party usually loses seats in the midterms. This, combined with the latest polling, means there is confidence among Democrats that they will at least win the House of Representatives.

"It's the cost of living, it's the undeclared war," Democratic strategist Mary Anne Marsh said of the key issues. "Every Republican who did not stand up to Donald Trump is about to realise the consequences of believing he was invincible."

If the Democrats do win the House, the party could try to block any legislation Trump wants to pass. That is unlikely to worry him, given he has already tried to bypass Congress as much as possible and rule by signing executive orders from the Oval Office instead.

Trump will be more concerned about the investigations Democrats will be able to launch if they take control of the House. They may also try to impeach some of his cabinet members, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth seen as a likely candidate due to the war in Iran.

Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.

Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.

Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina.

This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.

There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.

But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.

How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections, and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.

These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.

For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.

As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.

Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:09:18 GMT

This video can not be played

De Miguel died in hospital following serious injuries suffered in on-pitch collision

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.

The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.

De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.

Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.

Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said.

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."

Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal

Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.

Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.

The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.

Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.

The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.

The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.

Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.

Tenerife's president, Felipe Minambres, says the club's players will need "professional assistance" to help deal with the ordeal of one of their team-mates dying.

"We are all feeling vulnerable and deeply saddened right now. It's hard to even believe what has happened," said Minambres.

"We know, especially the players and the players' partners, that we will need support. We've already begun receiving offers of help today, and that support will continue.

"We will need professional assistance, but we also need the support of all our fans, because they are likely feeling the same way we are today."

Minambres added it had been a "truly unbelievable situation" and "an enormous tragedy that we have had to endure".

Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, issued a statement later on Tuesday which spoke of the club's shock and expressed condolences to De Miguel's family, club "and all those who were close to him".

"We are deeply affected by what has happened and we share the pain that the club is experiencing," it continued.

"From the very beginning we have maintained contact with them and we are at their disposal for anything they may need.

"What has happened has had a huge emotional impact on our players, the coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. These are particularly difficult times for everyone and we want to make sure that no one has to face them alone. That is why the club is providing psychological support to anyone who needs it."

Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."

De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.

"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."

Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.

"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."

This video can not be played

Real Madrid and Arsenal honour De Miguel with minute's silence

Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."

Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."

The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.

Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.

De Miguel scored 11 goals in 29 matches for Tenerife

De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.

After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.

He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.

The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.

De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

Fans have been leaving tributes for De Miguel at Tenerife's Heliodoro stadium

Real Madrid's first-team squad held a minute's silence for De Miguel before training on Tuesday morning

Arsenal's squad observed a minute's silence for De Miguel before training on Tuesday

De Miguel's daughter, Carla, was born in 2025

When will we know the US midterms results?

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:56:09 GMT

Millions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.

Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.

Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.

To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.

First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT). They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).

Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.

There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.

Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.

This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.

The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.

In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.

While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.

The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.

Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.

Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.

The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.

There are six Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report - Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas.

Of these, six are currently held by Republicans. The Democrats would need to win three of those seats, plus five classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

Polls have suggested Democrats have a chance in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

Democrats also need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent in a closely-observed race. The state was initially classified as a "toss-up" by Cook Political Report, but was reclassified as "leans Democrat" the day before the vote.

The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.

Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.

The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.

Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the key battleground states:

Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.

Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.

Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.

Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.

Every state and locality has rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, including how partisan observers can watch the count and, in some states, raise formal challenges.

Tight races will take longer, and create the possibility of recounts being triggered and legal challenges.

Mail-in ballots take longer to count, as officials need to process envelopes and verify signatures.

More than 30 states allow ballots to be processed before election day, but other states do not. In California, all ballots must be posted before or on election day and will still be counted if they arrive within seven days of the election.

In Alaska, ranked-choice voting could mean that tabulations take considerably longer than elsewhere in the country and the controversy over ballots could mean that legal challenges can complicate things.

Once every vote has been included in the final results, and after processes such as recounts have been completed, the election results are certified - first at the local, county, level and then state-wide.

The governor then typically signs the certifications for House and Senate winners to be sent to Congress.

Results can be challenged. Recounts can be requested by candidates in close races, and in some states recounts are automatically triggered if they fall within a certain margin.

Candidates can also file legal election contests alleging irregularities.

Congress has the final word. Losing candidates in both House and Senate races can file contests, with slightly different processes in each of the two chambers.

Both chambers can, theoretically, refuse to seat someone or order an investigation.

Outgoing members of Congress leave office on Sunday 3 January. Because that date falls on a weekend, the new members may take office on the same date unless Congress passes a law setting a different day.

Additional reporting by James FitzGerald, Yazmina García-Fernández, Tom Geoghegan and Mike Hills.

From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:50:14 GMT

Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.

On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.

Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.

Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.

During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.

Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."

In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.

Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.

Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.

"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."

Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.

"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.

Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.

Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".

While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.

Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.

She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.

"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."

Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."

For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.

This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."

Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items.

Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.

But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?

Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.

"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.

In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land.

In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.

"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

James Blunt on Traitors: I tried - and failed - to get banished

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:33:25 GMT

He may have made it to the final episode of this year's Celebrity Traitors, but James Blunt says he did his best to get banished from the show.

The singer-songwriter became a fan favourite for his 1980s leisurewear, outlandish conspiracy theories and military-style approach to tasks.

A dominating presence at the round table, he characterises himself as the "yapping terrier" to actor Michael Sheen's "mature labrador", as they sniffed out the traitors.

Behind the scenes, however, he was playing a different game.

"We all get paid the same, whether you're there for day one or day 23," he tells the BBC.

"So for most of the time, I was trying to... get the hell out of dodge. But no-one was killing me and no-one was banishing me!"

Blunt's cavalier approach informed his gameplay. He knew that outspoken players are often snuffed out first, and that his best bet was to keep a low profile.

"But that's also really boring," he says. "And so for me, I just thought, 'Let's just go around and come up with theories.'

"You don't see it in the edit, but I was telling everyone, 'It doesn't matter [who goes], just kill them all!'

"It's fine, as long as you're apologetic when you get it wrong."

He was wrong more often than he was right. But in the penultimate episode, Blunt and Sheen stumbled on to a theory that the quiet contestants were more suspicious than their outspoken brethren.

In a pivotal round table, they turned their attention towards comedian James Acaster, and picked apart his story of a "murder in plain sight" that had occurred nights earlier.

Caught in the crosshairs, Acaster simply confessed.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

Blunt says there was more to the sequence than viewers realised, hinting that Acaster was caught in a fib about a perfume bottle used in the murderous act.

"He didn't fall on his sword. That's what you saw, that's what you feel, but he didn't.

"You didn't see the full extent of the interrogation. It was heavy in there and it was clear-cut. He was pinned to a post. We got him. We really, really got him.

"I think how that played out hasn't really been revealed to you, but he didn't just say, 'Oh guys, you got me'."

In his exit interview, Acaster admitted the round table had been intense, but laughed off his uncloaking.

"It was sprung on me. It was a surprise," he said. "But I was glad that they caught me."

Blunt says the editing of the TV show is crucial to people's understanding of events.

And, with days and days of footage to sift through, not everything that happens makes it to air.

"There are elements [of the show] where I was screaming at the screen for a different reason than you," he laughs. "No matter what really went on in that castle, you're a victim to the edit."

Still, some of his favourite moments made it into the show, including actress and model Jerry Hall calling him "smooth like butter dripping off of hot corn".

"That was a very special one," he laughs. "And she also said, to my face, 'I'll take you home in your wetsuit'".

And what about Blunt's confession that he greased his nipples with butter before every physical task?

"I'm amazed you don't do that yourself, Mark," he shoots back.

In the end, however, he was voted off the show in its dying moments, when comedian Romesh Ranganathan couldn't shake the idea that Blunt was in cahoots with the traitorous Maya Jama.

Blunt maintains he was blindsided by the accusation, but bears no grudges.

"The ending was perfect. It had all the twists and turns. I wouldn't have wanted it any other way."

Still the question remains. If he wasn't that keen to go the distance in the castle, why did he enter in the first place? Was it simply for the experience, or did he simply want to promote his new music?

"I think you may have hit the nail on the head with the latter," he grins.

"I don't think otherwise I would have signed up to be imprisoned in a castle in Scotland."

There's a method in his madness, though.

In Blunt's own estimation, his eighth album, Airplane Mode, is his best work in years.

Now, musicians make that claim all the time. Blunt himself basically told me the same thing about his last album, 2023's Who We Used To Be.

But this time, he might have a point. After years of chasing radio hits and commercial success, he's gone back to writing from the heart.

The results are much more downbeat than you might expect from a man who's renowned for hilarious social media slapdowns and crowd surfing in inflatable dinghies.

Across the album's 12 tracks, he frequently sounds adrift, fretting about the state of the world and wrestling with "monsters in your head that you can't turn off".

"Darkness came like a tidal wave," he sings on the concerningly titled Reason To Die. "I'm paralysed by my body keeping score," he adds, over the portentous drums of Weight of it All.

The lyrics are informed by those negative, late-night thoughts that prey on your mind when you should be sleeping. Blunt says finally acknowledging them was a relief, after years of "trying to write happy upbeat radio singles".

"I don't have a therapist. I write songs as an exercise in voicing nostalgia and melancholy and the things I struggle with in the world.

"And, you know, the person you talk to the most in the world is the voice in your head. That's the truest conversation you're ever going to have, and that's who I was arguing with in the writing of this.

"I was going over the things that all of us struggle with: the burdens of growing up, growing older, having more responsibilities, having bills to pay, not knowing what the state of the world will be next year."

For all of his flippant humour, Blunt's demons are real.

In his 20s, he was an army captain stationed in Pristina during the brutal Kosovo war, and lost several close friends during the conflict.

Even after he left active service and became a successful musician, he was ostracised and ridiculed by his peers. He was later targeted in a tabloid newspaper sex sting, and was one of the many victims of the News of the World phone-hacking scandal.

The honesty of his new music reflects those experiences. And you can hear the rawness in his voice, too.

The musician who once quipped, "I sing like a girl", has a new depth to his vocals. On the new song Oh Daisy, there's even a Rod Stewart-esque rasp.

That, he says, is the result of a punishing 21-month tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of his debut album, Back To Bedlam (17.5 million copies sold and counting).

"I really damaged my vocal cords," he says. "I was pushing it too much, and my voice changed as a result.

"I actually now take singing lessons with different people – with an opera singer, even – and the [whole experience] has given my voice a bit of grit.

"Either that or my balls have dropped."

It's a typically self-deprecating jab. If anyone can laugh at themselves, it's James Blunt. And, however dark his new album gets, there's always a silver lining.

"This is not forever," he counsels himself on the closing track. "It's just for now."

"That song's a fist in the air saying, 'Yeah, we will endure'," says Blunt.

"I think I've been around long enough to know that I don't have to prove anything.

"The record label released my greatest hits album a couple of years ago, so if my greatest hits are already out, what am I doing now?

"I'm a guy on his own, writing songs with nothing to prove. That's a pretty good place to be."

Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored

BBC News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 06:01:23 GMT

Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.

A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.

"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.

But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.

It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.

Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.

"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.

"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."

Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.

"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.

She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.

The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.

Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".

But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.

"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.

The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

The nuclear waste repository in Finland designed to outlast modern civilisation

New Scientist November 03, 2026

There’s a timeless quality to the tunnels at Onkalo. And that’s the point. Carved into the rock more than 400 metres below ground, these passageways are part of a facility built for the long term. The extreme long term.

In fact, facilities such as Onkalo “should exist intact for at least 100,000, if not a million years”, says Allison Macfarlane at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who previously served as chair of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the US. “Those are geologic timescales.”

Onkalo is Finland’s answer to one of the more tricky questions posed by nuclear power: what do you do with the waste? We are going to have to get much better at answering it, given nuclear power is expanding again, driven partly by the hunt for low-carbon energy.

Advertisement

There’s broad consensus that burying the waste is the best option. But there is a catch. Radioactive elements can remain dangerous on timescales that make normal engineering look absurdly short-term. Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza is around 4500 years old. Some nuclear repositories will have to contain their contents for more than 20 times longer. Before the waste becomes harmless, civilisations may rise and fall, and ice sheets may come and go.

An earlier attempt to store waste on geological timescales failed spectacularly after just a few decades. The engineers at Onkalo, and at a handful of similar sites now being planned or built around the world, think they can do much better. So, as Onkalo prepares to accept its first waste shipments in the coming months, how exactly have the engineers future-proofed their facility?

Exclusive report: Inside Chernobyl, 40 years after nuclear disaster

The awkward thing about nuclear waste is that some of the most dangerous substances refuse to go away. Much of the material produced by the nuclear industry contains relatively low levels of radioactivity and can be handled with little drama.

But spent fuel and the materials used to build and shield the main nuclear reactor are another matter. Some of the radioactive elements they contain hang around for astonishing lengths of time. Iodine-129, for instance, has a half-life of almost 16 million years.

So, what do you do with it? Over the decades, researchers have entertained some spectacular ideas. One of the most eye-catching: blasting it into space.

“I have a one-word response to that, which is ‘Challenger’,” says Macfarlane. “We often send rockets up into space, and they blow up on the way. And if it’s carrying nuclear waste, that means that you get to breathe it and then greatly increase your risk of cancer.”

Given that possibility, in the end, the favoured solution is the same one we have been employing for decades: dig a very deep hole, put the waste inside and cover it up.

But even that’s easier said than done.

In 1967, authorities in what was then West Germany began storing radioactive waste in Asse II, a former salt mine. Over the following decades, more than 125,000 drums, mostly containing low- and intermediate-level waste, were stacked in chambers hundreds of metres underground. In the minds of the engineers, rock salt seemed like an ideal host. It is exceptionally impermeable to water and slowly deforms under pressure, meaning that if any cracks began to open up through which groundwater could flow, the rock could self-seal to keep the mine and its contents secure. But reality is rarely so simple.

By 1988, the operators had discovered that salty water was, in fact, flowing into the mine. The problem, as outlined in a 2011 report by the International Panel on Fissile Materials, was that the miners had excavated too close to the edge of the salt deposits and not backfilled enough of the caverns after they had finished with them. This weakened the underground structure and raised the risk of collapses, fracturing the salt faster than it could self-seal, and allowing water to seep in. The report suggested that the possibility of such collapses was flagged in 1979, but the warning was ignored.

The public became aware of the problem only in 2008. German authorities now have the unenviable task of retrieving the buried material: some 47,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste.

Asse II is about as stark a lesson in the difficulties of deep-time engineering as you could ask for. Getting radioactive waste underground is easy, but the devil is in securing it for time periods far beyond any normal engineering horizon. A barrier that looks reassuringly solid for a century may corrode, crack or shift over 1000 years. Stretch that timeline to 10,000 or 100,000 years, and engineering confidence drops.

One approach to this lack of confidence is to assume that extreme long-term storage might not, in fact, be required. Radioactive waste isn’t necessarily useless. Spent nuclear fuel still contains potentially valuable material. For instance, approximately 97 per cent of the material in used fuel can be recycled and mixed into fresh fuel, and future technologies may be able to extract even more use from it. Even if they can’t, people centuries from now may devise a better way to deal with the stuff.

Engineers in France are keeping that idea in mind. At an underground repository they plan to build in north-eastern France, known as Cigéo, a funicular railway will be on site so that nuclear waste can, in principle, be transported back to the surface in future.

Free newsletter

Cigéo, which is scheduled to be operational by the 2050s, will be carved into sedimentary mudrock, an impermeable material that limits the flow of groundwater and should keep the buried waste dry. But retaining the ability to remove nuclear waste would also act as an insurance policy, just in case problems similar to those at the Asse II repository emerge.

“People [in France] want to be assured that if something goes wrong with the site that they can remove all the waste,” says Macfarlane.

There is another concern about truly long-term storage: people living millennia from now may have no knowledge that the nuclear repositories exist, and they might accidentally drill into one of them, causing an environmental disaster.

People have come up with some wonderfully odd ways to avoid this outcome. Some researchers, aware that languages change or even fall out of use over long periods of time, think it is important to signal danger without written words. At the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico – the first and only operational deep geological nuclear repository in the US, which opened in 1999 – researchers considered building vast earthworks and ominous monuments, including a landscape of giant thorns intended to warn future generations not to dig there. But that forbidding landscape was never built. One obvious snag is that mysterious ruins have a habit of attracting curious humans on the hunt for buried treasure.

Macfarlane thinks the effort is better spent elsewhere. “Just give up. It’s a lot of hubris to think that, ‘Oh, I can design a sign that people in the future will understand’,” she says.

The French National Agency for Radioactive Waste Management, which is overseeing the Cigéo project, has something less theatrical in mind. Its engineers are testing sapphire discs that can be etched with up to 40,000 miniaturised pages of text and images. These discs, each 20 centimetres across, would be tough enough to survive heat, scratching and exposure to chemicals in the environment. If stored somewhere near the Cigéo site, such discs might alert future generations to the repository’s existence.

In Sweden, meanwhile, researchers working for the country’s nuclear waste management company have drafted a 42-page digital document detailing a nuclear repository being built deep below ground at Forsmark, a site about 130 kilometres north of Stockholm. The plan is to update, translate and pass the document down through the generations.

There might be alternative ways to keep the knowledge alive. Sweden’s nuclear regulator has also suggested that weaving knowledge of repositories into education and culture may prove more durable than producing physical documents. There are potential precedents for this: a decade ago, anthropologists reported evidence that information about sea-level rise that occurred at least 7000 years ago has been preserved in stories told by Indigenous communities around Australia’s coast. The researchers speculate that the stories survived because the communities employed a complex system of crosschecks, in which younger and older generations were both aware of the stories and corrected one another if any errors crept in.

But in Finland, researchers have taken a different approach. Decades ago, several possible sites for Finland’s nuclear repository were scrutinised. One thing the researchers were looking for is a subsurface region so devoid of useful resources, such as oil, that no one is ever likely to consider digging there. The idea is that engineers don’t have to worry about alerting future generations to a nuclear repository deep below ground in such a resource-free location. Instead, the repository can be sealed up and then forgotten.

On the island of Olkiluoto in south-west Finland, they found what they were looking for. And since 2004, this is where they have been working on the Onkalo repository.

“Even now, when arriving here, you have pretty much a modern industrial site,” says Petteri Vuorio, the facility’s development director. But as you travel deeper and deeper, the site begins to feel different. “The surroundings become quieter and the rock becomes increasingly present as you go underground,” he says.

The bedrock at Onkalo is just about the best you could hope for in a nuclear store, the Finnish researchers think. It is composed primarily of gneiss, an incredibly dense and impermeable metamorphic rock. To add to the engineering security, the rock was carefully mapped out to avoid any areas with major fractures or tiny structural weaknesses that might one day allow groundwater to seep into human-made caves. It is in these fracture-free areas that Onkalo’s kilometres of tunnels now lie.

But that rock isn’t enough.

A system of multiple fail-safes known as KBS-3, developed by the Swedish nuclear waste company SKB, is being deployed, too. Spent fuel is first loaded into a cast-iron container for strength. Each container is then sealed inside a copper vessel with walls 5 centimetres thick. Studies have shown that elemental copper remains virtually unchanged by radioactive and high-pressure environments, making it a good candidate for such a protective shield.

Next, the finished canister is lowered into a hole drilled into the bedrock floor of one of Onkalo’s disposal tunnels. Bentonite, a type of clay, is then packed around the canister. This clay swells when wet to create a dense and nearly watertight barrier, so if any water ever does find its way into the tunnels, the clay should ensure the nuclear waste remains dry. The bentonite also cushions the waste against any movement in the rock.

This combination of protective measures should, the engineers argue, provide the closest thing to a fail-safe system that can survive for millennia.

“The engineered barrier should do the job itself, but if, for any reason, it doesn’t, then you’ve got really good geology,” says Clare Bond, a geologist at the University of Aberdeen, UK, who has no operational connection with the project.

The rise of a new generation of radiotherapies means we will soon need much greater quantities of radioactive atoms. That’s why companies are scrambling to refine them from all manner of radioactive waste

In October 2026, the Finnish government granted a formal operating licence to run the Onkalo facility. In the months ahead, the first shipments of nuclear waste will arrive. Once Onkalo is completely full, all tunnels and shafts will be packed with more bentonite-rich material and sealed off. The facility will, quite literally, disappear back into the rock.

Years will pass, but the Onkalo site should remain sealed. Just 20,000 years ago, the site lay beneath a thick ice sheet, and over the nuclear repository’s vast lifetime, that may happen again – perhaps several times. “Weight from the ice disappears and the crust rebounds. And that can cause fractures,” says Bond. But she adds that significant research has gone into modelling the safety of nuclear repository sites like Onkalo under such climate shifts.

“There is still a lot to do, but we are happy so far,” says Vuorio. “Although there are still matters to solve, we are also quite close to the finish line.”

Onkalo may be the first bury-and-forget repository built with the deep future in mind, but it won’t be the last. There are plans for something similar in Canada, although construction is still some years away. Work has begun on the Forsmark repository in Sweden, and it will also employ the same multilayered protection system of copper, bentonite and bedrock. If all goes to plan, it should be operational in the 2030s.

The UK is further behind, still at the stage of selecting a site to deposit its nuclear waste – which includes the world’s largest stockpile of reactor-grade plutonium.

“The UK’s waste is varied and complex and is significantly different to the waste being disposed of in Finland, for example,” says Neil Hyatt, the chief scientific adviser to Nuclear Waste Services in the UK.

The country is currently evaluating two sites for a repository, according to Bond, both targeting impermeable mudrock in north-western England near the Sellafield nuclear site. Whichever is chosen, UK government documents suggest the plan is to build a permanent repository with a multilayered containment system broadly similar to the one that will be used at Onkalo.

At all these storage sites, engineers are being asked to think in terms of unfathomable timescales – an extraordinary challenge. But the truth is that only observers living in the distant future will know if these deep-time efforts prove to be successful. “Even after probably hundreds of visits underground, I feel humbled,” says Vuorio. “What we are doing here is something which has to be guaranteed to be like it is for thousands of years. This is something that is even hard to describe.”

Vibrating mattress helps clear Alzheimer’s protein from the brain

New Scientist November 03, 2026

Lying on a vibrating mattress while taking nitric oxide pills has shown promise for boosting the brain’s waste-disposal system. It caused the brain’s blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system’s clearance of a protein that accumulates during Alzheimer’s disease.

Other experiments into boosting the glymphatic system have involved ultrasound, pink noise and even intermittently inhaling high doses of carbon dioxide. “It’s important to come at this from as many angles as possible, to increase the chance of this translating to the clinic and benefitting patients,” says Christopher Brown at the University of Southampton, UK, who wasn’t involved in the latest research.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

But risky experimental approaches like taking nitric oxide and inhaling carbon dioxide shouldn’t be tried at home, says Vesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland. Regarding the latest experiment, which he led, Kiviniemi points out that “nitric oxide can reduce blood pressure, and if one happens to have low blood pressure to begin with, taking a pill might lead to loss of consciousness”.

Advertisement

Prior studies in mice have shown that vibrating the body activates a motion-sensitive protein called Piezo1, which is found in muscle cells in the walls of the brain’s blood vessels. This causes the vessels to dilate and constrict more strongly, which helps push waste fluid from brain cells through the glymphatic system, a network of channels that surrounds blood vessels in the brain and transports waste for disposal elsewhere in the body.

Other research has shown that nitric oxide, which is naturally produced in the brain, also dilates its blood vessels. This seems to make the surrounding glymphatic channels narrower, putting more pressure on the waste fluid so it exits the brain more quickly, says Kiviniemi.

Free newsletter

Combining these approaches, Kiviniemi and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn’t been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through.

Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer’s disease. “The treatment seemed to enhance the glymphatic system’s ability to clear beta-amyloid from the brain to the blood,” says Kiviniemi.

“A 35 per cent increase in circulating beta-amyloid 42 is a substantial and very interesting acute effect,” says Tuomas Lilius at the University of Helsinki, who wasn’t involved in the work. “It is certainly possible it could become biologically, and eventually clinically, relevant.”

The glymphatic system is the brain’s recently discovered network for flushing out toxins. Now, we’re uncovering surprising ways to boost it to protect brain health

Side effects were mild and minimal, with six of the participants experiencing issues such as nausea and headache. However, this could partly be due to the expectation of an effect from the nitric oxide pills. The researchers hope to overcome this in future work by including placebo pills.

Brain scans suggest the treatment enhanced the flow of fluid along glymphatic channels, probably by widening the brain’s blood vessels and making them pump more strongly, says Kiviniemi.

But other mechanisms could also be at play, says Christopher Brown at the University of Southampton, UK. For instance, this intervention may slow the breakdown of beta-amyloid 42 by the liver, leading to higher amounts in the bloodstream, he says. Future studies could get around this by injecting markers into cerebrospinal fluid, which moves through the glymphatic system, to more directly measure its flow, says Brown.

Additional experiments by Kiviniemi and his colleagues tested either only the mattress vibrations or only the nitric oxide pills on the same participants, at least a week before or after they underwent the combined approach. Based on brain scans, these solo interventions seemed to have less than half the effect on the glymphatic system than when they were combined.

The researchers now hope to trial the combined approach in 60 people with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease next year, which could produce results in the following two years.

If that goes well, they hope to conduct a trial where a similar group of people has the treatment regularly for several months, rather than as a one-off intervention. This should be long enough to detect any improvements in cognitive abilities, like memory and problem-solving, says Kiviniemi.

Boiling frog syndrome is often called a myth – but is it?

New Scientist November 03, 2026

The boiling frog tale is too good an allegory for our modern times to ignore. It goes like this: frogs will obliviously stay in water as it gradually warms until they eventually boil to death, blissfully unaware that their environment has become incrementally deadly. It is easy to see why this story gets wheeled out by climate change activists or democracy campaigners, along with the full spectrum of self-help peddlers who give advice on everything from bad relationships to poor diet to toxic workplaces.

As a metaphor, it is almost as frequently cited as a parable for our times as it is decried as a ridiculous myth. As a journalist who has spent decades writing about the natural world, I’d always heard that it wasn’t true. Or is it?

I am here to break some news – I have personal, first hand, long-term evidence that frogs will indeed stay in water as it slowly heats until they die.

Advertisement

Deadly fungus makes sick frogs jump far, possibly to find mates

Let me just say from the outset that I love frogs. Ever since I was old enough to poke my hand into a puddle or a creek, I have been catching tadpoles and frogs. But I understand that not everybody is as comfortable around the amphibians as I am.

One of my very earliest frog memories was grabbing one from under a brick during a summer holiday at my grandparent’s shack on the coast of New South Wales, Australia and running over to the adults sitting around a barbecue fire drinking beer. Prone on a banana lounge was one gout-stricken adult who I’d never liked, but I was still keen to show him my frog. As I opened my hand, it hurtled free and in a huge parabolic arc flew straight into Uncle Gout’s lap, who leapt to his feet screaming in equal parts terror and agony.

Fast-forward decades later and 30 kilometres north to my own property where I have installed an outdoor timber hot tub surrounded by hundreds of acres of wild forest. It’s a new-fangled hot tub and instead of chlorine, the water is kept clean and chemical-free using ozone and a UV lamp. As far as wildlife are concerned, it is hundreds of litres of pure rainwater, a place to sneak inside cracks and hide from my resident red-bellied black snake (Pseudechis porphyriacus).

I heat the water using a wood fire and it is an extremely slow process. If I have been away for a while in winter, it can take an entire day to warm the water from less than 15˚C (59˚F) to around 38˚C (100˚F).

Ever since I installed the tub, I have had to share it with my local frog species, Peron’s tree frogs (Litoria peronii). Sure, I initially worried about what would happen to these interlopers in my hot tub, but I believed that the boiling frog syndrome was unscientific.

I also know that some species are attracted to higher ambient temperatures as a way to ward off fungal infections. So, I decided to soak away my concerns. Afterall, what kind of creature, with ready avenues of escape and a decent-ish brain, would let themselves slowly cook to death?

But at the end of those early days when my family and I would first clamber into the tub, I would find dead frogs floating, splayed out with rigor mortis and ghostly white in the hot water.

So now each day, before I light the fire, I catch every one of the hot tub squatters, moving them to a perfectly delightful, actual frog pond nearby – along with the occasional giant millipede (of whom I am scared) and spiders (for whom I feel healthy respect). And then, at frequent intervals during the heating process, I lift the lid and make sure there are no slow-cooking stragglers.

It is a pretty funny ritual, as it must be the same half-dozen individuals who make the short journey each evening from the pond back to the hot tub, only to be caught and moved each morning. It happens pretty rarely now because of my diligence, but occasionally a frog does still avoid detection, and I find it dead at the end of the day – a victim of its sacrifice to the self-fulfilling boiling frog fable.

So, what is going on?

A quick search reveals that the science on which the boiling frog story is based is thin on the pond, mostly down to a series of bizarre 19th-century experiments, including one where lobotomised frogs were compared to those with their brains intact as the water around them was heated. These early experiments showed that, for the most part, frogs will indeed leave dangerously warm water unless the heating is very slow.

In 1875, a scientist called Carl Fratscher showed that frogs stayed put when the water they were in was warmed from 20˚C to 38˚C over 2 hours and 15 minutes. But when a large flame was used to raise the temperature from 26˚C to just 29˚C in a mere 5 minutes, they tried to escape.

This doesn’t seem to have been rigorously tested since, and it is easy to see why such an experiment wouldn’t be conducted today. One researcher commented, when approached for this story, that they “hope no one has knowledge of this, as it’s not the sort of experiment you’d easily get past an ethics committee”.

Key finding could save endangered Darwin’s frog from extinction

Despite Fratscher’s upsetting experiments and my hot tub observations, Jodi Rowley at the Australian Museum in Sydney, says the frog-boiling myth is just that. “It’s a well-quoted saying, but in most situations, frogs would perceive the increase in temperature, become more active and likely jump out of the water,” says Rowley. “In fact, frogs are highly sensitive to even small, gradual changes in temperature in both the lab and the field, and are some of the first animals to respond to climate change.”

Marco Gallio at Northwestern University in Illinois, inspired by the boiling frog parable, studied fruit flies to see what happened when they were slowly heated.

“Our work shows that the fly brain has circuits that are especially tuned to respond to rapid, but not slow, temperature change and that alert them to escape even before the conditions reach physically dangerous limits,” says Gallio. “So, if the rate of change is faster, they escape quicker.”

He and his colleagues believe these results are generalisable to other species. But he, too, thinks that frogs will eventually escape if it becomes dangerous.

Which leaves me caught between a frog and a hot, wet place. I know what I know and, at my property, the boiling frog parable is very real. I am stuck in a Groundhog Day loop of living my 5-year-old self’s best life, catching frogs each morning to save my amphibious tub buddies from themselves.

Advertisement

The Aratasaurus individual studied by the team wasn’t yet fully grown, with an estimated body length of just over 3 metres, and weighed about 34 kilograms.

“The fossils we worked on are not display specimens by any means, so they don’t look very interesting,” says Grice. “If you look at them, you think there’s just a bunch of bones and there’s probably not much in there.”

Grice cut thin sections of bone, mounted them onto glass slides and used hydrochloric acid to remove surrounding rock – and she was shocked at what she saw.

“I was jumping up and down,” says Grice. “I ran up to my head of school’s office and was so excited that he gave me a whisky to calm me down. No one has ever seen dinosaur red blood cells in high resolution before.”

The cells she found were abundant: in a single slide, just a fifth of a millimetre wide, there were 20 blood cells. All of the cells were within fossilised blood vessels, providing further evidence that they really were red blood cells.

The team also had to rule out the possibility of any contamination, especially from the sediments in which the fossil was preserved, which were dominated by algae.

The cells found outside the bone were dominated by chlorophyll-derived compounds, whereas those inside contained haem-derived molecules, which strongly suggests that the latter cells weren’t a result of contamination.

The researchers also compared the blood cells to those of the closest living relatives of the dinosaur fossil, birds and crocodiles. The Aratasaurus red blood cells are significantly larger. This could indicate that the cells swelled during fossilisation, or that the species grew much bigger than the fossilised specimen.

Susannah Maidment at the Natural History Museum in London says previous studies reporting red blood cells in fossils tens of millions of years old are contentious, with some researchers suggesting they could be the result of bacteria or artefacts of the fossilisation process. “This paper is further evidence that fossilised soft tissues such as red blood cells can preserve over geological timescales,” she says.

Grice says the discovery may mean that other nondescript dinosaur fossils that have been locked away in museum collections may hold profound secrets. “There’s drawers and drawers of fossil material, which don’t look very nice,” she says. “This kind of work opens up a whole new opportunity to unlock those collections and bring modern technology and molecular techniques to these specimens.”

New Scientist November 02, 2026

Struggling with a difficult mental task? Zapping the brain region linked to our motivation to make a mental effort might help – for a while. People who had this part of their brain stimulated by electrical currents excelled at a difficult task, but also became more mentally fatigued afterwards.

“Their performance is much better; however, this good performance comes with lower motivation in the end,” says Hongmei Xia at the University of Munich, Germany.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

Xia and her colleagues put electrodes on the heads of 31 volunteers with no known health conditions. During a half-hour session in an MRI scanner, the volunteers spent 20 minutes doing the 3-back memory test, where you have to remember and identify the third item back as an ongoing sequence is presented to you – a very demanding mental task. They were then offered €1 for doing an easy test or €2 for a harder one.

Advertisement

During the 3-back memory test, the electrodes delivered transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to a region of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to randomly chosen volunteers, who were unaware they were receiving it.

Other studies have shown the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is involved in controlling the cognitive effort we make. “Our dorsolateral prefrontal cortex helps us to work hard,” says Xia.

The volunteers who had tDCS reacted faster and more accurately than those who didn’t receive this stimulation. For instance, their average reaction time was 0.98 seconds, compared with 1.12 seconds with sham stimulation.

Free newsletter

Xia thinks stimulating the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex will boost brain performance generally. “I can imagine any cognitive task will be better, but afterwards you will feel more fatigued,” she says.

After the tests, the volunteers who got tDCS had higher levels of the neurotransmitter glutamate in their dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, according to a non-invasive technique called magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The higher their glutamate levels, the more likely they were to choose the €1 task over the €2 one.

Some researchers think mental fatigue is a result of the buildup of glutamate, which can harm cells at high levels. Xia thinks her team’s findings are the strongest evidence of this yet. The findings suggest it is important to take a break when you feel mentally tired, she says.

Xia thinks future studies should also look at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in people with conditions such as depression, which can affect motivation.

We often think that our ability to be curious stems from our complex, human brain – but what if curiosity shapes that complexity?

“I think the claim that the stimulation made people ‘work harder’ is well substantiated,” says neuroscientist Emile Radyte at Samphire Neuroscience, a UK-based company exploring the use of tDCS to treat conditions such as premenstrual syndrome. But the study doesn’t prove that higher glutamate levels were the cause of the greater mental fatigue, she says.

Radyte says her trials have shown that if productivity is hindered by conditions such as premenstrual syndrome, applying tDCS over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can restore it. But she isn’t sure about using it to boost mental performance. “A 20-minute laboratory task does not establish a net productivity benefit over a working day,” says Radyte.

It is a good study, says Nilli Lavie at University College London, but the greater mental fatigue could be a result of using more neural energy, rather than the buildup of glutamate. It’s also hard to precisely target the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with tDCS without an MRI scanner to guide you, says Lavie. “Drink coffee instead,” she says.

PNAS DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2534136123
