Banks Peninsula: Christchurch’s biggest electorate is a swing seat

New Zealand Herald November 03, 2026

Vanessa Weenink beat Tracey McLellan by just under 400 votes in 2023. Photo / Getty Images

By Keiller MacDuff of RNZ

It’s all on in Christchurch’s biggest electorate, the swing seat of Banks Peninsula.

Covering a vast and diverse area, the peninsula switched from red to blue for the first time in more than 20 years at the last election, by a slim margin.

The electorate covers tourist hotspots such as Akaroa, the bohemian enclave of Lyttelton, the industrial city-fringe suburb of Woolston and Halswell’s swiftly growing subdivisions, as well as some of the city’s most exclusive neighbourhoods, such as the coastal communities of Sumner and Redcliffs and hilltop Cashmere.

It’s also one of the country’s most engaged electorates – boasting the highest percentage of eligible enrolled voters and, at the last election, the highest voter turnout.

When National’s Vanessa Weenink beat Labour’s Tracey McLellan in 2023 by just under 400 votes, it was the first time the electorate had swung blue in 24 years.

Weenink and McLellan are back to contest the seat, alongside the Green Party’s Craig Pauling, Alliance candidate Kyle Turnbull, Act’s Zachary Wellman and Amy Turner of the New Conservatives.

The electorate skewed older than the national median – 53 years for Banks Peninsula compared to 38 years nationwide, had a high percentage of home ownership (83% to the national rate of 66%) and had an enrolment rate of 98% compared to 91% nationally.

In the last election, 84% of Banks Peninsula’s enrolled voters turned out to vote, compared to 78% nationwide.

Jemma Hooykass recently returned to New Zealand from 20 years overseas and was taken aback at how much election chatter there was.

“I feel like it’s the conversation everywhere, and in places I wouldn’t expect like the gym, drop-offs with the kids, dinner parties, even just now I’m here on a play centre visit and we were just having our morning hui and everyone was talking about it and who they’re voting for.”

She had researched parties’ policy positions and took her civic duty seriously.

“I wouldn’t want to just show up and tick a box without knowing what I’m doing.

“It’s special being able to vote, and I’ve lived in many countries where you can’t, or you can’t take that for granted.”

Halswell voters were united on the need for better infrastructure in the city’s largest and fastest-growing suburb.

Peter moved down from the North Island three years ago.

“Infrastructure is going to be a problem. We’ve got all these houses coming in over here. Yeah, well, it’s not just here. I mean, it’s all over Canterbury and yeah, probably the countrywide, isn’t it?”

He’s not convinced the electorate was more engaged than any other, and was most concerned about minor parties delaying the formation of a new Government.

He wanted to see a tweak on the current arrangements rather than a wholesale change.

“Well, a slight change, not a major change. I mean, the Labour Party’s certainly not done us any favours in the last term they had.

“Some of the minor parties would be good - not too much change, but they’ve certainly got some good ideas.”

Halswell resident Neil said he was a little nervous about the outcome.

“I’m feeling ... a little bit apprehensive about what coalition party might be scraped together, either National and their cohorts or Labour and their cohorts.”

Education and health were the key issues from his perspective.

“Being a teacher and a wife who’s a nurse, that’s what we’re keeping a close eye on, and obviously the cost of living, which affects everybody.”

He planned to hit the golf course on election day, and “not give it a second thought until night time”.

Joseph Quested has lived in the electorate for more than 15 years, and loved the sense of community he’d found in Lyttelton, which he said leaned strongly to the left.

“There’s one National Party sign up in Lyttelton, just on the corner of the street down there, and it’s been vandalised every single night since the moment that it got put up.”

The environment, Palestine and the cost of living were among the most important issues for young people, he said.

He felt polling often got the outcome wrong, and was basing his predictions more on vibes.

“I think that the person who is going to win an election is ultimately going to be the person who has the most swag, the most ris [charisma].

“Obviously, if it’s going to come down to like Labour or National, I definitely want Labour to win, but I think Chris Hipkins is a deeply swagless individual, you know, I don’t think he has much charisma.

“I would be voting for the Green Party either way, but I wish the Labour Party would put up somebody with a little bit more juice in the tank.”

Janine Clarke said the strong and engaged community in Diamond Harbour was one of the things that attracted her to the area.

People were definitely interested in the election, with a well-attended meet-the-candidates evening and a solid showing by the candidates at various events.

“I think a lot of people are looking for something that isn’t sort of same old, same old, bouncing back and forth.”

Many Diamond Harbour residents had an interest in conservation and the environment, she said.

“We live in a beautiful place, we want to keep it beautiful.”

She could sense some cynicism at the process seeping in, but that made voting more important than ever, Clarke said.

“I guess sometimes that people get a bit disengaged when it becomes like that and that’s actually the time we need to get engaged because if we just do the same thing we get the same results.”

Clarke said she planned to take a broader view of her vote.

“I’m personally probably not as affected by cost of living issues, but I know there are a lot of people that are, and it’s not just about me.

“It’s about making New Zealand a better place for everybody. And that way, if everybody’s kind of at least a bit happier, then we’ve done a good job.”

Peter Langlands lived in Woolston, and was a frequent visitor to his favourite Lyttelton cafe.

He said his Green Party vote was “pretty hardwired”, with conservation and the health system among his chief concerns.

He was against commitments from some parties to cut taxes.

“It’s a real false economy in the long term. When people have got a good health system, their wellbeing is better, their productivity is better, and ultimately we just have a far better system moving forward.”

Like much of the electorate, he will be watching closely on Saturday.

“It will be certainly one to sit down on the couch with a box of popcorn, this one.”

New Zealand Herald November 03, 2026

For more than a decade, Christchurch man Mike Bryce has dedicated his own time to helping people in their most vulnerable moments.

But now, the volunteer emergency medical technician (EMT) is facing the prospect of rebuilding his life-saving equipment after a medical bag containing more than $10,000 worth of specialised gear was stolen from his truck outside his Halswell home.

Bryce, who volunteers for Hato Hone St John, discovered the bag was missing when he went to his truck yesterday morning.

The theft has left him without equipment he relies on to respond to emergencies, sometimes in the middle of the night.

Over the years, he had built up the stolen emergency first-response medical kit, investing more than $10,000 in essential and specialised equipment.

“I travel a lot with work and stuff, you come across so many accidents on the side of the road, and you just end up buying your own gear,” he said.

“To do CPR on someone and to get them back, or someone in real trauma – whether they’re a bad person or a good person – to help someone, the feeling and what we’re doing for the community is so important.”

Bryce’s journey into emergency medical volunteering began about 25 years ago, when he started volunteering in search and rescue operations and assisting during the Christchurch 2011 earthquakes.

“During the earthquakes, we were doing medical stuff, and I was outside my skillset, so I decided to learn about being an ambulance officer,” he said.

Bryce volunteers as an EMT a few nights a week in North Canterbury, alongside his fulltime job in a senior management role at a construction company.

Contact our South Island newsroom

Keeping the equipment in his truck was also essential to responding quickly when an emergency call comes through.

Bryce said having the equipment readily available can make a significant difference when someone’s life is on the line.

“I’ll get a call at 2am and someone’s rung 111 because Dad’s having a cardiac arrest,” he said.

“You don’t have time to spend 10 minutes loading your vehicle and putting everything in the car.”

Now, with his medical bag gone, he faces the prospect of replacing the equipment himself, a costly and time-consuming task on top of a demanding job.

But for Bryce, the loss is about more than just the financial cost of replacing the equipment; it’s also about being there to help people.

“Just bring my gear back. No questions asked, no police involved. I just need the gear back so I can help others,” he said.

“We all make bad decisions at times, but it’s not the bad decision; it’s how you respond to that bad decision. So just bring my gear back.”

A Givealittle page has also been set up to rebuild Bryce’s first response bag.

Every dollar raised will go towards buying vital medical supplies and equipment needed to rebuild the kit and ensure Bryce can continue to help others, alongside other volunteers.

“It’s not just about me; it’s about the tens of thousands of people that give so much of their personal time and are immensely physically exhausted but still keep going to help others in need,” he said.

“We’re volunteers. We do it to help the community.

“I just want my gear back.”

Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 20:00:13 GMT

Agriculture, youth visas and emissions agreements nearly tied up under PM’s plan for a much closer relationship with Brussels

The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?

Andy Burnham is preparing to announce billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU covering everything from youth visas to pet passports under his vision of a much closer relationship with the bloc.

With the prime minister scheduled to meet his European counterparts in Brussels on 20 November, officials have all but agreed three deals that would allow farmers to sell freely to the continent and travellers to take their animals abroad more easily.

Although parts of the agreement will not be put in place until 2028, those close to the talks insist the process will not be derailed by disagreements on European industrial policy or UK university fees.

Elements of the deal, which will see the UK pay the EU for access to its emissions trading scheme, face criticism from those who argue Britain is signing up to the same rules it was seeking to avoid when it left the bloc.

However, Burnham said on Tuesday that the agreement would boost the UK economy by £17bn – an increase of 0.4%. His advisers believe it will also strengthen his attempts to forge much closer ties with, and even potentially rejoin, the bloc.

The prime minister told the Economist on Tuesday: “A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now that is a number that you cannot ignore.”

And he told ITV: “Public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”

Burnham will meet Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, the president of the European Council, in Brussels later this month when the leaders are expected to announce the deals.

They include an agricultural agreement, which the government believes will be worth over £5bn to the UK economy by 2040; access to the EU’s emissions trading scheme; and a youth visa scheme for tens of thousands of people under 30.

Officials on both sides say the final text for all three deals is close to being agreed, though some key details need to be finalised. These include how many young people should be allowed to travel under the mobility scheme.

Both sides are understood to have agreed that each European member state should get its own quota under the scheme, to spread out the benefits and potential costs.

Under the proposed agricultural deal, UK companies and travellers would no longer have to get a certificate to transport live animals, including pets, into Europe. Those wanting to bring domesticated animals into the bloc would be issued with a pet passport, eradicating the need for complicated paperwork each trip.

UK producers would be allowed to continue selling some products that are banned under EU law, such as certain pesticides, for a “transition period”. Trade in other products, including live molluscs and Scottish salmon, would be freed up.

Under an agreement on emissions, the UK will pay the EU billions of pounds to avoid a cross-border carbon tax, which comes into place next January. Under a separate agreement the UK will join the EU emissions trading scheme to avoid being trapped.

And under the “youth experience scheme”, Britain and the EU would issue visas to people under the age of 30 to live, work and travel in each other’s territories. The UK is negotiating an emergency brake-style mechanism to make sure that if a member state refuses to issue its quota of visas, the UK will restrict the number of their nationals looking to travel to Britain.

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Officials on both sides have now started talks over a separate joint statement setting out areas of future cooperation, including on industrial policy and tuition fees. A draft of that agreement seen by the Guardian would seek to conclude an agreement on charging European students lower fees within six months.

The Guardian revealed earlier this week that the UK was willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for any financial loss as a result – but only if the EU agreed to grant Britain access to its protectionist Made in Europe scheme.

The draft statement, which has been prepared by the EU and not yet agreed by the UK, describes the two sides as “trusted partners” – language which the UK believes will allow it to participate in Made in Europe.

But European countries are pushing Britain to sign up to higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a move UK ministers and businesses are resisting. The European draft text says both sides will “cooperate closely and explore further solutions”.

It also says the UK is likely to pay a financial contribution to the EU’s “cohesion” budget to help poorer member states – though this has not been signed off by the UK and is understood to be more likely as part of a future agreement.

The EU has also raised concerns about the UK’s plans for an accelerated programme to deport “foreign national offenders from the UK to the EU”, which it is pushing London to drop.

The agreement being announced later this month forms one half of Burnham’s attempts to reset the British conversation over Europe.

The prime minister is also planning a major announcement setting out his vision for how the UK could interact with the union in the future, including possible re-entry.

Downing Street has said this would take place “around the time of the summit” – though it has not yet been decided whether it will be before, during or after.

‘Well-known’ man fails in legal attempt to block Guardian and ITN publishing sexual allegations

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 19:48:43 GMT

Anonymity of individual, whose lawyers had sought injunction citing suicide risk, remains in place subject to any appeal

A “well-known individual” has failed in his attempt to stop two media organisations from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities towards young women, the high court has ruled.

The legal team for the anonymous individual, known in court only as PPT, had claimed he was “highly likely” to attempt suicide if the Guardian and ITN published the allegations, which he denies.

PPT’s legal team said he had attempted to kill himself twice since being contacted about the allegations in May. On the second occasion he absconded from a secure hospital to do so, they said.

The judge in the case, Mr Justice Nicklin, concluded he was satisfied that a decision to permit publication of the claims, the anticipation of publication and publication itself “would each materially increase the claimant’s risk of suicide”.

“That increase would be very substantial,” he said.

However, he found that it was for the state’s health services to protect PPT from harm in the form of mental health treatment, rather than the court’s responsibility to protect him by stopping the allegations from being published.

The claimant was seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

“The court has not assumed responsibility for the claimant’s psychiatric treatment or safety in the relevant sense,” Nicklin’s ruling states. “In the present case, the state has assumed responsibility for the claimant’s immediate safety through the psychiatric hospital and mental health services.

“The claimant is detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. The hospital exercises direct control over his care, observation, treatment, access to means of self-harm, leave and eventual discharge. It has assumed responsibility for the very risk with which article two is concerned.

“The evidence establishes that the hospital can provide significant protection. Inpatient treatment cannot eliminate the risk, but it materially reduces the likelihood of suicide.”

Nicklin said he had to balance the claimant’s rights with the media outlets’ right of freedom of expression.

The claimant had also made a claim under article eight of the ECHR about the impact his death, serious self-harm or a prolonged psychiatric admission would have upon his relationship with his son.

Nicklin said the claim had “very substantial weight”, but had to be balanced against the rights of the media companies to publish.

He said an injunction “would constitute an exceptionally serious interference” with their rights.

“It would prohibit the defendants from publishing the results of their investigations into allegations of serious wrongdoing by a prominent individual,” he found. “It would also prevent the sources whose accounts form part of those investigations from communicating their experiences to the public.”

The anonymity of the claimant remains in place because the judge granted him permission to appeal against the ruling.

Nicklin’s ruling stated that the Guardian and ITN allege that the claimant used his power and status as a well-known public figure to “establish contact with young women, who were also considerably younger than him, and engage, and/or seek to engage in inappropriate sexual activity”.

They claim the alleged incidents took place over several years and that some of them, if proved, could amount to criminal offences.

The judge emphasised that the current case did not examine whether the allegations against the claimant were true, but only whether the court should prevent the media outlets from publishing them.

He said the proposed journalism “did not lose its public interest value” merely because the allegations were disputed.

Nicklin also pointed to the implications of granting an injunction based on the risk of suicide.

“The principle contended for would apply whenever the court was satisfied that otherwise lawful publication would create a sufficiently grave risk of suicide or psychiatric harm and that restraint was the most effective means of preventing the trigger,” he found.

“The evidence does not identify a point at which publication would become safe merely through the passage of time. The relief sought would therefore be of uncertain and potentially indefinite duration.”

Nicklin rejected a proposal for the injunction to remain in place with a reassessment of the claimant’s condition after 18 months.

“The evidence does not … provide a clinical basis for selecting that or any other period for reassessment, or for concluding that treatment would by then have reduced the publication-related risk sufficiently,” he found.

Why are fridges being hacked and what could be next? - The Latest

Sarah J Maas’s long-awaited return to her bestselling romantasy series has smashed UK sales records, with A Court of Splintered Harmony becoming the fastest-selling adult fantasy novel since accurate records began in 1998.

The novel, the sixth in Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses (Acotar) series and her first return to it in more than five years, sold 188,914 copies in the UK between publication day on 27 October and 31 October, according to NielsenIQ BookData. That also makes it the fastest-selling hardback novel since Dan Brown’s Inferno, which sold 229,000 copies in its first week in 2013.

“Harry Potter has the record for the highest ever weekly sale for a fantasy novel, but it’s the biggest sale since our records began [in 1998] for an adult fantasy novel,” said Philip Stone of NielsenIQ.

Rebecca Yarros’s Onyx Storm held the previous record, selling 155,141 copies in its opening week in January 2025. According to Maas’s publisher, Bloomsbury, A Court of Splintered Harmony amassed the biggest single week of sales for any adult fiction title in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015.

The US author is one of the most prominent writers of romantasy, the genre blending romance and fantasy that has come to dominate bestseller lists in recent years. Strong sales of romance and fantasy helped UK fiction revenue pass £1bn for the first time in 2024. The genre’s readers are largely young women, and much of its growth has played out on TikTok, where hashtags related to Maas have more than 14bn combined views.

The novel went straight to No 1 in the UK’s overall book chart, Maas’s third time at the top. When she last topped the chart, in January 2024, House of Flame and Shadow, part of her Crescent City series, sold 44,761 copies in its opening week.

The figure counts English-language print and ebook editions in the US, Canada, the UK and Australia, but not audiobooks or translations. Maas’s global English-language sales across all her series now exceed 100m copies.

Fans turned out in force for the release, with bookshops across the UK hosting parties and opening past midnight. Waterstones alone hosted 60 midnight launches and 80 early openings and release-day parties across its shops.

“As one of our most pre-ordered books of the year, excitement for Splintered Harmony was at fever pitch, and the astounding first week of sales has reflected this,” said Lucy Jakes, the science fiction and fantasy buyer at Waterstones. “It was amazing to see the hype translate into thousands of Sarah J Maas fans gathering in bookshops.”

Acotar is one of the biggest franchises in publishing. The first book, which reimagines Beauty and the Beast, came out in 2015, and its sequels follow Feyre through the faerie realm of Prythian.

The new book is the first part of a four-part story. The next two parts are contained in A Court of Forgotten Melody, out on 12 January.

The Guardian view on apologising for slavery: a necessary process has at last begun

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:31:26 GMT

Andy Burnham’s commitment to a structured dialogue with Caribbean governments is a step forward, but they need more than words

There was a risk, in the run-up to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) this week, that important discussions could be derailed by the UK government’s refusal to apologise for slavery and the slave trade, combined with its continuing rejection of calls for financial reparations. For the Caribbean governments and campaigners pushing for these steps, the siting of the biennial gathering in Antigua and Barbuda offered a vital opportunity to press their case and raise awareness of the challenges that they face.

That deadlock was broken when Andy Burnham wrote in the Guardian at the weekend of his “sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”, and pledged to listen to calls for a formal apology as part of a structured dialogue. While he reiterated the UK government’s position that financial reparations will not be offered, he also indicated a willingness to discuss aid, investment and the restructuring of debt. King Charles did not say sorry when he addressed Chogm on Tuesday, but a very necessary process of reconciliation and redress has at last begun.

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, pointed to continuing disagreement on the reparations question. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community, said that “apology without repair is incomplete”. And while the new drive on debt promised by Mr Burnham is welcome, it is shamefully overdue. Last year’s UN development finance conference did not achieve the hoped-for breakthrough and the UK opposed proposals for a new process to tackle the worsening debt crisis. The context of rising climate threats and broken promises of climate finance to support a transition away from fossil fuels only serves to strengthen the Caribbean countries’ case.

Mr Burnham’s announcement of Gordon Brown’s involvement in debt negotiations was a promising sign, but so far there is no detailed plan. The difficulties are enormous. High interest payments have undermined the beneficial effects of earlier debt forgiveness, with record-high costs trapping poor countries in a cycle whereby they cannot afford to invest in the health, education and renewable energy that they desperately need. While problems with aid go back decades, the Trump administration’s defunding of USAID was a massive setback. Disappointingly, there is no sign that Mr Burnham will reverse the UK’s own aid spending cuts, which have hit Commonwealth countries and nature protection projects hard.

Historians continue to uncover new information about Britain’s involvement in slavery; William Pettigrew, for example, recently named King James II as “the most important English slave trader of the 17th century”. But while enslavers, investors and traffickers enriched themselves, and provided seed funding for the Industrial Revolution, the Caribbean was left impoverished by the cruel system that the colonists built. Now, demands for this legacy to be properly recognised are coinciding with the climate crisis, to which Caribbean islands are highly exposed through their vulnerability to hurricanes.

King Charles recognised as much when he spoke of the “monstrous injustice” of slavery and the “catastrophic reality” of global heating’s effects. But it falls to Mr Burnham to follow through on the statements of recent days. Structured dialogue is a step worth taking, but Caribbean countries are entitled to expect actions as well as words.

The Guardian view on Labour’s growth obsession: a different economics is possible

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:30:56 GMT

The latest edition of Radical Thinking, the Guardian’s new podcast, should be required listening at a Treasury still stifled by outdated orthodoxies

As prime ministers have come and gone at bewildering speed in recent years, the search for elusive economic growth has become the overriding fixation of the British political class. In the lead-up to the 2024 general election, Sir Keir Starmer declared that “growth must become Labour’s obsession”, given the financial constraints that any new government would be under. The scale of Labour’s progressive offer, it was made clear, would be umbilically linked to its ability to generate a significant uptick in GDP.

“Growth in every postcode” is also the early mantra of Andy Burnham’s government. The prime minister swept to power partly by running on Greater Manchester’s record as the UK’s fastest-growing city region while he was mayor. Echoing Mr Starmer’s approach, Mr Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, told the Labour party conference in September: “Without growth, there is no social democracy.”

But as the economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal suggest in the latest edition of the Guardian’s new Radical Thinking podcast, that is a flawed and politically unhelpful linkage to make. In a transformed geopolitical environment, they argue, the notion that former levels of growth can be restored is likely to prove a chimera. Just as importantly – as the contrast between Manchester’s booming city centre and hard-pressed towns such as Oldham and Wigan illustrates – better growth rates would not solve entrenched problems of affordability in places unlikely ever to become hubs for advanced manufacturing or financial services.

Yet neither of those assertions mean that an ambitious egalitarian politics must be ruled out. “We need to say: ‘How do low-income places work?’,” Prof Williams says. “What do we need to do to get them to work better?” Or as Prof Johal puts it: “What are the basics, the necessities that we need … for people to have a decent civilised life?” At the most fundamental level, a more ambitiously redistributive fiscal approach can bring bills down for the less well-off. More broadly, shifting resources into the essential building blocks of every local community – transport, utilities, care networks and other social and physical infrastructure – can improve everyday lives by restoring collective control over public goods.

Mr Burnham’s signature move as mayor – the decision to take Greater Manchester’s buses back under public control and cap fares – suggests a shared agenda here. But the prime minister has sent mixed messages when it comes to “Manchesterism” – the place-based economic strategy that he wishes to export to the nation. As the role of the United Arab Emirates in the city’s modern development comes under scrutiny, Mr Burnham’s version of “business-friendly socialism” is a political philosophy in need of greater definition. Devolution should involve funnelling local power downwards and outwards, rather than upwards to Abu Dhabi-type investors in the indiscriminate pursuit of growth.

A greater focus on the “foundational” economy described by Prof Williams and Prof Johal can help with that project. One of Mr Burnham’s last acts as mayor was to sign off on a mayoral development corporation for the town of Middleton, near Manchester. Its agenda is being shaped by residents and local business owners, with the aspiration that local economic networks can be “rewired” and the provision of everyday essentials be reconfigured and improved. Given proper backing from Westminster, social democrats do not need to wait for growth before they can begin improving lives.

Even if US democracy can be salvaged from Trump, Europe is moving on

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:07:14 GMT

It will take decades to rebuild trust in a country that removed a tyrant once – and then reinstated him four years later

When Joe Biden entered the White House in 2021 it was possible to believe that Donald Trump’s reign had been an aberration. “America is back. The transatlantic alliance is back,” the new president declared to relieved European leaders shortly after winning the 2020 race. It was true, but not for long.

Trump’s defeat proved that US democracy was mechanically operational, not culturally robust. His supporters tried violent subversion to prevent the inauguration of a successor. A second term should have been unthinkable. Republicans who failed to denounce the 6 January insurrection should have been unelectable. Instead, within four years, US voters reinstated the champion of a failed coup against their cherished constitution as commander-in-chief.

That is worth remembering in any analysis of midterm congressional elections. Voting was under way at the time of writing. Opinion polls in the run-up favoured Democrats. But it is a measure of how grievously Trump has imperilled democracy that peaceful completion of that process, followed by a fair count, cannot be anticipated with confidence.

The most that can be said is that the elections were not aborted, nor did they look blatantly rigged on the eve of polling, which gives hope that the balloting process can still function in theory. That is no protection against a president with a record of denying results that displease him and a party that cravenly endorses every lie and coercion he deploys to consolidate his power.

With two years left in his second term, Trump has ample scope to punish disloyalty and reward sycophants. Facing a choice between election integrity and partisan venality, precedent suggests few Republicans prefer the path of constitutional virtue. That moral collapse in the ruling party is salient for some voters, but that group – the anti-tyranny constituency – were always going to vote Democrat. In the swing-voting middle, Trump is a drag on the Republicans because people feel let down on the economy and disrespected by a president who is more interested in the construction of a White House ballroom for himself than the affordability of everyday goods for everyone else.

A disciplined and sophisticated fascist would have focused on suffocating domestic opposition and dismantling institutional checks on the presidency, instead of launching a strategically inept and economically self-sabotaging war against Iran. That miscalculation has damaged Trump. It upset “America first” ideologues who thought he stood against forever wars in the Middle East. By precipitating closure of the strait of Hormuz, it landed higher bills on voters whose motive for voting Republican in 2024 had been the spike in inflation preceding that poll.

Democrats can’t afford to be fussy about different flavours of anti-Trump vote. If the economy is what people care about, that is the campaign to run. If a quixotic, megalomaniac foreign policy choice made in February leads indirectly to the election of a Congress better equipped to hold a rogue president to account, that would obviously be better than the scenario where the same failure passes with impunity.

But it leaves the argument incomplete in the same way that Biden’s 2020 victory was insufficiently decisive. The case that defenders of US democracy still haven’t landed is the one that explains Trump’s bad decisions as the inevitable consequence of his beliefs, not just disappointing meanders away off the true path.

If US society were truly and passionately wedded to the principles enshrined in its constitution, a campaign exposing Trump as a persistent aggressor against that foundational ethos would be unbeatable. But it has been tried and beaten.

Before Biden stepped down mid-race in 2024, he sought to frame his bid for re-election as an existential contest for the soul of the US political system. Trump was a despot, he said, whose embrace of the 6 January insurrection was a clear disqualification from ever being allowed near the Oval Office again. “Whether democracy is still America’s sacred cause is the most urgent question of our time,” he told a rally in Pennsylvania. When Kamala Harris took over as the Democratic nominee, she made the same point. Trump was “unhinged and unstable”, seeking “unchecked power”, she said weeks before polling day. America decided the price of eggs was a more pressing concern.

Perhaps Trump’s second term can achieve what the first one didn’t. Maybe the extra exposure to a more virulent strain of the virus is generating antibodies in the US body politic that the initial four-year dose couldn’t produce. If so, we won’t have proof of it any time soon. A nation that swerves dictatorship by luck, because the aspiring dictator lacked the strategic acumen to complete his mission, doesn’t look immune for the long term.

It is a lesson US allies learned from the false comfort they took when Biden said the old America was back. Slowly, European democracies are adapting to a world in which they cannot assume US friendship. Reliance on the US defence umbrella and advanced technology is now recognised as a strategic vulnerability to be urgently addressed.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

For Britain, Trump is an engine driving closer integration with Europe. His trade policy, combining innumerate protectionism and territorial rapacity, has destroyed the flimsy case for Brexit that posited nonexistent transatlantic deals as alternatives to the EU single market. White House indulgence of Vladimir Putin and scorn for Nato makes it hard to credibly sustain the idea of UK leverage through a “special relationship” with Washington.

Some restoration of trust in a post-Trump America is feasible. But so is the spread of Trumpian nationalism through Europe. The election of far-right governments could strain and ultimately even break postwar 20th-century institutions that were founded with vows of determination never again to let enemies of liberal democracy plunge the continent into spirals of hatred and war.

That history was meant to be an inoculation on both sides of the Atlantic. But when it mattered, the 20th-century parables didn’t sway US voters. The warnings went unheeded when familiar authoritarian intent appeared, lightly camouflaged in modern celebrity style, speaking in all-American idiom. The challenge now for European democrats is to study that lesson – the cautionary tale of America’s fragile defences against tyranny in the 21st century – and turn it into campaigns that prevent the same thing happening here.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls in referendum on Trump’s agenda

Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. In the charts below, blue shapes on the right signal a good night for the Democrats, and red shapes on the left signal that the Republicans have done well.

Before the election, the Cook Report classified six Senate races as genuine "toss-ups". The Democrats need to win at least three of these, alongside the other races they are expected to win.

Democrats are now favoured in enough House seats to take the chamber without winning any of the 18 seats the Cook Political Report classes as “toss-ups”. If they win every seat they are expected to win, they will comfortably win a majority. The balance of power now turns on whether Democrats hold the 18 seats rated “lean Democratic”. Republicans, favoured in 195 seats, would need to sweep all 18 toss-ups and flip five Democratic-leaning seats to win.

Republicans are defending a majority in the 435-member House. Democrats hold 212 House seats and need 218 to win control. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms and face re-election every even year.

Lead indicates who is currently ahead in the vote count. Win indicates states where a winner has been called. Flip indicates states that switched party allegiance compared to the previous election.

Cartogram map source: The Downballot. Each House seat is the same size regardless of its geography. In redistricted seats, more than one candidate may be marked as an incumbent if they represented part of the redrawn area before redistricting occurred. In redistricted seats, AP will work out whether a seat has flipped based on the previous districts that overlap the new one - and this can mean a seat can be counted as a flip even if an incumbent wins it. Where a race ends in a runoff vote, if the two leading candidates are from the same party, the race will be classed as being won by that party already.

The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?

The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.

The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.

How is the Senate elected and how do they work?

The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.

Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.

In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.

Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.

In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.

Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.

How are governors elected and how do they work?

Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.

In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.

Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.

The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.

Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.

Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

Primark lacks fizz as it approaches its go-it-alone moment

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:58:35 GMT

After a profits dip, the chain’s demerger from its sister food company still makes sense but is unlikely to reveal tons of value

Primark brings forward home deliveries plan by two years as profits slide

The business logic for demerging Primark from Associated British Foods’ greater Ovaltine-to-Twinings empire – an event due to happen by the end of next year – is impeccable. Read this year’s results statement and you wonder why the controlling Weston family took 20 years to get behind the idea.

One paragraph can be about a yeast plant in India or the impact of high gas prices on sugar-refining margins; the next can jump to Primark’s new “digital flywheel” or the progress of the “By Coleen” collection. Even by conglomerate standards, food staples and discount fashion has always been an odd mix. Separating into two FTSE 100 companies, with stand-alone governance, makes sense.

But it would be hard to say the rejig will reveal tons of value, another reason conglomerates often give for doing the splits. Primark obviously isn’t a hidden jewel because it already makes two-thirds of the group profit – and it isn’t currently on sparkling form either.

Or, at least, it’s not in continental Europe. A like-for-like sales decline there of 4.7% for the financial year is jarring even in the context of “weak” consumer sentiment. The way ABF tells it, the continental operation is simply a year or so behind the refresh treatment that has been administered on the UK stores. We’re talking sharper digital marketing campaigns, a rejig of ranges, the introduction of click & collect and so on.

The trouble is, the same explanation was given in January, when the gap between the home performance and that on the continent became apparent. Ten months later, the story remains largely the same. The UK and Ireland are in positive like-for-like sales territory (of 0.5%) but the continent is still miles off. Market conditions in Germany, Italy and Spain were all described as “very challenging”.

Since Britain is now the priority for a home delivery service to capture “incremental” shoppers, one can imagine the gap will remain wide for some time yet. Perhaps online-only operators such as Shein, Temu and Zalando are simply more of a headache on the continent.

None of which alters the underlying strength of the Primark machine. Never mind the U-turn on the economics of home delivery, there are still physical stores being opened, including in the US. This is still a formidable operation with almost £10bn of annual turnover.

But the potential for profit growth tends to be a metric would-be new investors in newly liberated companies look at.

On operating profits, Primark stayed above £1bn (just) for the year, but the number was 11% down on a year ago. For this year, the forecast is for a same-again profit margin of 10%-ish. There is a sense, even while opening new stores, of working hard to go roughly sideways.

No new money will be raised in next year’s demerger, so timing is irrelevant in one sense. Shareholders will get what they already own, just in two parts; there will be no real need for investment banking hype.

All the same, the overall ABF, as currently constituted, is forecasting a second year in a row of lower earnings because the food ingredients side, especially sugar, is still sticky. Meanwhile, the £1.9bn of share buy-backs over the past four years have come to an end as the group is in long-term investment mode.

There could be another 12 months until the big split, which allows time for things to perk up. But in current “macroeconomic headwinds” conditions, ABF is travelling slowly to the historic separation. It’s still the right thing to do – just don’t expect fireworks.

Britain must have the courage to face its legacy of slavery

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:50:23 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Andy Burnham in which he says that people today can’t be held personally liable for the country’s historical wrongs

In his opinion piece (30 October), Andy Burnham argues that British people today cannot be held liable for historical wrongs “in which they played no personal part”. On one level, he is right. But he confuses two very different things: personal liability and the continuing responsibility of the state.

When slavery was abolished in the British empire in 1833, the government borrowed £20m – an extraordinary sum then – to compensate enslavers for the loss of their supposed property. Some 40,000 claims were made. The British taxpayer carried the cost, and the resulting public debt was not finally cleared until 2015.

Around 3,000 people in Britain received about half of the compensation fund. The state had effectively used public money to preserve the wealth of a privileged elite, while leaving the victims of slavery uncompensated.

If the state could identify enslavers and establish their claims to compensation in 1833, it cannot be beyond the capacity of today’s state to examine how that wealth, and its enduring legacy, might be addressed. The historical records are remarkably detailed, after all.

The state cannot claim continuity when honouring its obligations to enslavers while disowning any responsibility towards the enslaved. It is the same institution, enduring across generations.

Nobody is suggesting that today’s citizens should inherit personal guilt for the actions of their ancestors. But neither should the wealth accumulated through slavery be treated as a private inheritance, cleansed of its origins simply by the passage of time.

The descendants of enslavers, many of whose families remain among Britain’s wealthiest, cannot just divorce their inherited privilege from the injustice that helped create it. They too have a responsibility to confront that legacy. Giselle Dye Edinburgh

Andy Burnham celebrates British resistance to slavery while refusing to recognise the totality of the system against which people resisted. Recovering these histories matters, including that of enslaved people’s struggles. But we also need to understand how chattel enslavement and imperialism developed a global political economy organised through racial hierarchy, capitalist exploitation and patriarchal power.

These processes shaped who could own property, whose labour could be appropriated, and whose lives mattered. Their consequences persist in the distribution of wealth and power today. This system harmed people differently. Enslaved Africans and colonised peoples endured dispossession and violence on a scale incomparable with workers’ exploitation in Britain, but their struggles were interconnected.

Patriarchy sustained this order by exploiting women’s labour and controlling reproduction. Ecological destruction accompanied the treatment of land and life as resources for extraction.

Imperial competition drove these processes; wealth extracted through empire enriched Britain, disproportionately benefiting its landed elites. And yet Burnham writes of climate change, women’s rights and the cost of living crisis as if these issues are disconnected – as though each can be resolved independently within the very system that generated the harm.

Reparatory justice doesn’t depend on individuals having personally committed violence; it begins with these relationships. Most of us never had the opportunity to learn how they shaped past harms and continue to harm others and ourselves. An adequate response requires material redistribution and debt cancellation, alongside public education and discussion.

A parliamentary inquiry that tells the truth of the British empire is critical: how it developed, who was harmed and who benefited, how its structures persist and what repair now requires. Past solidarity should encourage us to confront these connections; celebrating earlier generations’ courage while refusing to see the wood for the trees leaves the structures they challenged far too comfortably intact. Dr Asha Herten-Crabb University of Warwick

Andy Burnham is open to an apology for Britain’s role in slavery, but rejects financial reparations. He argues that historical wrongs “happened in a different age under different laws” and that British people today played no personal part in them.

For centuries, Britain was a leading slave-trading nation. Burnham instead emphasises its leading role in the abolition movement, which began in the 18th century. The question, however, is whether the absence of personal involvement removes responsibility for injustices whose consequences persist.

Past injustices matter today if they have left morally relevant traces in the present, meaning that there are people today who suffer from the past injustices and people who gain. There is, for example, a direct link between slavery and the slave trade on the one hand, and the current poverty and underdevelopment in the Caribbean on the other. There is also a link between the incomes from slavery and the slave trade that rolled into the British economy in the 17th to 19th centuries and present prosperity.

In principle, if someone gains and someone else suffers from a historical wrong, and the heir of the perpetrator is aware of this relation, there is a moral duty for the one who gains to compensate the one who suffers. Therefore Britain has a moral duty to compensate the Caribbean nations that suffer from past injustices. An apology is not enough, but compensation can of course take various forms. Göran Collste Emeritus professor of applied ethics, Linköping University; author, Global Rectificatory Justice

Andy Burnham’s openness to offering an apology for British involvement in slavery is a welcome development. But despite his recognition of its “brutal and barbaric violation” of the enslaved, he still manages to make an “honest conversation about the legacies of slavery” seem like an act of political largesse rather than an objective audit of structural inequality.

If he really understood how transatlantic slavery “still shapes our world today” he might reflect on some of its local ironies. For example, the fact that, though not “liable for historical wrongs”, British people nonetheless, through taxation, serviced the debt that compensated enslavers (some of the wealthiest people in the country) until as recently as 2015. He would recognise the insult added to that injury for some of those taxpayers, who were descendants of the enslaved.

In fact, if Burnham truly understood historical legacies in the Caribbean and elsewhere, he might consider cancelling Commonwealth debt repayments altogether, rather than proposing to lengthen the term over which they are repaid. He might recognise that the “cup of sorrow” referenced in his quote from the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson did not disappear in 1807 at the end of the slave trade or in 1833 with emancipation, and would comprehend the extent to which slavery shaped colonial attitudes and practices, replacing a barbaric yoke with an authoritarian one.

He would see that the effects of slavery are not something to be recognised only in an annual ritual of remorse during Black History Month; neither are they redeemed by politically empty declarations to “end global poverty and inequality”, while denying the legitimacy of some of the reparative means to even attempt it. Paul McGilchrist Cromer, Norfolk

Any deal would mark a significant shift for the USOPC, a non-profit organization that, unlike many national Olympic committees, relies heavily on sponsorships, licensing ⁠and other commercial revenue streams rather than government funding.

The plan has been in the works for months, according to minutes of USOPC board meetings which showed the proposed commercial entity would be named United States Olympic and ⁠Paralympic Ventures (USOPV).

“[USOPC CEO Sarah] Hirshland reported encouraging feedback from preliminary discussions with potential investment and strategic partners,” the minutes said. “Prospective partners generally validated ​the vision for the USOPV and strategic rationale underlying the initiative.”

The ‌USOPC is being advised by investment ‌bank Raine Group, according to Sky News, which said the venture could be valued in the billions of dollars.

Raine did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment.

The potential deal comes as the United States prepares to host the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles and seeks to capitalize on growing investor interest in sports assets and intellectual property. Team USA consistently tops the medal table at the Summer Olympics and brings NBA stars, high-profile track athletes and famous names like Simone Biles to the Games.

The move underscores how sports leagues and governing bodies are increasingly turning ⁠to private capital in a bid to unlock the value of their commercial rights and secure access ​to resources to fund future growth.

King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:32:55 GMT

Speaking in Antigua, the king did not give explicit support for reparations but said he wanted to ‘address past wrongs’

King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.

“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past.

“The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”

Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs.

But the king stopped short of an apology or explicit support for reparations, instead pointing to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage.

“For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.

Though speaking as head of the Commonwealth, and this speech would have been drafted by Charles personally along with his advisers, palace aides have indicated there would be “no surprises” in it for the UK government.

Andy Burnham refused to be drawn on whether the UK might offer further financial contributions to the Commonwealth stopping short of direct reparations.

The UK prime minister told reporters: “I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations, and I made that quite abundantly clear in the piece that I wrote in advance of coming here.

“But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got, green finance. That’s what we’ve done under all governments, and in my view, we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth.”

Pressed on whether this could mean additional financial contributions that would weigh on the taxpayer, Burnham said: “Well, you’re getting ahead. What we need to have is that meaningful dialogue where we take time to listen, and let’s be clear: the Commonwealth is an important part of our trade too.

“It’s a two-way arrangement. You know, trade is up between the UK and the rest of the Commonwealth in the last year quite significantly, actually. So you need to see it in that way as well. It benefits Britain to be here, listening to people, building that new partnership, and that’s good for growth in Britain.”

Reparations are not formally on the agenda of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), where trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and opportunities for young people were among the stated priorities of the 56-member bloc.

But sustained campaigning by Caribbean governments and a growing international reparations movement have propelled the issue to the centre of political debate surrounding the gathering.

Opening the summit in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, the country’s prime minister, Gaston Browne, said “fairness” required an “honest engagement with our shared history” and called for meaningful and respectful dialogue on reparatory justice and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism.

Burnham had said he was open to Britain apologising for slavery, with officials holding talks with national leaders in Antigua about what that could entail.

He has also proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

But Caribbean leaders have stressed that dialogue must extend beyond an apology. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), described an apology as an “essential first step” but said an “apology without repair is incomplete”.

He said any structured dialogue must allow consideration of the entirety of Caricom’s 10-point reparations plan, including public health, education, cultural restitution, psychological rehabilitation, debt cancellation and monetary compensation.

Britain’s royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology. A palace spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the king to announce a change in government policy.

According to the AFP news agency, Burnham discussed slavery with the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral meetings the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.

They discussed how Britain was “offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade”, including the “next steps”, Downing Street said.

Outside the heavily secured summit venue, protesters gathered with placards declaring: “We know what you did and we can see you,” and “You say appalling atrocity, yet you refuse to apologise.”

One protester, Lenworth Johnson, said that if the king’s constitutional position prevented him from apologising, the British government should authorise him to do so. “We feel an apology is necessary,” he said.

Another, Radcliffe Robins, said the wealth enjoyed by Britain and other western powers was built in part on enslavement. “It is absolutely necessary that his majesty the king and the royal family apologise for the brutality and the injustice that they have imposed on us,” he said. “And with that, we ask for reparations.”

Another protester said the demonstration was intended to ensure those entering the summit knew campaigners were “watching them and listening to what they’re saying and what they’re doing”.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda Reparations Support Commission and one of the organisers, said: “One whose heart is filled with horror and whose soul bears the most profound personal sorrow must surely be moved beyond words – beyond repeated emotional expression without acceptance of responsibility.

“Genuine moral consciousness demands apologies – the acknowledgment of wrong, the acceptance of responsibility and the commitment to pursue reparations. Unfortunately King Charles III does nothing of the sort. He has again failed the people who recognise him as king.”

The demonstrations followed a reparations event on Monday hosted by the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations alongside campaign organisations.

Its chair, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, welcomed debt relief but warned against presenting it as reparations.

“Reparations was never about personal guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions that still stand,” she said. “Aid is not reparations, because aid leaves the power with the giver. Agency was the crime. Agency has to be the remedy.”

The meeting was followed by a candlelight vigil on an Antiguan beach commemorating enslaved Africans brought to the island. The Rev Bonnie Smith, president of the Antigua Christian Council, asked those gathered to remember people torn from their homes, separated from their families and forced across the Atlantic into enslavement.

“Their names may be absent from our records, but they are not absent from your love,” she said. “Their voices may have been silenced, but their lives have never ceased to matter.”

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, meanwhile framed the campaign as part of a wider struggle for peace and justice.

“We are concerned about the unleashing of terror and violence upon innocent people,” he said.

“We believe that reparatory justice that calls for human decency, equality and justice for all is the philosophy that will hold us together as humanity going into this 21st century.”

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair Campaign, the reparatory justice movement, said he believed Charles’s expressions of sorrow over slavery were sincere, but was disappointed he had not gone any further than his previous remarks.

“The apology hasn’t come. And there’s no talk about reparatory justice. So to that extent, this speech to me was a disappointment,” he said.

The king’s reference to support for health, education and infrastructure, Gonsalves said, concerned subjects already covered in the agreements in the UN sustainable development goals.

“What we are saying is that there has to be, additionally … a special carve-out in respect of reparatory justice,” he added.

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:28:49 GMT

Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe.

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NSCS) said it was working with the affected companies but the national impact was minimal.

Speaking at the launch of the NCSC’s annual review on Tuesday, its director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that. At the moment, the impact is minimal.”

Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to malicious operations linked to Russia.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday – with some rising to as high as 50C (122F) – and several companies confirming they had been hacked.

Similar incidents were reported in France last month. It has emerged that the cyber-attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to the internet with default passwords.

No UK grocery chain has been directly affected so far.

Chichester said the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was working with organisations to identify loopholes in their technology and close them before hackers exploited them.

He said the NCSC was not able to comment on who might have carried out the attacks, but that they were not AI-enabled and had used vulnerabilities that had been “out there for a long period of time”.

The NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, said the fridge attacks represented the “foothills” of an enlarged cyberthreat that companies and the public faced as AI systems highlighted flaws in IT networks that owners were not aware of or had neglected to patch.

“There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he added.

The agency’s chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, said everyday domestic devices connected to the internet would be susceptible to hackers in certain situations. He said manufacturers needed to be encouraged to make their technology safer, and consumers needed to accept paying more for safer equipment.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said some of its more than 300 members had been affected after becoming “collateral” in the hack.

The industry body said no meat had been lost in the refrigeration hacks but the incidents were a “reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets”.

One meat supply company saw its cold units rise to up to 100C while another two reported their units had started to defrost. The association said the affected units were empty at the time.

A fruit and vegetable wholesaler in London was also affected but prevented the attack from escalating by pulling the internet connection to its cold storage units out at the wall.

Alex Pearce, managing director of Langridge Organic, said the hackers had changed the parameters on a number of units, setting them to defrost for more than four hours at 150C. However, Pearce and his staff intervened before any stock could be damaged.

“It clearly must have been easy to get in [to the system] because the simple solution was to unplug ourselves from the internet,” he said.

Pearce said Langridge uses the same fridge control system, developed by a US software company called Copeland, that was involved in the French supermarket incidents. The Grocer news website first reported the Langridge incident. Copeland said it is talking to affected customers and has recommended software fixes.

Cybersecurity researchers said attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – whose systems were also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – were similar to recent operations linked to Russia. Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cyberdefence firm Lupovis, said it had recorded 256 attempted attacks from 91 different sources between 20 October and 30 October after setting up online “honeypot” traps that are indistinguishable to attackers from real Danfoss fridge controllers. The attackers attempting to take over the dummy controls remained anonymous, but most of the authentication attempts used the manufacturer’s publicly documented factory-default username and password credentials.

They also used what Bellekens called “bulletproof” hosting, which means using internet service providers that are particularly tolerant of malicious activity, often ignore abuse complaints or make it difficult for authorities to disrupt their customers’ operations. “What caught our attention was the overlap between infrastructure involved in the recent probing activity and infrastructure we have previously associated with Russian-linked malicious operations,” he said.

“While we are not able to pinpoint a group yet, the number of actors that fit this bill is relatively small and the bulletproof hosting we have seen being used by these actors for probing was also being used by Russian groups some time ago.”

Tenerife footballer Jesús de Miguel dies aged 30 after on-pitch collision

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:17:29 GMT

Police homicide division opens judicial proceedings

He was struck in the chest when challenging for ball

Spanish football was in shock on Tuesday after the Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in the second division. The homicide division of the national police has opened judicial proceedings into a possible involuntary manslaughter, a routine procedure after any death not by natural causes. The chief public prosecutor in Santa Cruz de Tenerife told the state news agency EFE that it was “very difficult” for a case to come to court.

Tenerife announced that De Miguel had died at 8am on Tuesday after he had been taken into intensive care on Monday afternoon. He did not regain consciousness after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

The collision occurred in added time at the end of Andorra’s visit to Tenerife, a game put back 24 hours because of the risk of torrential rain. With the score 2-2, in the 96th minute, a long ball was played away from the Tenerife area and up the pitch. De Miguel chased it into space and Owono came a long way out of his goal, jumping forward, with his right knee up, and crashing into the attacking player inside the centre circle.

Owono was sent off, walking straight to the touchline. De Miguel was left unconscious, with players from both sides appealing for medical assistance. The match was abandoned by the referee, Manuel Ángel Pérez Hernández, having run into the 108th minute.

Medics restored De Miguel’s pulse in the ambulance and transferred him to the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz. Tenerife said he was able to breathe unassisted and was stable but that he remained unconscious and in a critical condition. At 5am the club announced De Miguel’s condition had worsened neurologically.

“CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesús de Miguel Alameda on Tuesday 3 November 2026 at 8:00am,” said a statement released at 9.31am. The statement described the club as “broken by pain, with a lump in the throat and unable to believe that this is true”, and accompanying the forward’s “devastated family, loved ones and everyone associated with Tenerife who mourns this cruel end … there are no words of consolation”.

The former Barcelona defender Gerard Piqué, who is Andorra’s majority shareholder and attended the game, wrote on social media: “I am so deeply sorry, to my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús.” The club’s president, Ferran Vilaseca, told reporters: “This has had a huge emotional impact on our players, coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. Our sincerest condolence arriving on the Spanish mainland after midnight, still unaware of the outcome.”

The chief public prosecutor in Santa Cruz de Tenerife, José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui, told EFE it was “very difficult” for a legal case to be taken up given that the impact happened in the course of the game. A formal legal complaint could still be brought. Sentences for involuntary homicide range from three months to four years of imprisonment. There is no precedent of a footballer facing legal proceedings as a result of a challenge in the course of a game.

According to federation protocols Owono could face a 12-game ban, with the disciplinary committee due to decide.

The report from the referee said: “In minute 90+6, player no 25 Ferrer Owono, Jesus Lazaro, was sent off for the following reason: for impacting sharply upon an opponent with his leg high and excessive force in dispute of the ball. The player was treated on the field of play, which he then abandoned on a stretcher. At the close of this report, no medical certificate had been presented.”

Tenerife have asked to postpone their next two games, against Granada on Saturday and Badajoz in the cup the following week. Andorra have requested that their meeting with Mallorca at the weekend be postponed. The Spanish football federation announced the postponement of all games due to be held on Tuesday in the Copa del Rey and the Copa de la Reina.

Clubs across Europe, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, paid tribute to De Miguel. “Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times,” Barcelona said. Real Madrid said they sent “condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones”.

De Miguel had played most of his career in Spain’s third tier, at Leganés B, Inter Madrid, Fuenlabrada, Navalcarnero, Unionistas de Salamanca and Castellón. He was Castellón’s top scorer when they were promoted to the second division in 2024 and joined Tenerife in 2025.

US president makes surprise election day announcement, saying country does not ‘need’ $4bn annual payment

Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.

In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, the US president said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it”.

“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.

Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”

Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.

Israeli officials appeared to be taken by surprise by the announcement, and leading members of the opposition said it showed the damage that Netanyahu had done to the US-Israel relationship. The announcement comes at a crucial moment after Netanyahu’s party lost its majority in the Knesset in last week’s elections and the opposition is trying to cobble together a coalition to replace him.

“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right rival to Netanyahu who is seeking to replace him as prime minister. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”

“A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not dismantle it,” wrote Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats opposition party. “Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis, putting Israel’s future at risk.”

Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as foreign military financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.
