Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, in which US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.

Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”

During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it?

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:00:51 GMT

People everywhere are searching for the reason behind their sudden bursts of anguish or homesickness

Women: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed?

Some say it feels like a sudden burst of anguish; others liken it more to homesickness. The sudden onset of a sinking, upsetting feeling due to nipple stimulation is anecdotally known as Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS), and for Sandra, it can be triggered by something as commonplace as putting on a shirt.

“I was probably a child when I first noticed: ‘Why does touching my nipple make me sad?’” says the 28-year-old. The sensation seemed to happen at random, and without the words to describe it, she kept it a secret. It wasn’t until college that she worked up the courage to Google it. “I realized I wasn’t crazy,” she says.

There are many others like Sandra (who, for privacy, has asked to use a pseudonym). Breastfeeding mothers, queer lovers and cis men alike have all sought an explanation for this phenomenon.

Sad Nipple Syndrome is often discovered in private. People describe it as a sudden dysphoria (a profound state of unhappiness or uneasiness) that follows nipple stimulation. It is often resolved within a couple of minutes, but can cause confusion and disruption.

I spoke to four people who experience SNS, and each described similar negative feelings. Sandra described it as “dread, a nostalgic sadness or the feeling of a bad memory”. Salma Zaky, a New York-based comedian who has talked about her SNS on stage, says she can “tell if a woman has gone through it – they’ll light up or clap”. Zaky likens it to a mix of homesickness or nostalgia.

For Sandra, the most common trigger is a light, unexpected touch when changing clothes or towel drying. Its intensity can vary depending on the circumstances. For instance, if she triggers the feeling on her own with light touch, “the negative feelings tend to persist for more than just a few seconds,” says Sandra. If there is sustained friction with her clothing, she sometimes feels “deep grief”.

Their sentiments are echoed in thousands of online posts asking whether anyone else experiences the “nipple touch of doom”. In the absence of a formal clinical diagnosis, most people’s understanding of Sad Nipple Syndrome has come from word of mouth or chatter online.

“Reddit was helpful in just being like: ‘Oh, I’m not an insane person,” says Zaky. “Other people feel this too.”

SNS is not an official medical diagnosis, and scientific research remains in short supply. That said, awareness is growing, even among researchers and medical practitioners.

As with many conditions that primarily affect women’s intimate or hormonal experiences, there is not much medical curiosity, funding or research. “While there is no explanation yet, we can assume that the hormone oxytocin is somehow involved, since nipple stimulation leads to its release,” says Dr Vladimír Kraus, PhD, Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Pavol Jozef Šafárik University.

Oxytocin is often referred to as the “love hormone”. Largely responsible for bonding and increased emotional connectivity, it is triggered by physical touch like hugging, massage or sex, and also after uterine contractions during childbirth or breastfeeding. When it comes to its role in SNS, Kraus theorizes that “some subtle changes may cause the [oxytocin signaling pathway] to go haywire and [could] be responsible for the surprisingly prompt and very negative feeling experienced”.

There are no SNS-specific studies, but there are two more well-studied conditions that are similar enough to help us understand it. The first is dysphoric milk ejection reflex, or D-MER, which occurs during breastfeeding. It is an emotional response to the milk letdown, the moment where milk starts flowing out of the milk duct. People commonly describe the sudden rush of emotion as homesickness, sadness, loss of hope, worthlessness, shame and guilt, according to Alia Macrina Heise, an international board-certified lactation consultant and an expert on D-MER in Naples, New York. “It is disruptive to the duration of lactation and to the mother’s experience of breastfeeding and bonding,” she says.

SNS and D-MER present identically, and are also similar to post-coital dysphoria, says Heise. While SNS and D-MER are focused on nipple stimulation, the negative feelings people experience with post-coital dysphoria occur after the hormonal spike of orgasm. Anyone who has one of these conditions “will describe the embodied emotional sensations basically exactly the same way, even though the cause and the trigger is different”, says Heise.

The prevailing theory is that these three conditions involve a “hormonal cocktail inside the body”, says Heise.

The two most relevant hormones are prolactin and dopamine. This cocktail Heise refers to affects every human in a multitude of ways. “Prolactin and dopamine have a known relationship inside the human body – male, female, breastfeeding, not breastfeeding, in sexual arousal, in orgasm,” says Heise. Prolactin also contributes to weight control, immunoregulation, stress adaptation and maternal behavior.

Meanwhile, dopamine drives the brain’s reward system, playing a key role in movement, pleasure, desire, motivation and thinking. “Dopamine is often called prolactin’s gatekeeper,” explains Heise. In order for prolactin to flow into the body, dopamine has to allow prolactin through in order to complete one of its many jobs.

It’s possible that what happens in SNS, D-MER and post-coital dysphoria has to do with the way prolactin and dopamine go about their daily duties. One possible explanation is “inappropriate dopamine activity”, says Heise, who first heard a colleague mention SNS in the 2000s. “With dopamine being a mood stabilizer, that inappropriate activity is causing a mood destabilization that lasts for a very short amount of time.”

There is a growing body of research focused on D-MER, but to truly understand these conditions, we need more specialized studies. Without a clearer picture, sufferers are left feeling alone and “crazy”. Even if they work up the courage to ask their doctor about it, most medical professionals don’t have enough experience with these conditions to recommend treatment.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Techniques for reducing the severity of symptoms are mostly experimental. “One of the tricks that we’ve found helps the most by also targeting the dopamine system is cold therapy,” says Heise, who’s worked with thousands of breastfeeding mothers with D-MER. “Mothers drinking ice water or putting cold wraps around the back of their neck and cooling down their face and mouth receptors before letdown significantly eases the symptoms because it increases prolactin levels.” But whether this trick works for people with SNS is unknown.

Unexplained physical phenomena can be confusing and distressing, especially when they involve intimate body parts. The impact of SNS goes beyond the brief sensations, to shame and confusion over what they might mean.

Without formal answers from the medical community, many have developed theories about the causes, including forgotten sexual trauma, questions about one’s sexuality and marital doubts. These unfounded explanations can do real harm.

Kraus says SNS has rarely come up in his practice, but those who experience it often feel concerned “about their mental state or fear that they don’t like their partner or sex”.

As with all sexual preferences or personal boundaries, clear communication is key, experts say. It may also feel challenging or personal for partners of people who experience SNS.

“This isn’t about you, and it isn’t rejection,” says Dr Jennifer Lincoln, a board-certified OB-GYN and author in Portland, Oregon. “Talk about it outside the bedroom, agree on a signal to pause or change what’s happening, and let the person with the reaction lead.”

It can be tricky to bring up something you might not even know the name for, feel ashamed of or confused by. But talking about it can be helpful.

“Even just naming [Sad Nipple Syndrome] helps a lot, because many people think they’re going crazy – or with D-MER, that they are a bad mother,” says Lincoln. Similarly, shame can arise when SNS leads to negative experiences during sex and intimacy.

“I just avoid any nipple stuff during sex now, and it’s completely fine,” says Zaky.

“It pretty much has not impacted my sex life at all,” says Sandra. “I think the hardest part was simply feeling like a weird freak, and having a reaction that can’t be explained.”

Ivana Rihter is a writer in Chicago whose work has appeared in Vogue, Vanity Fair, Slate, Nylon and more

Datacentres are deeply unpopular – so the geniuses at OpenAI are rebranding them

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:58:55 GMT

These resource-guzzling centres drive up utility bills and are hated across the political spectrum. Cue a clunky, but potentially influential, new name for them

Jesus may have turned water into wine, but Donald Trump has done one better: he turned Lake Ontario into Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico into the Gulf of America. And then, for his next trick, he insisted we all stop talking about artificial intelligence (AI) and call it superintelligence (SI) instead.

Those, of course, are only a few of the name changes the president has ushered in. When he’s not golfing or commenting on senators’ buttocks, president Trump loves a rebranding project. Which makes sense: coming up with a new name is far easier than making meaningful improvements to people’s lives.

Trump isn’t alone in thinking a rebrand can distract from bigger issues. The tech industry seems to be on a mission to pepper every inch of the earth with datacentres that will facilitate our glorious AI-powered future. One slight problem: the hoi polloi are not quite so enthusiastic. People around the world are increasingly nervous about AI. Meanwhile, a majority of Americans across the political spectrum hate datacentres with a passion; so much so that they have become one of the biggest talking points of the midterms. There are various reasons for this anger, but the big one is that a lot of people blame the resource-guzzling centres for driving up the cost of utility bills. And so, with Trumpian logic, the great minds at OpenAI have come up with a brilliant solution to their very bad image problem. They will rename datacentres … wait for it … compute campuses.

Did a consultant (or ChatGPT) land on this new alliterative formulation because it sounded a smidgen warmer, a bit more human, than datacentres? I presume that is the case, but the official explanation is somewhat more convoluted. “Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we’re building for AI,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Business Insider on Sunday. “These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work.”

As someone once said, nobody ever went broke by underestimating the intelligence of the American people, but do the geniuses at OpenAI really think the public is stupid enough to be swayed by a few new buzzwords?

I won’t speculate as to what these people think, but I will concede that names do matter. The Affordable Care Act (ACA), the major US healthcare reform passed in Barack Obama’s first term, is one obvious example. When the ACA was being debated, Republicans started calling it “Obamacare” to try to make it seem as if it was a self-serving power grab by the president. This wasn’t an entirely successful ploy, but it did cause a lot of confusion. A 2017 Morning Consult study found that a third of Americans had no idea that the ACA and Obamacare were the same things. About 80% of Republicans strongly disapproved of Obamacare while only about 60% strongly disapproved of the ACA. “Very slight variations in how you describe something can change people’s minds,” the co-founder of Morning Consult noted at the time.

That said, I’m fairly certain that a new name for datacentres isn’t going to win hearts and change minds. But that’s OK: the tech industry has other tricks up its sleeve and a number of helpful partners in crime. Fox News, for example, seems to be going out of its way to do PR for the industry. According to a new analysis by Media Matters for America, the volume of pro-datacentre claims made by Fox News personalities and guests increased 420% after 18 August. That’s not a random date; it’s when the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent out a memo warning that animosity towards the industry could hurt pro-datacentre Republican candidates in the midterms.

As the propaganda proliferates, I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’re simultaneously seeing the gradual criminalisation of opposition to AI. In June, the Intercept reported that Philadelphia police were scanning “social media looking for posts opposing AI datacentres” because of a supposed risk from “domestic violent extremists”. Meanwhile, in August, Futurism counted at least 37 arrests from protests related to datacentres so far this year, many for petty infractions. Since that analysis, there have been a number of other reported arrests. It seems the powers that be think that if people can’t be brainwashed into loving the “compute campus” next door, they can always be scared into shutting up.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

All aboard with Kaptain Kemi, lost at sea on the good ship amnesia

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:45:17 GMT

Launching a defence plan on a rusty sloop, and dogged by a UK Iron Dome that never was, the Tory leader has forgotten her party’s 14 years in power

HMS Wellington. A decommissioned Grimsby-class sloop from the second world war. A warship that has been moored on the Thames, going nowhere for the best part of 80 years. Today’s venue for the leader of the opposition to explain why the Conservative party hollowed out defence spending throughout their time in office. Sorry. Scrub that. To welcome in a brave new world order. Come aboard the good ship Badenoch. There are times when you wonder if the Tory media team have been infiltrated by Labour HQ. Still, we might as well enjoy it while we can.

After a brief introduction from the loyal but dim Lieutenant “Steady as she goes, chaps and chapesses” James Cartlidge, who – for reasons not even he fully understands – is the shadow defence secretary, Kaptain Kemi appeared to take over the helm. “Why have I brought you here?” she began. A good question. Though if she doesn’t know, it seems a bit much expecting us to have the answers. Maybe this was more of a rhetorical cry for help. It wouldn’t be the only time her memory failed her on this latest public outing.

A pause. Still no one had a clue what we were doing. Most people had only come because they had been asked. It’s a worry when the host doesn’t remember sending out the invitation. Kaptain Kemi allowed herself to take in her surroundings. Being onboard evoked euphoric recall of a time of empire. When most of the globe was painted red, and Britain ruled the world. That was a time and a history of which we could all be proud. Instead, we now lived in a world where our entire navy was out of action, good only as an entertainment venue, available for corporate events. The irony escaped her.

Let’s hear it for the Britannia Shield, said Kaptain Kemi. Trying to inject some energy into a speech that was already sinking fast. James had come up with the Britannia Shield, she added. Which should have been a warning in itself not to take it seriously. Commander Cartlidge had only really envisioned it as a couple of drones being piloted from his back garden. He had never thought that anyone would take it seriously. It was something he had thought up in the shower while preparing for his speech at the Tory party conference.

“Why do people keep comparing it to the Iron Dome?” she asked. Yet another question. Her memory was now failing her in real time. At this rate she would be lucky to make it to the end of the event without a psychiatric intervention. It doesn’t matter whether it’s an Iron Dome or not, Kaptain Kemi insisted. Let’s try to help her out. Oh, that was it. We had compared it to an Iron Dome because that’s how both she and the Tory party had described it on X and in press releases. Now we were being given a hard time for taking her at her word. You can’t win.

Kaptain Kemi then wandered into a long ramble about how things were all terrible and how Shabana Mahmood had weakened our borders by putting in place immigration controls that were far tougher than anything the Tories had ever done. Luckily, she appeared to have no idea how embarrassing the speech had just become. An extended cry for help. Living proof of terminal cognitive decline. She tried to cheer herself up by asking some more questions.

“Where is the prime minister?” she said. It was nice of her to show an interest in Andy Burnham’s whereabouts. And at least she knew the answer. “Antigua!” she yelled triumphantly. A victory that was short-lived as it soon became clear she thought he had gone there for a holiday rather than to attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting.

Kaptain Kemi also moaned about the country having experienced no rise in living standards throughout the 14 years of Tory governments. Some of which she served in. Though that too appears to have been wiped from her memory. Brain fade. She ended with another questions. “We are a new party, aren’t we?” Er, no. You’re not. At the last count the Conservatives were nearly 200 years old. Still, good guess. You had a 50-50 chance and you got it wrong. It can’t be long before the producers try to sign up Our Kaptain for next year’s Celebrity Traitors.

That just left time for a few questions for the media. Kaptain Kemi was dead against any form of dynamic alignment with the EU on food products. Any hint of regulations to make it easier to trade with our neighbours was a red line. Trade should be made as difficult and as expensive as possible. That was what the British public had voted for. If Brexit was to mean anything, it was the right to impoverish yourself. Which was why she would be stockpiling water after declaring war. It turns out that the only terms on which Kaptain Kemi would visit China was if she had bombed it into submission first. I’m not sure she has quite got the hang of this diplomacy thing.

The longer the session went on, the more delusional Our Kaptain became. It wasn’t long before she was offering her thoughts on making an apology for Britain’s part in the slave trade. “Saying sorry is always a weakness,” she said. The first rule of any contested area is never to admit liability.

Slavery was so old history. Centuries old. Countries needed to move on. And don’t forget, we want some credit for ending slavery. Swings and roundabouts. The idea that a confident nation could address both the good and the bad it had done and apologise where necessary didn’t seem to have occurred to her.

Come the end, Kaptain Kemi seemed just as confused as the rest of us. Still no real answer to why so many people had gathered on HMS Wellington. We were here because we’re here because we’re here. Maybe the reality was more prosaic. It had all been an exercise in rehabilitation. Occupational therapy for the leader of the Tory party. Shame she won’t remember it.

The art prescription: how 60 minutes in a gallery each month could transform your life

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:36:19 GMT

Are you getting your RDA (recommended dose of art)? Along with 10,000 steps and five fruit and veg a day, this small, enjoyable change could make you much healthier – and happier

Name: Art.

Age: Art has been around for thousands of years. The drawings in Blombos Cave in South Africa, for example, are estimated to be about 73,000 years old. But this is less about how old and more about how often, and for how long.

OK, how often, and for how long? Sixty minutes a month.

Cave painting? No. Well, if you like, sure (though ask the owner and check for bears first). But this is about experiencing art.

Like going to a gallery? Exactly. Or a museum.

For an hour a month? Minimum.

To make me more cultured and interesting? Maybe. But mainly because it’s good for you.

Who says? A study by the Art Fund charity, and more specifically Daisy Fancourt, a professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London, who wrote the foreword to the report, as well as the book Art Cure: The Science of How the Arts Transform Our Health.

And what does Fancourt have to say? “Regular engagement and meaningful encounters with art are now recognised as an important contributor to our health and wellbeing.”

It makes art sound like your five fruit and veg a day, or 10,000 steps. It’s meant to. It’s being called RDA – recommended dose of art. Fancourt says of visiting museums and galleries: “The evidence suggests they should be viewed as health-promoting behaviours, alongside having a balanced diet, regular exercise and spending time outdoors.”

OK, but one study, by a charity that exists to get people to go to galleries … Another study, published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, working with data from 2,148 adults in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, found a 48% lower risk of depression for people going to museums, theatre and cinema once a month. You want more?

You’ve got more? Another study, published in the journal Brain, Behaviour and Immunity, found “evidence that authentic art viewing engages biological processes linked to stress reduction and immune modulation”.

“Authentic” – is that relevant? Yes, the interesting thing about this study is that it compared the physiological impact of viewing original artworks in a gallery with looking at reproductions in a laboratory.

And? The positive effects were “not observed when the same works were viewed as reproductions”.

So the Starry Night phone wallpaper, which I see about 17,000 times a month, doesn’t count as my RDA? No.

Do say: “Thanks, I’ve been feeling great ever since my GP prescribed the Barbara Hepworth show.”

Don’t say: “And they do great doughnuts in the gallery cafe.”

Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:24:29 GMT

George Madgwick, party leader on Hampshire county council, faces charges related to four teenagers between 2008 and 2021

Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

George Madgwick, 37, who is a councillor in Portsmouth and leads the Reform group on the council, was a prominent voice linked to recent protests in the town connected to the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats.

A Crown Prosecution Service statement said the charges followed a police investigation into allegations connected to four complainants, aged 16 and 17 at the time, and were alleged to have taken place in Portsmouth and Wales between 2008 and 2021. On 6 January, officers arrested a man at an address in Wandsworth, London.

The charges comprise 12 allegations of rape; eight of actual bodily harm; two of assault by penetration; two of sexual assault; two of controlling and coercive behaviour; two of making an indecent image of a child; one of distribution of an indecent image of a child; one of stalking; one of making threats to kill; one of false imprisonment; one of criminal damage; one of theft; and one of causing or inciting the sexual exploitation of a child.

Madgwick is scheduled to appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November. A CPS spokesperson said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute George Madgwick for serious sexual offences, including multiple counts of rape. He has also been charged with making a threat to kill, false imprisonment and stalking.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”

A Reform spokesperson said: “Cllr Madgwick has been suspended from Reform UK with immediate effect.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “These charges are truly shocking. Nigel Farage must urgently tell the public whether he was aware of Councillor Magdwick’s arrest, or of any of the appalling allegations he is accused of.

“If he was, the Reform leader must explain why he thought it was appropriate for Madgwick to stand for his party, hold a local leadership role, and to work as a Reform member of staff.”

Madgwick began his political career as an independent on Portsmouth city council, winning his seat in 2021. In 2025, he joined Reform UK, and a year later he became a Hampshire councillor, representing the North East Havant area.

He was one of 20 Reform councillors to be elected, placing them third behind the Conservatives, who run the authority, and the Liberal Democrats. Madgwick became leader of the Reform group, and chair of the council’s corporate services and resources select committee.

In September, when masked protesters connected to the far right activist Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, blocked roads in Portsmouth over the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, Madgwick was at the scene and spoke to the media.

While saying it was important any protests were peaceful, Madgwick said local people were “not happy, and rightly so” about the arrival of asylum seekers. He was involved recently in an incident in which protesters gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel after mistaking Pakistan’s under-19s cricket team for asylum seekers, liaising with hotel staff and persuading protesters to leave.

Madgwick called the hotel to mediate between staff and the assembled crowd, and said at the time that it was a “massively unfortunate incident”. He added, however, that he believed the incident was understandable given recent coverage of asylum seekers arriving in the city via small boats.

I’d all but forgotten my ‘altercation’ with Nigel Farage. But since he mentions it, here’s what happened

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:06:04 GMT

His boorish behaviour towards me typifies the politics of Reform UK: this is a party full of disdain for parliament, its people and its traditions

Caroline Voaden is the Liberal Democrat MP for South Devon

I got an unexpected message last week from a former colleague whom I haven’t heard from in 20 years. I was all over her TikTok, she said, so she reached out to say hi. Such was the furore caused by Nigel Farage bizarrely raising an incident that took place in the House of Commons nearly six months ago that I suddenly found myself trending on social media. That had not been on my bingo card for budget week.

I was at home, having just got back from London, when I received a message telling me that Farage had referenced “the incident”. I looked at the footage of his press conference and was completely dumbfounded. Because this “physical altercation”, as he described it, was something I’d chosen not to discuss in public at the time, and something that, if I were him, I’d have kept quiet about.

But, no, not Nigel. Here he was, scrabbling around for excuses to explain why he wasn’t in the chamber for the budget, and this had to be the strangest one he could possibly have used. And it made absolutely no sense.

For clarity’s sake, this is what happened.

On the day of the king’s speech, MPs process through to the House of Lords to listen to it. Leaders of all parties, including smaller ones, lead the procession, but on this occasion Farage didn’t seem to get into place in time. So he was stuck behind a load of MPs also trying to join the procession.

I was on a flight of stairs and he demanded to get past. I told him to wait his turn like everyone else and he clearly didn’t like that, so he grabbed me by the arm and I ended up shoved to one side so he could push through. My colleague thought I was going to fall down the stairs, so he grabbed Farage and had a word with him about his behaviour. I reported it to the parliamentary authorities and they asked him to apologise in writing. That never happened – of course – and I chose not to say anything about it publicly.

So, yes, there was an altercation. Was it caused by “aggressive” Lib Dem MPs, as a Reform UK source later claimed? Hardly.

The whole thing makes me wonder: why bring it up now? Why bring it up at all? I think it’s a perfect reflection of the type of politics that typifies Reform UK. The politics of grievance, the repetitive mantra that the “establishment are out to get us”, but, more importantly, the disdain for parliament and its traditions.

For a man who claims he wants to become prime minister, Farage’s aversion to spending time in parliament means that he will go into the next election with very little knowledge about how the place works, how to leverage its power and what lies behind its traditions. He has spoken less in parliament than any other comparable party leader and voted about half as much as the average MP. He is a stranger in the place he aims to command.

I’ve never believed Farage would be PM, even when his party was polling in first place. Because much of what the PM does is the hard yards behind the scenes – the kind of stuff Farage hates – and, in reality, very little of the job is the glory bit in the media.

As leader of the Lib Dems in Europe, I worked “alongside” Farage in the European parliament – though he barely showed his face in Brussels. He attended just one out of 42 fisheries meetings, despite being the member chosen to represent the UK fishing industry. For all his bluster about being on the side of UK fishers, he hardly ever showed up to be their voice at the table because that seemed too much like work – too boring, too mundane, not glamorous enough for a man who loves the limelight.

And it’s much the same in London. Last Thursday he showed up at business questions, where MPs can ask the leader of the house about the following week’s Commons business, and had to ask a colleague how it worked. We’re halfway through this parliament, and Farage is still apparently getting to grips with the basics of what happens in the House of Commons.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It’s a sign of the disdain in which he seemingly holds parliament and the work we do there. Yes, it’s old-fashioned. Yes, there are traditions that have probably seen better days. And, yes, we could – and I’d argue should – modernise the way we work. But if you want to be PM, or even leader of the opposition, it’s fundamental to understand what goes on there and respect how the place works. And part of that is respecting your colleagues – all of them, regardless of party or political persuasion, age, race or sex.

I’ve been asked whether I thought Farage would have acted in the same way if I’d been a man. I think it’s highly unlikely. We’ve all heard what Sarah Pochin MP has said about the alpha males at the top of Reform UK and the problem they have with women, and the boorish behaviour I’ve experienced pretty much sums this up.

For Farage to float the idea that he chose not to go into the chamber to listen to the budget in case he got involved in another altercation is quite simply laughable. There may be nine Lib Dems to every one Reform MP, but we’re not spoiling for a fight. We’re just getting on with the day job – which does involve sometimes being in the chamber, Nigel.

Caroline Voaden is the Liberal Democrat MP for South Devon

West Ham want promotion – so it’s time to call in an understated club legend

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:55:01 GMT

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

While Football Daily hasn’t actually seen much of West Ham this season, we’ve noted enough of their results to presume they were doing OK in their attempt to bounce back to the Premier League after relegation. Less than a third of the way through the Championship season under Nuno Espírito Santo, they’d already spanked six without reply past both Wrexham and Lincoln, while scoring three or more in wins over Wolves, Derby and Bolton. However, it turns out that of the 13 matches they’ve played in a league that is famously difficult to get out of (unless you were Sheffield Wednesday last season), they have actually lost three times and currently sit in eighth place, a whopping six points off leaders Middlesbrough. Given the context of such an unbridgeable chasm, it is small wonder West Ham fans woke up to news that Nuno had been unceremoniously bounced out of the London Stadium with a P45 in hand.

Coming on the back of consecutive home defeats by Southampton and West Brom, Tuesday’s news won’t have come as a huge surprise to Hammers fans, treated to the sight of a sad Nuno on the London Stadium touchline on Saturday, eyes glazed and grey beard glistening in the early evening mist as he stared blankly in the direction of several celebrating Baggies. “West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team head coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect,” droned a club statement. “Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.”

Determined to secure one of the two automatic promotion places up for grabs, West Ham have decided to nip any prospective long-term slump in the bud by approaching Scott Parker. An understated club legend of sorts, the 46-year-old is best known for wearing expensive Thom Browne four-bar ripstop blouson jackets in his technical area while masterminding immediate promotion to the Premier League for the only three English clubs he has managed thus far.

Indeed, it is a testament to the breezy optimism of certain West Ham fans on several Social Media Disgraces that they are already discussing how dismal Parker’s Premier League record is, while arguing over who should replace him when he becomes the first top-flight gaffer to get sacked in 12 months’ time. With their team having scored 33 goals in their opening 13 games this season, West Ham fans can now presumably look forward to seeing them bag the same number in their remaining fixtures as they clock up 33 consecutive, risk-averse 1-0 wins. It may not be the fabled West Ham way but it will do until the next guy comes along.

The family of Jesús de Miguel is grateful for each and every expression of support received, and also requests, from the bottom of their hearts, the utmost respect for their privacy during these terrible times” – Tenerife have announced the death of striker Jesús de Miguel, who died after a collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in Spain’s second division. As King Charles visits the Caribbean, is the reparations movement approaching a tipping point?

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:25:20 GMT

The British monarch has been stalked by protesters during his visit to the Bahamas, Antigua and Guyana – and they will only become more insistent as time goes on

Don’t get Cotton Capital delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The sun is starting to set in the Bahamas and the loud wash of the tide, which is always audible on Nassau’s Western Esplanade, is beginning to be drowned out by the sound of excited screams. King Charles is visiting the Caribbean archipelago, for which he is still the head of state, for the first time in more than 50 years and a youth rally attended by schoolchildren makes for a particularly welcoming crowd.

Some have described the king’s nine-day tour of the Bahamas, Antigua and Guyana amid growing calls for reparations as a significant risk that may accelerate his removal as head of state from the six remaining Caribbean Commonwealth countries in which he still serves.

King Charles was in the Bahamas before travelling to Antigua for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting (Chogm), which is usually a collegial gathering of leaders, but has only just managed to keep enslavement and reparations off the formal agenda.

As the summit gets under way today, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin talks about a formal apology with countries affected by Britain’s role in transatlantic enslavement.

Those talks will include plans for a “debt reset” for Commonwealth countries facing higher costs on their debts.

Writing last week in the Guardian, Burnham indicated he is open to the possibility of a formal apology, going further than any UK prime minister has before. However, he rejected demands for financial reparations, saying that British people cannot be held liable for what “happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part”.

Fresh from his trip to the Bahamas, the king is expected to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” on the lasting pain of the transatlantic trafficking of African people as he opens the summit.

‘The noise is getting louder and louder’

Given the mounting pressure before the summit, the fanatical atmosphere in Nassau may be a surprise, and a relief. “It’s a celebrity effect, isn’t it?” says the Guardian’s Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan. “Shaking the king of England’s hand – that’s something that they will remember for ever.”

Still, beneath the sheen and structure of organised royal engagements, Natricia tells me that something has shifted. The venue, Clifford Park, marks the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973, and on a sandy stretch of the Esplanade opposite called Fish Fry, a small but visible group of protesters pick up the mantle. Their colourful signs read “pay us what you owe us”, and “reparation, repatriation, restoration is a must now”.

Sharon Purser-Cooper, who attended the protest organised by the Rastafari organisation Ethiopia Africa Black International Congress, tells me that she will not name an abstract figure for reparations; rather, she wants to see investment in healthcare, education, agriculture and infrastructure.

Like many, Purser-Cooper wants a formal apology.

“We are demanding an apology from England, and, by extension, all of the 52 countries that abstained from the vote to apologise to the people whose ancestors they slaughtered, raped and plundered,” she tells me.

The UK and EU members were among those that did not vote in March on the UN resolution to describe the transatlantic chattel slave trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and call for reparations as “a concrete step towards remedying historical wrongs”. Purser-Cooper says: “We are not begging for anything, we are making a demand.”

Protests are not a new occurrence during Caribbean royal tours, Natricia tells me, with calls for reparations after the then Duke and Duchess of Cambridge to Belize, Jamaica and the Bahamas during Queen Elizabeth II’s platinum jubilee visit in 2022. “But now we have a call coming from the centre of politics, from government, from civil society, from academics. And it’s more organised. The noise is getting louder and louder, and much harder to ignore.”

The UN motion is not the only significant development in the reparations movement in the past 12 months. In September, the king referred a petition to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, after pressure from a delegation of Jamaican politicians. The petition, which will be heard by the privy council in March, seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

Still, many see the prospect of reparations as an impossibly abstract demand. The Bahamians that I speak to broadly express apathy towards the king, or mild disgruntlement at the cost of the visit. The campaigners see their task as to make things concrete. Natricia tells me: “In the Bahamas, there have been recent devastating hurricanes. Imagine you’re a mum in Trinidad or Barbados: you have bills to pay, you have your child going to school, the cost of living and other challenges. Top of your mind is going to be about providing for your family and your health.”

While the cost of this year’s trip is unconfirmed, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge’s 2022 visit cost the Bahamas $636,000 (£505,620). The Caribbean might ask if there is something else that could be done with that money.

I ask Natricia if this Caribbean tour represents a tipping point for the reparations movement and if so, why at this moment in history? “If you asked me about this a year ago, I would have a very different answer,” Natricia tells me. “I am still really in awe of what has happened in the last year … The Rastafarian movement started this call, and they often make the point that initially, they were considered as being on the fringes.”

But things can change quickly. “You’re talking about really young countries,” Natricia says. “Where I come from, St Vincent and the Grenadines, we got our independence in 1979, around the same time as most Caribbean countries. You almost have to start from there in terms of defining who you are as a nation, bearing in mind that slavery and colonisation has taken so much away from people in terms of their identity.”

Either way, the conversation has begun. The very fact that the monarchy and British party leaders have been pushed to make statements on reparations and a formal apology looks like a possibility, signals a shift in the parameters of the debate. “The more they resist, I think, the more insistent people will become,” Natricia says. “This is not going away.”

British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham

‘Reparations now’: King and Burnham face protests at Antigua Commonwealth summit | Natricia Duncan

Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund| John Collingridge

Barack Obama pays tribute to Manchester cotton workers and cites them as an inspiration | Chris Osuh

Deceptively simple’: Gullah Geechee art exhibition illustrates that beauty lies in the details | Adria R Walker

Manchester | The inaugural Sarah Parker Remond lecture, presented by Manchester arts charity SICK! Productions and Manchester City Galleries, has launched an annual commitment to celebrating global majority women whose leadership, creativity and activism has shaped Manchester.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

The acclaimed performance poet, writer, librettist and arts curator SuAndi opened a new chapter in the city’s Black history with the lecture, Sarah’s Sistahs, at Manchester Metropolitan University’s Grosvenor East Theatre.

Last month’s event marked the bicentenary of Parker Remond, the abolitionist, suffragist and international campaigner. Born in 1826, she spoke at the Manchester Athenaeum in 1859 during her anti-slavery lecture tour of Britain.

SuAndi drew inspiration from Remond’s belief in the power of testimony to fight injustice, asking whose voices have inspired social change, and whose contributions remain overlooked.

In a lecture that addressed memory, race, gender and the fight for equality over continents and centuries, SuAndi said: “Are not all our merits still determined, if not negated by race and gender, as the old strategy of divide and rule still influences society? What we all need to believe is that we are all treated equally, but are we?” Chris Osuh, community affairs correspondent

Sea Islands | We Were Fridays, a multidisciplinary project led by the cellist Jeffrey Zeigler, explores Gullah Geechee music from South Carolina and the connection to his ancestral roots. An amalgamation of music, theatre and dance, We Were Fridays premiered in Brooklyn in September and October.

The work that has been years in the making began when Zeigler learned as an adult that his father’s family, who he knew little about, were the descendants of formerly enslaved west Africans who retained their distinctive culture and customs. We Were Fridays merged music, oral history and genealogical documents to illustrate the preservation of ancestry.

Zeigler is joined in the musical project by the visual artist Sister Sylvester and the choreographer Reggie Gray. Last month’s event at Weeksville Heritage Center in Brooklyn, a site dedicated to preserving one of the first free Black communities in the US, included workshops on photography, textile-making, quilting and choreography. It ended with an evening performance. Melissa Hellmann, senior reporter on the Guardian US’s race and equity team.

Jamaica | Last month, campaigners scored a surprise victory in one of five court battles over free public access to Jamaica’s beaches. They are fighting to repeal the 1956 Beach Control Act, a colonial law enacted six years before Jamaican independence that gives the state ownership of the island’s foreshore and seabed. It means anyone wanting to use or develop a beach needs government permission. Campaigners argue it has led to beaches being sealed off to locals for luxurious hotel developments.

In October a court granted a temporary injunction preventing the government from continuing to restrict access to Little Dunn’s River in St Ann while the case is ongoing. Campaigners from the Jamaica Beach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem), which was set up in 2020, have welcomed the ruling and said it had given them hope. “This victory means a lot for the Jamaican people. It means our case is strong,” said Dr Devon Taylor, the group’s founder.

The Jamaican government has said it plans to appeal against the decision.

If you want to know more about this issue, I recommend watching this excellent video, Why Jamaicans Can’t Access Their Own Beaches, from our It’s Complicated series, which breaks it all down. Angela Foster, assistant editor

When I heard that, as a response to Lloyd’s of London unearthing new evidence on its historic links to slavery, the insurance company had commissioned an orchestral work, I wasn’t sure what to expect.

Though the task had been handed to a Black composer, David Önaç, Atlantic Requiem was to be performed by the London Symphony Orchestra. Hardly a typical example of reparative justice. Could a piece of music really help atone for slavery and its legacies?

Lloyd’s insured ships and their human cargo during the transatlantic trade in the 18th and 19th centuries. I’d expected some kind of sorrowful but soothing sound experience, lamenting on the injustices of slavery. It was very different. From the start it grabbed the attention: a cacophony of discordant, syncopated jabbing sounds.

Unnerving, jarring, unpleasant even, giving the listener a feeling of continuous discomfort. And above this “noise”, three singers read out words extracted from 18th-century court testimony and insurance documents: on African lives valued at £45; on an enslaved woman who contracted smallpox being thrown overboard tied to a chair; on the captain’s regret over losing “so good a chair”. The disconnect between the dull language of bureaucracy, and the brutalised lives of those under discussion. The banality of evil.

A jolting experience leaving the audience somewhat shellshocked. And a very creative and impactful way to mark this centuries-long horror. Joseph Harker, senior editor, diversity and development

‘A trailblazer in the truest sense’: poet Grace Nichols wins £10,000 Pioneer prize

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:46:05 GMT

The Guyana-born, British-based writer takes home the Royal Society of Literature prize honouring women writers over 60 who have broken barriers

The poet Grace Nichols has been named the winner of the 2026 Royal Society of Literature Pioneer prize, a £10,000 award that recognises women writers over 60 who broke through at a time when the literary world was less open to them.

Nichols, 76, who was born in Guyana and moved to the UK in 1977, made her name with I Is a Long-Memoried Woman, which took the Commonwealth poetry prize in 1983, and The Fat Black Woman’s Poems, a collection published the following year. Her poems have been GCSE set texts for decades, and she has written extensively for children as well as adults.

The Pioneer prize was established last year by the then president of the Royal Society of Literature (RSL), Bernardine Evaristo, who donated the £100,000 she received from the 2025 Women’s prize outstanding contribution award to fund it for 10 years. The award will rotate between forms each year, and this year was given for poetry. The winner of the inaugural Pioneer prize was the novelist, playwright and activist Maureen Duffy, who died in May.

Nichols’ poems draw on Guyanese folk tales, oral tradition, landscape, and on the history of slavery. She was also one of a group of West Indian poets whose work tackled racial tensions during a time of inflammatory immigration debates in Thatcher’s Britain. Her other collections include Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Woman (1989), Sunris (1996), which won the Guyana poetry prize, and Startling the Flying Fish (2005). She has also published a novel, Whole of a Morning Sky (1986), as well as books for younger readers including Come on Into My Tropical Garden (1988) and Give Yourself a Hug (1994). Several of those were anthologies she co-edited with her partner, fellow Guyanese poet John Agard.

Ruth Borthwick, the chair of English PEN, who led the judging panel, called Nichols “one of our most important contemporary poets”, who had developed “her own poetic language – an earthy mix of Creole and standard English”.

“Grace showed the way for generations of poets from the diaspora to make the cultural connections between the Caribbean and Britain,” Borthwick said.

Borthwick was joined on the panel by the poet Sarah Howe, who said: “Grace Nichols is a legend, a trailblazer in the truest sense. Her work spans continents and traditions, alive to orality and shapely on the page, light and weighty at once. Her work blends the rhythms and stories of her Caribbean heritage with a unique vision of modern Britain.”

Nichols said she had been surprised to get the call from Borthwick. “I am honoured and delighted to have the RSL Pioneer prize bestowed on me and grateful to poetry for all that it’s given me, as well as to the judges and my parents who made books a part of our lives,” she said.

Judith Palmer, the director of the Poetry Society, also on the judging panel, said Nichols “was probably the first poet who really lifted poetry off the page for me”.

When she established the prize, Evaristo said: “It’s very easy to forget the feminist struggles of the past and the intrepid women who paved the way for successive generations, and it’s important to celebrate our trailblazers while they are still around to enjoy it.”

after newsletter promotion

Nichols, who is a vice-president of the RSL, received the Queen’s gold medal for poetry in 2021. Her next collection for adults, The Tracks of My Name, will be published on 19 November.

She will be celebrated at an event at the British Library on 1 March 2027.

They fell in love on The Simpsons and married in real life. Meet the French Homer and Marge

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:33:12 GMT

They have brought TV’s most famous cartoon couple to life in France for the last 38 years. Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau tell all about working and living together for so long, still being lovebirds – and rarely arguing

The Simpsons is the biggest cartoon comedy in the world, with suburban couple Homer and Marge at its heart. From their beginnings as high-school sweethearts to the travails of married life, they’re an unbreakable pair. Gag-heavy as it may be, it’s also a series with plenty of sentimental plots, from Homer giving up his beloved Duff beer for a month to prove his love to Marge, to Marge composing a heartfelt poem to a dying Homer (miraculously, he makes it through his sushi-induced food poisoning).

Not even the temptations of a brunch-loving bowling instructor called Jacques or a doughnut-guzzling redhead called Mindy could get between them. Plus, of course, they enjoy the occasional “snuggle” (even on a miniature golf course … ).

Now in its 38th season, The Simpsons has also been a huge hit across the globe, meaning hundreds of international actors have voiced this much-loved couple. Among them are Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau, who – as well as playing Marge and Homer in the French dub of The Simpsons since 1990 – met through the show and ended up getting married.

“Matt Groening called us the second most famous couple in the history of animation,” says Peythieu. “There were the actors who voiced Minnie and Mickey Mouse [the late Wayne Allwine and Russi Taylor], and then there was us. Meanwhile in Los Angeles, he said, everyone he worked with was getting divorced …”

The pair record their scenes together with a director in a Paris dubbing studio over 10-12 days a year. But clearly The Simpsons is a 365-day-a-year commitment, from appearances at galas and conventions to the gifts they receive from adoring fans. Both are adamant that they wouldn’t carry on without the other, which means a definite non to AI taking over in the future. “We’re not for artificial intelligence – we’re for artistic intelligence!” says Augereau. There will always be roles that require a human soul, she adds, and – for Peythieu and Augereau – this role has given them each a soulmate to boot.

Philippe Peythieu: We met at a casting call in 1989 – it was only six months after The Simpsons had debuted in the US, so it wasn’t a success there yet. We auditioned, and then six months later – by fax – we found out we had got the roles.

Véronique Augereau: Philippe and I didn’t know each other well at all. When we were trying out, we crossed paths in the hallway at the dubbing offices and greeted each other but we were just colleagues – we weren’t even friends at that stage. There’s a video of us at a wrap party for the first series and we’re just walking right past each other, not even speaking, let alone stealing any glances!

PP: Voilà, that’s how this beautiful story began. The recording process brought us closer together, since we were working in the darkness of the studio, and so we became more than friends … We had to be very discreet in the beginning, because this was a professional setting, but eventually word got out and we were inseparable from that point on. As for the series, we never imagined it would last so long. But the success also contributed to the success of our relationship.

VA: In terms of what actually attracted us to each other, it’s hard to say, but I think the atmosphere around the recording sessions helped – there was always a friendly, funny vibe. Personally, I find the show and the storylines extraordinary, and incredibly intelligent. I think we really loved this show and were enthusiastic about it from the get-go. We liked the spirit of the series, and that humour that could be quite biting.

VA: Marge isn’t a fan of Homer’s over-the-top antics, but deep down she knows that he is her one and only love in life. Ultimately, she has a lot of tenderness and affection for this man, whom she knows is devoted to her and to their children. He is completely in love with his family – even if he doesn’t remember his children’s names all the time …

PP: Through the seasons there have been rifts, but every time they’ve found their way back to each other. If you look at the film [The Simpsons Movie, released in 2007], Marge decides to leave Homer, but ends up forgiving all of his foolish mistakes in the end. Their love grows stronger – they’re able to separate then find each other again.

VA: A critic in France, Romain Nigita, actually wrote a book called Les Simpson ou le paradoxe du donut intemporel (The Simpsons, or the Paradox of the Timeless Doughnut), to which we wrote the preface. [The book is about the show’s relationship with time, and how it never changes yet always seems relevant.] He writes about Marge and Homer’s first meeting in high school – Homer smoking in the bathroom with Barney, Marge burning her bra at a feminist protest, before the pair cross paths at the high-school prom. That’s when Homer says: “I’m sure we were meant to be together. Usually when I have a thought, there’s a lot of other thoughts in there ... something says yes, something says no ... But this time, there’s only yes! How can the only thing I’ve ever been sure about in my life be wrong?”

VA: Across all of these seasons (we will soon be dubbing season 38), this couple is still standing!

PP: Despite his doubts, his worst gaffes and the tests of time, Homer is certain of one thing: Marge is the love of his life!

VA: We love the bedroom scenes when they’re in their room with the lights off and you can only see their eyes moving around.

PP: Those scenes that can be a bit cheeky but they’re handled very well – the show addresses sexuality but with a lightness of touch, affection and humour.

PP: When you’re this hooked on The Simpsons, it’s hard to be critical of the show. It would also be difficult to rewrite its history – it’s a show that has defined an era. Besides, we love these characters unconditionally, so whatever they do we would always forgive them! Homer also resembles us – I think, as a man, I’m a bit like him, and he’s a bit like me in some ways. What you see is what you get with Homer, and yet he still manages to surprise us …

VA: I don’t love the Halloween specials, personally.

PP: She finds them scary. There was a Halloween episode where they sent up The Shining – I loved that one.

VA: We share the same values ​​in life and move forward together, bound by a very strong connection.

VA: We often stroll down the street arm in arm, and people always say, “Hello, lovebirds!” or – if I’m alone – “Oh, not with your husband today?” I don’t want to say that people have this idealised vision of us, but when we meet fans at conventions they always say the same sorts of things to us too. Whether in The Simpsons or in real life, it seems that many people see us as this devoted couple that they enjoy spending time with.

PP: We’ve had the opportunity to meet Matt Groening and the team several times, and they’ve always told us that the French version is one of the best, because we’ve understood the spirit of the series, and the fact that we’re husband and wife has added that little extra something to it.

VA: People tell us, you were the soundtrack to our childhood. Fans will tell us that we represent this perfect couple in their eyes – every Saturday night we were in their homes, on their TVs, so for some people we were almost like surrogate parents.

VA: It’s not from set, but at a charity gala in Switzerland we were given a huge portrait of Marge as a Playboy bunny [a callback to the episode The Devil Wears Nada].

PP: I’ve lost count of the amount of times I’ve been given doughnuts.

PP: What they teach us is that – come what may – it’s all about this strong bond that they have. It’s a bond that’s almost indestructible despite life’s difficulties and the differences that sometimes come between them.

VA: They show us that love is about forgiveness.

PP: And accepting the differences between both people.

VA: You have to be on the same page in life too … with us, we have the same tastes, like contemporary art, food …

PP: We’re bon vivants! We love life. We rarely argue, and if we do it’s usually about trivial things.

VA: That’s why it’s lasted all these years – we’ve been together nearly as long as The Simpsons!

China’s first AI-generated film is a flop. Some still see it as the future of cinema

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:32:54 GMT

Chinese investors placing high value on AI despite unpopularity of Sanxingdui: Future Past

China’s first fully AI-generated movie has flopped, earning just 1.7m yuan (£191,000) at the box office despite costing “tens of millions” to make, according to its producer.

But is it any good? The Guardian watched Sanxingdui: Future Past in a virtually empty cinema in Beijing, and found it no worse than plenty of human-centred mindless action flicks.

OK, well maybe a bit worse.

Sanxingdui tells a confusing tale of a future society in which every decision has been outsourced to algorithms and AI, leading to a global catastrophe. The only way to avert the impending doom is to unlock the hidden code that is hidden in the Sanxingdui, bronze sculptures linked to the ancient kingdom of Shu. Cue astronauts racing through ancient Egypt and archeologists diving through space-time vortices.

Use of the production company’s in-house AI scriptwriting tool, called Bowen, was evident in lines such as, “That is the superbrain superintelligence that costs $10m dollars a month to subscribe to”, and, “Avoid that thing!” when a plane was about to crash in an incident foretold by the evil algorithm. But the sole other audience member and I agreed that it exceeded our very low expectations.

All of the film’s visuals and some of its sound effects were created using AI, while it was edited by humans.

Many of the characters were uncanny – uncannily life-like for the most part, and uncanny valley for the remainder. The Chinese characters seemed much more realistic than the white people. All of them struggled with running (which they do a lot). They uniformly fell into that steady, smooth gait of video-game characters. One of the main characters, an astronaut called Wu Xingyan, looks creepily like Tilly Norwood, the controversial “AI actor” who is “starring” in an upcoming Hollywood feature film called Misaligned.

But despite Sanxindui’s unpopularity, people who work in the film industry believe that it’s just the beginning of AI cinema in China.

Sanxingdui flopped because “the movie isn’t entertaining”, said Yu Yaqin, an independent film critic in Beijing. At least in the short term, “AI films will continue to be produced in China because investors place a high value on AI,” she said.

One person who works in screenplay development in Beijing said that the majority of projects she has been approached by in the past few months have been for AI films. “Chinese investors believe this is the future,” she said, not least because AI films have the potential to be much cheaper than traditional productions.

“What used to take 100 people to do, now can be done by five people, and the rest won’t have any jobs,” she said.

One state media commentary said that although Sanxingdui was “riddled with flaws and imperfections,” it may “yet go down in cinematic history as the starting point of what came next”.

Chinese audiences are no stranger to AI-generated content. Tens of thousands of AI-generated microdramas, one- to three-minute-long dramas that are designed to be watched on mobile phones, are uploaded to streaming platforms each month. The industry, which didn’t exist a few years ago, is now worth an estimated $3bn. That is still much smaller than the traditional film industry, but a sign of the direction of travel.

Sanxingdui’s poor performance may also be because people don’t want to pay 50 yuan (£5.60) for a cinema ticket when they can watch similar content on their phone for free.

“AI-generated microdramas are selling a way to kill time, while films in cinemas are selling an experience worth spending time on,” wrote one film blogger.

“Perhaps audiences are still more willing to spend money on films that offer a more unique experience,” said Yu, hopefully.

Additional research by Yu-chen Li

‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis?

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:21:51 GMT

With globe-spanning artists – including Charlotte Church doing angry electropop – the Flow project is hoping to make an impact at this month’s Cop31

Amid tense and long-winded negotiations, and with the future of the planet at stake, emotions can often run high at Cop climate summits. But last year, when the annual conference arrived in Brazil, one UN official was unexpectedly moved to tears by five women singing about the power of water.

“She gave me a massive hug after the event and said, ‘We need to bring music into Cop,’” says Nikita Llerena, the project manager for Flow, a music collective that’s hoping to bring art to the centre of the climate movement. What started as a handful of musicians meeting over Zoom last year has grown into a full-length album that unites female artists from around the world, including Charlotte Church, Maxine Peake and Nadine Shah. This month, members of the collective will return for Cop31, in Turkey, where they have been promoted to a slot at Global Cultural Action’s opening event.

“We are moving beyond awareness,” says Llerena. “Cop is now starting to realise the importance of art and culture to bring the climate debate forward. We can reach levels of human subjectivity that data alone cannot.”

The album focuses on the common theme of water, and is co-produced by Grammy winner Jennifer Decilveo. The artists have roots in Bangladesh, Canada, the UK, India, Brazil and beyond. Shingai, vocalist and bassist for the pop-rockers Noisettes, draws from her Zimbabwean heritage, singing in Shona about the importance of environmental conservation.

It’s an ambitious project in scale and intent. From heatwaves and wildfires across Europe to devastating flash floods in Nepal, the consequences of rising global temperatures have never felt so urgent. But can art bridge the gap between statistics, lived experience and meaningful political change?

“Music is the most powerful way to help people connect emotionally with what is happening,” says Church. Her song on the album – My Mother, the Ocean – begins as a hypnotic ode to water, developed from a sound-healing piece, before breaking into a distorted, electropop expression of mourning and rage. Amid the all-too-evident effects of global heating, says Church: “There’s an enormous amount of grief, at our separation from the natural world, at what’s being lost, and the fear and existentialism that’s wrapped up in all that. It requires people to feel, and so much of modernity is pushing us away from feeling.”

The album will also soundtrack a documentary that charts the experiences of women on the frontlines of the crisis. Márcia Mura, an Indigenous teacher from the Brazilian Amazon, is one of them. As a child, she could drink water directly from the Madeira River. Now, she says, the area resembles “a state of war”, damaged by severe floods and droughts that were exacerbated by local dams and pollution.

For Mura, a member of the Mura people, the inclusion of Indigenous voices in initiatives such as Flow is crucial. “The Indigenous people in Brazil have a slogan: ‘Nothing about us without us,’” she says, speaking through an interpreter. “It’s very important that we speak for ourselves, especially the women who are protagonists of this struggle.” Her point reflects research by UN Women, which found that women and girls are disproportionately affected by disasters, but it also speaks to Mura women’s spiritual relationship with water. “Women in the Amazon are the defenders of the waters,” she says, and these days, that goes beyond cultural tradition. Mura helped set up the Mura Collective, connecting women from different territories to share resources and defend their local waters. “When we protect the river, we protect our lives.”

Flow ends with a spoken-word piece, written and performed by Peake. It tells the story of a woman who, like Mura, harnesses her ancestral connection to water to protect her local riverbank from corporate development. In her telling, the woman is victorious.

Peake hopes Flow will inspire people to feel less helpless amid climate doomerism – to recognise that they, too, can make an impact. “Even if you don’t spark a revolution, it’s about slowly chipping away,” says Peake. “If enough people throw enough pebbles into the sea, we can cause a tidal wave.”

Flow is released 5 November via EarthSonic. Cop31 takes place 9-20 November

The Joy of Six: Glenn Maxwell’s greatest innings for Australia

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:00:45 GMT

From the miracle of Mumbai, gamechanging centuries and a rare Test ton, here are half a dozen of the Big Show’s most destructive knocks

Glenn Maxwell has bowed out from international cricket, leaving behind a trail of destruction razed by his most blistering innings and unconventional shots. Yet for all the outrageous highlights and gamechanging knocks, the 38-year-old’s legacy is tainted by an unshakeable feeling that he remained an unfulfilled talent.

The Big Show was denied a farewell appearance for Australia when overlooked for their T20 squad to face England this month before bringing the curtain down on his international career. But the three-time World Cup winner already has a long list of show-stopping performances to point to including arguably the greatest ODI knock of all time.

The career-defining performance brought together all the ingredients that made Maxwell one of a kind. Impeccable hand-eye coordination. Inventive stroke play and a 360-degree game. A knack for saving his best for the biggest stages and for when his team needed him most. And brute force made to look like a natural gift but finely crafted behind the scenes.

Maxwell was unbeaten on 22 as Australia slumped to 91 for 7 in pursuit of a 292-run target in a must-win game against Afghanistan at the 2023 ODI World Cup. There was little hint of what was to come with Australia on the brink of an early exit until captain Pat Cummins joined Maxwell at the crease and the all-rounder unleashed a stunning knock to turn the contest on its head. After suffering from cramps that left him barely able to walk and collapsing to the turf with 10 overs still remaining, Maxwell needed fluids and long periods of treatment just to continue batting. With his feet stuck to the crease like they were deep in cement he somehow plundered 201 not out from 128 balls with 21 fours and 10 sixes to lift Australia into the semi-finals and one step closer to what had seemed the most unlikely World Cup triumph.

Maxwell had been out of sorts when he stepped in for the injured Aaron Finch to open the innings in a T20 international for the first time in September 2016. He immediately looked at home at the top of the order with a 65-ball mauling of Sri Lanka in Pallekele. Maxwell set the tone as he dipped into his bag of tricks with a reverse sweep for the first six of the match. He cleared the rope another eight times and added 14 boundaries as he first reached a half-century in 27 balls, then took only 22 more deliveries to bludgeon his maiden T20I ton. Maxwell carried his bat to finish unbeaten on 145, while Australia’s 263 for 3 surpassed Sri Lanka’s record score in a T20I amassed against Kenya, and equalled the then highest total in the T20 format.

Maxwell is one of only six Australians to score a century in all three formats despite only playing seven Tests and none on home turf. The clean-striking powerhouse showed he had gears in his game as he steeled himself for a gritty knock against India in Ranchi in 2017. Maxwell waited until the 56th delivery he faced to hit his first boundary before turning to his more familiar approach to hammer a first – and what would be his only – Test ton with 104 from 185 balls. He played only three more Tests as his red-ball potential remained untapped, while his aggressive counterattacking approach was arguably ahead of its time.

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

Maxwell had shown he had X-factor but was yet to put it all into practice in a starring role until he broke through for a maiden international hundred to light up the SCG. His 51-ball century against Sri Lanka in 2015 was then the quickest by an Australian in men’s ODIs as well as the second-fastest in World Cup history. Maxwell blasted 10 boundaries and four sixes before being dismissed for 102 as – not for the last time – his match-turning knock came in a must-win match for Australia at a World Cup. He was part of the XI that would go on to lift the trophy, before he added two more crowns when hitting the winning runs at the 2021 T20 World Cup and 2023 Cricket World Cup.

Maxwell’s Magnum Opus would come later in the tournament but he first brought his A-game to an Off Broadway clash with the Netherlands at the 2023 World Cup. He made the most of facing a less threatening attack in New Delhi as he blazed his way to a 40-ball century for the quickest at a men’s Cricket World Cup and what remains the fastest for an Australian in all ODIs. Maxwell only faced his first ball midway through the 41st over but still had enough time to punish the Netherlands and raced to an unbeaten 75 by the end of the 48th. He then exploded with 4, 4, 6, 6 off the first four balls of a Bas de Leede over, and brought up his scintillating century with a hook over fine leg from a no-ball full toss.

Maxwell was still riding high from the 2023 World Cup when he hammered a strong West Indies attack in a T20I at Adelaide Oval early the next year. He started slowly but soon stepped through the gears with sixes from switch hits and reverse sweeps as he raced to a half-century from 25 balls. Maxwell matched that pace through the next stretch to bring up his ton from 50 deliveries and finished unbeaten on 120 runs off 55 balls with eight sixes. It was Maxwell’s fifth T20I century to set a record he still holds with Rohit Sharma for the most among all men’s batters, but his unstoppable form would end there in what would be his last ton for Australia.
