‘The output of a lunatic asylum’: what the Bloomsbury group can tell us about mental health

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:52:41 GMT

From Virginia Woolf’s horrifying views on eugenics to James Strachey’s seminal translations of Freud, the Bloomsbury set didn’t only experience mental illness, they shaped how society thinks about it

‘As an experience,” Virginia Woolf wrote in 1930, “madness is terrific and not to be sniffed at … In its lava, I still find most of the things I write about.”

Woolf’s 1941 suicide by drowning in the River Ouse, her pockets weighted with stones, is usually framed as evidence of her tortured genius. But a new exhibition at Charleston in Lewes radically excavates this narrative while challenging ideas about mental illness.

Curator Hazel McMichael describes the Bloomsbury group as a “case study for looking at a mad community”. She explains: “We wanted to look at how aspects of psychiatry and psychoanalysis were echoed in the group’s everyday lives and art.”

Aligning with the “mad pride” movement of the 1990s, the exhibition reclaims the word “mad” as a point of pride and political identity, much like “queer” or “crip”. McMichael’s aim is not to deny the tragedy of Woolf’s suicide, which followed at least two other attempts, but to ask: mad according to who?

Woolf’s mental health issues were not anomalous in her circle, but her treatment – mainly private care at home – meant she could continue working. Meanwhile her peer, the artist Helen Coombe, studied at the Royal Academy and enjoyed early success, but her career dissolved on her admittance to the Retreat, an asylum in York where she spent the last 26 years of her life. Coombe was the wife of the critic and (much lesser) painter Roger Fry. In 1910, Fry curated the seminal exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists at Grafton Galleries, London, which was roundly accused by critics of being “the output of a lunatic asylum”.

Charleston displays paintings from that exhibition alongside rarely seen examples of Coombe’s work, including exquisite designs for stained glass and a drawing of a female Narcissus (a recurring, psychoanalytically informed motif in the show). In 1883, Coombe petitioned the RA to allow women to study partially draped figures. When Vanessa Bell, Woolf’s sister, began her studies there in 1901, she directly benefitted from Coombe’s activism. Bell’s prolific output is the subject of a forthcoming exhibition at Tate Britain, alongside Duncan Grant, her friend, lover and co-owner of Charleston, the Bloomsbury group’s countryside base. You can’t help but think: what might have become of Coombe without institutionalisation?

Photographs of the Retreat show light-filled rooms and displays of patients’ handicrafts. In correspondence with Coombe’s doctor, Fry pushed for the integration of colour and art in the treatment of patients. It’s a far cry from an 1897 image of the crowded women’s dining hall at St Pancras Workhouse, where Bell’s servant Mary Elizabeth Wilson ended up following a period of severe mental disturbance. We know of Wilson because of Bell’s comedic account of her life – “Mad Mary” – which Bell read aloud to the inner echelons of the Bloomsbury group in 1921 at the Memoir Club. Woolf’s diaries also refer to Wilson’s “servant’s hysteria”.

Wilson’s presence adds welcome nuance to the ever popular Bloomsbury story, which often celebrates the group’s revolutionary spirit without acknowledging the privilege that facilitated it: access to “a room of one’s own” and magnificent homes such as Charleston. But Wilson’s story remains secondhand. “Madness is often an invisible phenomenon,” McMichael says, “haunting objects in ways that are difficult to pin down”.

Contemporary responses brilliantly plug these gaps. An installation by the Mad Heritage Collective, a group with experience of mental illness and neurodivergence who co-produced the exhibition, features a text composed of cut-up extracts of Bell’s “Mad Mary” essay. Louisa Fairclough’s sound piece, The World Went Out of Tune With Itself, viscerally recreates the artist’s seven-year experience of psychosis. Discordant electronica made, Fairclough explains, “from within madness”, is layered with notes recalling obsessive, paranoid thought patterns.

While the tortured genius narrative casts Woolf as exceptional, mental illness recurred in her family. Among hundreds of family photos of Woolf’s siblings, only two survive of her half-sister, Laura Stephen. A hazy photograph of a girl, head downturned to obscure her features, evokes a haunting absence when displayed alongside handsome oil paintings of Woolf and other celebrated relations.

Another photograph was taken on Laura’s admittance to Earlswood Asylum in 1893, aged 22. McMichael notes: “Patients were photographed in formal attire, which appeared to dignify them, but the doctors in charge used patient portraits to document facial features for racial classifications.”

Laura was diagnosed with hereditary “imbecility” because her grandmother had attempted suicide. But her Earlswood case notes describe her repeating the words “bed”, “boys” and “family”, suggesting a link to the sexual abuse we know Woolf and Vanessa Bell suffered at the hands of their older half-brothers.

The notion of inherited madness prompted complex conversations among the research groups at Charleston. McMichael notes that while many “found solace in the potential genetic roots of neurodivergence, others wanted to focus on how pathologised ways of thinking, feeling and acting are responses to a maddening world”.

The subject also evokes the Bloomsbury group’s often overlooked history of eugenic attitudes, which the show addresses head-on. The economist John Maynard Keynes, a frequent Charleston guest, was vice-president of the Eugenics Society. “Only healthy seed must be sown!” blares a 1930s Society poster. Woolf wrote horrifyingly in 1915 of encountering an “ineffective shuffling idiotic” group of learning-disabled adults who she declared should “certainly be killed”.

The Bloomsbury group didn’t just experience mental illness, they were at the forefront of changing ideas around it in Britain. Adrian and Karin Stephen, Woolf’s brother and his wife, were prominent psychoanalysts. The Hogarth Press, founded by Woolf and her husband Leonard, published Freud’s Complete Psychological Works under James Strachey’s editorship.

Strachey – a sometime lover of Maynard Keynes – made the consequential decision to use the Latin “ego” and “id” for Freud’s German “das Ich” (I) and “das Ees” (it). This, says McMichael, “transformed self-explanatory language into clinical jargon, shaping the way we think about consciousness.”

The group’s extraordinary output was also impacted by therapeutic encounters. TS Eliot started writing The Waste Land in 1921 following a breakdown, and while undergoing treatment from Roger Vittoz in Lausanne. Diagrams illustrate Vittoz’s technique of “brain control”, which focused on sensory experience, simple repeated movements and exercises. The academic Matthew Gold’s revelatory work argues that the fragmentary, rhythmic echoing in The Waste Land (birdsong is “twit twit jug jug”) were a product of Vittoz’s methods as well as existential dissolution.

Whatever the medical profession has us believe, psychiatric labels reflect social attitudes. Homosexuality, for example, was classed a “mental disorder” for the majority of the 20th century. In keeping with Charleston’s spirit, Mad Bloomsbury leaves space to celebrate transgression from norms. Duncan Grant’s naked Spanish Dancer costume was worn with wig, heels and painted face at a typically fabulous looking Charleston party. Grant’s painted jigsaw of a rosy, spanked bottom also features, alongside tender 1970s portraits of young queer friends Grant found late in life through Brighton’s Gay Liberation Front.

The exhibition’s quieter moments speak to non-medical methods of managing distress. McMichael says: “We talked of how fundamental animals and nature are to being able to function in our day-to-day lives.” Grant’s portraits of beloved pets join Vanessa Bell’s sketches of a woman and her dog, made for the cover of Woolf’s 1933 novel Flush, which was inspired by the spaniel Vita Sackville-West gifted Woolf. The writer’s cross-stitched tapestry handbag nods to Woolf’s comment in a 1912 letter to Leonard: “knitting is the save of life.”

In exploring the Bloomsbury group’s relationships to mental health, the exhibition expands our understanding not only of a fascinating milieu, but of the mind and its diverse workings.

Mad Bloomsbury is at Charleston in Lewes from 4 November to 11 April

British people don’t need to apologise for slavery – but the government does

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:52:30 GMT

Andy Burnham’s intervention is important. Because when it comes to Britain’s role in the transatlantic trade, the collective amnesia is stunning

Departing from his predecessors’ stances, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, surprised us all when he stated he was open to listening to calls for an apology for the UK’s role in centuries of transatlantic enslavement. King Charles is expected to speak with “unflinching honesty” and “sincere sorrow” about the UK’s role in the transatlantic slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda today. Burnham was quick to add that financial reparations were off the table. But he was in favour of discussions about debt restructuring – one of the key concerns of the Caribbean community (Caricom) and the African Union. The opposition, led by Kemi Badenoch, argued that apologies were a distraction.

Beyond political bickering and point-scoring lies a deeper question. Why does Britain struggle to fully understand its colonial past and to grapple with the negative impact of its legacies? One the one hand, the country celebrates its historical conquests as far back as the Battle of Hastings and applauds the wealth that derived from the products of colonisation, such as cotton. On the other, it refuses to accept that harm was caused to populations whose lands it forcefully occupied – and that the trafficking of African captives has changed how we think and what we assume about different racial groups to this day.

The king and the PM clearly understand that Caribbean countries, and the Commonwealth as a whole, are among Britain’s most important relationships. The group of 56 Commonwealth countries represents about a third of the world’s population with more than 2.7 billion people. Because of their historical links to Britain, these countries play an important role in the UK’s global influence and soft power. Refusing to apologise and work together towards a reparatory justice plan is a diplomatic and political mistake. In the long run, it also has a knock-on effect on trading partnerships, as Burnham seems to acknowledge.

The question of repair continues to be framed along the lines of financial compensation. That framing fails to consider how the past is weighing on the present and future of British citizens. Repairing includes building a society that is honest about its traumas and ready to work towards reconciliation. In these times of recession, drawing on existing resources could help address points raised by Caricom and the African Union. For example, the return of cultural heritage could be facilitated by having a discussion in parliament about the British Museum Act 1963 and the National Heritage Act 1983, which prevent the British Museum, Natural History Museum, V&A and Science Museum from permanently returning certain objects from their collections.

A fair reparatory justice plan would help tackle issues such as education, climate justice, health inequality and so on. Perhaps the PM has been paying attention to Caricom’s focus on green energy and climate resilience. His pledge of £40m to Caribbean projects is a very significant step towards mending fences and furthering dialogue on climate justice. Education could also be an important part of the plan precisely because part of the British public doesn’t understand why apologies are required, let alone why taxpayers should pay the bill for financial reparations at a time of national and even global economic recession. Lack of knowledge – of how the trafficking of African captives for more than 300 years helped shape British institutions such as parliament, the Church of England, universities, the banking system, royal societies and so on – has led many to wonder why they should apologise for their ancestors.

Transatlantic enslavement centuries ago relied on the labour of enslaved Africans, and it made Britain very wealthy. The institution of slavery classified populations based on a racist hierarchy. It developed the so-called scientific racism of the 19th century, which led to the 21st-century eugenicists’ stances that still influence current debate about belonging and identity.

Tracie Jolliff, an organisational development consultant who specialises in dismantling systemic racism, puts it like this: “There appears to be a collective amnesia when it comes to harms towards people with black skins as compared to other atrocities that have been well documented. Racism still shapes the way the descendants of those same African people are treated today.”

For Jolliff, the ideas that informed and perpetuated transatlantic enslavement never went away; they simply morphed into more subtle, but still life-limiting structural racism. The evidence and outcomes of that can be seen in the ways that British citizens who are black are disadvantaged in housing, health, education and the criminal justice system. Similarly, Marvin Rees, a former mayor of Bristol who is involved with the Repair Campaign, says, “Individuals today are not responsible for their ancestors’ wrongdoings. It is, however, important to make a link between individuals and institutions. Individuals inherited institutions and institutions bestowed advantages.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Arguments that position reparations as a subject of the distant past are overlooking the facts. UK taxpayers have been paying back the colossal sum that compensated the owners of enslaved people after the Abolition Act 1833 – a bill that was only repaid in full in 2015. It’s not British people who should apologise, but the British government that used taxpayers’ money to compensate those who profited from trading in people.

Because of the legacies of this trade, many descendants of those responsible for transatlantic enslavement are still part of the financial elite of this world. Some of them, like the Heirs of Slavery, are attempting to engage with the question. The UK government should work with families whose ancestors received compensation in 1837 and who are ready to work towards a restorative justice plan – and with institutions such as the Church of England, Lloyd’s of London and universities that have started to do the work. Combining resources is the way forward now.

Black communities who have their life chances negatively affected by systemic racism were also paying the bill for the owners of their ancestors until 2015. So, if the debt to the slavers can endure without question into this century, surely repair for the legacies of ongoing systemic injustices should be dealt with on similar terms.

Olivette Otele is a historian and distinguished research professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London

24-year-old woman dies after collapsing in final stages of New York City Marathon

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:36:08 GMT

Father says Rachel Apa died from rhabdomyolysis

Runner was former college athlete in ‘perfect shape’

A 24-year-old woman died after collapsing during the final stages of Sunday’s New York City Marathon, her father has said.

Rachel Apa’s father, Steve Apa, told the New York Times his daughter was in Central Park, two miles from the end of the race, when she collapsed. It was Rachel’s first marathon and she was running as part of the Parkinson’s Champions team in honor of her late grandfather, who suffered from the disease.

Steve Apa told the Times that his daughter had played field hockey in college and was in “perfect health, perfect shape”.

Rachel, from Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was being cheered on by Steve and her mother, Michelle Apa, on Sunday.

Michelle Apa filmed her daughter smiling at mile 14, but at mile 18 later Rachel texted her father, writing “Ow”. A mile later she texted him: “Ow, ow”. At mile 23, Steve texted “final stretch” to her but she did not reply. She collapsed soon afterwards and was given CPR by a member of the public. Race medical staff then used a defibrillator on Rachel before she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center. Doctors there tried to save her but she died at 9.40pm. Her father told the Times that Rachel had died from rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition that can be brought on by heavy exercise in which muscles break down.

“It’s unfathomable,” Steve Apa said.

Rachel had recently started an MBA program at Charleston Southern University.

“We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday’s race,” the New York Road Runners, who organize the race, said in a statement. “Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner’s family, friends, and the entire running community.”

New York Road Runners said the last time a participant in the race died after a medical incident was in 2024.

‘His voice was too queer – so they silenced him’: how Spain’s national poet Lorca finally became a gay icon

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:15:48 GMT

The significance of the poet and playwright’s homosexuality was repressed in Spain for decades – but a spate of recent work, including the film La Bola Negra, is redressing the balance for a new generation

Patricia Langa parades on to an invisible stage in a basement room of Instituto Cervantes in central London, locked into the character of Conchita, a professional mourner loosely based on the sorrowful heroines of Federico García Lorca’s 1936 play, The House of Bernarda Alba.

“His voice was too loud, too queer, too alive for those around him, filled with jealousy and hatred,” she tells her imagined audience. “So they silenced him.”

Langa (who uses she/they pronouns) is rehearsing her cabaret-cum-drag ode to Lorca, which they will perform as part of the Festival of Queer Spanish Culture, taking place in London this November. Combining flamenco, lip-sync and poetry, the show imagines a funeral for the poet and playwright, 90 years since he was killed by Franco’s nationalist regime. His body was never found.

The performance feeds into a growing embrace of Lorca among Spain’s LGBTQ+ community. From viral Booktoks, drag memorials, documentaries, book clubs and, most recently, the Oscar-tipped film La Bola Negra, the Andalucían poet has emerged as an increasingly important queer icon in Spain.

For Langa, studying Lorca’s work through a queer lens has led to a deeper, more personal, connection with it. “He went out there and told stories that are not typical,” she says. His first play, The Butterfly’s Evil Spell, about the forbidden love between a cockroach and a butterfly, serves as one example. “A lot of his work is about being different. There is something quite magical about understanding these little tricks that he used to share something that maybe he publicly didn’t feel he was able to.”

Born near Granada in 1898, Lorca rose to be one of Spain’s greatest writers in his lifetime. Although there was speculation about his homosexuality, allegedly a factor in his murder, Lorca was never openly gay. Homosexuality was violently oppressed during the Franco regime, and Spain was one of the last western countries to decriminalise same-sex relations – sentences for which were only cleared in 2001.

In the decades after Lorca’s death, any mention of Lorca’s queerness was hushed by his family and Spain’s literary circles – academics and writers who feared being denied access to the family’s archives and university resources, would pussyfoot around the topic as a result.

“If you went around saying that Lorca was gay, the door was shut,” says Ian Gibson, one of Spain’s most respected Lorca biographers. Gibson refers to a biography written by Lorca’s brother, Francisco, published posthumously in 1980, as an example. “In that book the word homosexual doesn’t appear. There is no allusion to his sexuality.” Gibson’s own groundbreaking biography of Lorca came out in 1985 to critical acclaim. “I put homosexuality in the centre of the picture,” he says, “and that was the end of my relationship with the family.”

Gibson’s subsequent 2009 book, Lorca y el Mundo Gay, delved deeper into the poet’s sexuality and has been a key resource for readers looking to uncover more about Lorca’s queerness. In Berkana, a queer bookshop in Madrid’s gay Chueca district, copies of a pink-tinted reissue of the book from 2026 line the window display. “In Spain, we didn’t speak about his sexuality for many years,” says the bookseller, who says that the popularity of La Bola Negra, Spain’s highest grossing film of the year, has led to a rise in demand for Lorca-related work. La Piedra Oscura, the play by Alberto Conejero on which the film is based, has become an unlikely bestseller.

An Irishman who moved to Spain in the 1960s in pursuit of studying Lorca – and subsequently became a citizen – Gibson is honoured in La Bola Negra through the character played by Glenn Close. True to accounts of the film, his interest in conveying the truth around Lorca’s sexuality stems from his own personal circumstance: his brother, Alan, was gay, and died in a psychiatric clinic after a lifetime of trauma growing up in a puritanical methodist family in a wider closeted Irish society.

“[My brother] has influenced my life at a very profound level and obviously is the basis for my fascination with Lorca,” says Gibson, who is 87, over a cocido Madrileño stew in Lavapiés, his longtime home. “I don’t think it’s the least bit strange that Lorca is now a gay icon, I think he should be. And they’ll tell you across the right that he’s apolitical, but that’s bullshit.”

Recently, Lorca’s queerness has also entered the Spanish political arena. Encouraged directly by Gibson, Spain’s incumbent leftwing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has appropriated Lorca’s ideals as part of his current political campaign, in the run-up to a tense snap election that will take place this November.

At a campaign speech in Granada on 24 October, Sánchez referred to the success of La Bola Negra, before reciting one of Lorca’s poems. “This is the Spain of Lorca, the Spain that embraces the diverse and different,” he said, addressing the crowd in a white shirt with the slogan La Fuerza del Amor (The Force of Love). Sanchéz faces tough competition from a unified right, with both the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox having campaigned to roll back LGBTQ+ rights across the country.

The past 40 years have seen Spain reckon with much of the horror inflicted by Franco on the LGBTQ+ community, moving to become one of the most progressive countries on gay rights. (It was the third country in the world to legalise same-sex marriage in 2005.) However, the current rise in far-right homophobic attitudes has sent shock waves through Spain’s gay community, which fears a regression to Francoist attitudes.

Lorca’s sexuality has become increasingly significant in this current political climate – a point that La Bola Negra confronts directly, addressing the damaging consequences of the intergenerational trauma imprinted on Spain’s queer community as a consequence of silence and shame.

Its star, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, more widely known as Guitarricadelafuente, wished the film had been released when he was young. “Growing up in Spain there weren’t many references,” says the gay musician. “Lorca’s desire was so profoundly linked to his art, it can’t be separated. It was something that we didn’t learn in school.”

Set across three different timelines, inspired by Lorca’s life and work, La Bola Negra focuses on Lorca’s intimate relationship with Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, and his unfinished play La Bola Negra – his only work with an explicitly gay protagonist. Meanwhile, La Nieve – the original song Lafuente wrote for La Bola Negra, which reached the Top 10 of the Spanish charts – takes cues from Lorca’s Sonnets of Dark Love, which is thought to be dedicated, at least in part, to Rapún.

La Nieve is a favourite for the best original song award at next year’s Oscars, and is also the soundtrack to a queer-led viral trend where young Spaniards film themselves at the cinema before watching La Bola Negra and then afterwards in tears.

“What this film can shed a light on, and what moved me when I watched it, is acknowledging those stories that weren’t able to happen, ever. Those impossible stories hidden in the ground,” says Lafuente. “I think this is a testimony of those stories and that it can help people see we cannot go back to that. Even though we think we’ve achieved so much, we cannot take the freedom that we have for granted.”

Langa, who watched the film while visiting her family in Barcelona, was among those in tears – and says the film has reaffirmed her admiration for the poet. “Lorca left us more than his poetry. He left us a way of seeing the world: finding beauty where others see shame, humanity where others see difference, and possibility where others impose limits.”

Patricia Langa performs To Lorca With Amor at The Divine, London, on 21 November. La Bola Negra is in US and Australian cinemas now, and in UK cinemas from 6 November

Shabana Mahmood has barely softened her plans – Britain’s immigration regime is now a theatre of cruelty

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:14:54 GMT

The home secretary’s reforms merely reinforce the lie that migrants are to blame for all of the UK’s problems

Five years ago, Shabana Mahmood called for a “general amnesty” for undocumented migrants. “That’s not official Labour party policy yet,” she mourned, “but myself and a group of other Labour MPs are continuing to make the argument.”

Now home secretary, she is introducing one of Europe’s most punitive immigration and asylum systems. The standard qualifying period for migrant workers to gain secure residence will double to 10 years, which will be twice the length set out in almost all EU countries. The standard wait for refugees who claim asylum in Britain outside designated resettlement routes will be 20 years, four times the usual five-year qualifying period in Germany, Spain and Italy.

But even this is misleading. As the Home Office notes: “There are no visa routes to enable people to claim asylum in the UK from overseas.” As it further adds: “A person must be present in the UK to claim asylum here.” So accessing this punitive process by regular means is in essence impossible.

Mahmood has reopened an exceptionally limited resettlement scheme, with Afghan women and girls and Palestinians expected to account for about a quarter of referrals. The latter is a shamelessly cynical sop to progressive voters infuriated by Labour’s complicity in Israel’s genocide. And previously exceptions have been made for travel to Britain for humanitarian reasons: from Ukraine, Hong Kong and Afghanistan. But if you’re seeking to flee persecution in, say, Iran, Eritrea or Somalia, you cannot legally apply for asylum. Arriving by small boat is your only shot. For those who do and have their asylum claims accepted, a wait of up to 30 years for permanent residency beckons.

Eleven years ago, Mahmood spent three days at a refugee camp in Greece and wrote about her experiences in the New Statesman. “You would run,” she told her readers. “I would run. They are running. We must do our part to help them.”

Bear in mind that Britain receives fewer asylum applications per capita than the EU average. Bear in mind, too, that nearly seven in 10 of the world’s refugee population are hosted by low- and middle-income nations. Remember also the role of Britain in violence that has caused destabilisation and accelerated population movements – such as the wars in Iraq and Libya, the latter of which Mahmood voted for.

Yes, there has been a partial retreat on social care workers, with those who entered the route before May 2025 and meet the relevant conditions able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. But consider how the social care sector has already been plunged into crisis by Britain’s “cut off its nose to spite its face” immigration policies. New international recruits plunged from 105,000 to 30,000 in the space of two years – while the sector has nearly 100,000 vacancies. Mahmood’s concessions will not reverse that crisis.

Here is why these policies are such a travesty. The fundamental breach of trust is a violation of any principles of natural justice. When Mahmood’s Conservative predecessor Theresa May introduced a £35,000 settlement salary threshold in 2012, she exempted migrants who had obtained qualifying work visas before April 2011. Mahmood, on the other hand, is applying the 10-year baseline to many of those already lawfully resident. That’s despite many migrants and their families having made plans around what was promised to them. Half a million people will be hit by this promise-breaking.

What of the rampant classism of someone who earns more than £125,000 qualifying in only three years, while someone below £50,000 normally waits 10? The New Economics Foundation once released research that found that a childcare worker generated up to £9.50 of social value for every pound they were paid; a hospital cleaner created £10; a recycling worker produced £12. A City banker, on the other hand, destroyed £7 of social value for every pound they generated; that was £11 for an advertising executive and £47 for a tax-avoidance accountant. But these exorbitantly paid occupations have a three-year pathway, compared with 10 years for underpaid crucial workers.

Mahmood has at least recognised that nurses, teachers and care workers offer contributions that cannot be captured by salary alone. But why doesn’t this principle apply to other workers?

Then there’s the supposed party of labour undermining the collective bargaining power of workers by keeping them dependent on employer-sponsored visas for a decade. Even the Home Office has admitted that settlement can improve wages because workers have the freedom to change jobs. These plans will damage migrant and British-born workers alike. “This creates downward pressures across sectors as a whole,” the Trades Union Congress notes, “as sponsorship impedes workers’ ability to campaign for better pay and conditions or fight back against poor treatment.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Then there’s requiring migrants to have gone five years without accessing specified state support before qualifying for settlement on the standard route, or face a longer wait – although the exact scope and exemptions are not yet clear. People with disabilities could be punished, while parents may be forced to impose hardship on their children in order to gain permanent residency.

All of this is based on a pernicious lie that both media and political establishments have promoted in Britain: that immigration is responsible for our country’s problems. Not the financial sector, which plunged the country into a disaster from which we have never recovered. Not greedy exploitative bosses not paying their workers properly after the labour movement was permanently hobbled in the 1980s. Not an economic order rigged in favour of Big Finance and assets instead of productive industry, or politicians who won’t build the housing we need. No, it was migrants who became the scapegoat.

Well, now that a hostile environment has well and truly been constructed for migrants, who will the scapegoaters have to blame?

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

The candidates who will decide the US midterm elections

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:46 GMT

The 2026 US midterm elections feature firebrand progressives trying to stake out new territory, moderate Republicans struggling in the shadow of Donald Trump, and a host of scandals that have made races closer than they should be.

These candidates could shape not only power in Washington, but public and political understanding of what works – and wins votes – in different places across the country. Can a Democrat win in red Kansas? Could Texas finally flip away from Republicans? Will abuse allegations or absenteeism tank incumbents? How important is capturing online attention?

And how can Republicans run away from Trump, their party’s leader, and modern architect, as his popularity wanes?

The lessons learned – and the candidates who teach them – will play into the 2028 presidential election and alter the makeup of Congress at a critical time for both parties

Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official on the left of the Democratic party, beat a moderate member of Congress to win the party’s nomination for US Senate in Michigan, in a race clouded by tens of millions in outside spending. He is facing Republican former congressman Mike Rogers in one of the country’s most-watched races. Michigan is a swing state: while the Senate seat they are fighting for has been held by a Democrat for 12 years, the state narrowly backed Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. El-Sayed’s brand of tough talk and the simplicity of his campaign slogan (money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All) have made him a progressive star – and a frequent punching bag on the right, where prominent figures led by the president have leaned into Islamophobia to criticize him.

Republican US Senator from Maine

Susan Collins isn’t new to the US Senate. She has been serving since 1997, and is now seeking a sixth term. A moderate Republican, she is a dying breed in the current Maga-tinged Washington during Trump’s second presidency. Maine is a battleground state: Kamala Harris won the state by a clear margin over Trump in 2024. Now Collins, 73, is trying to hang on to her seat in a race that Democrats have targeted as a key to winning back control of the Senate. She initially faced Graham Platner, a Democrat who dropped out of the race after facing rape allegations. Now, Troy Jackson – a former logger who served in the state legislature – is trying to topple the longtime senator.

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Kansas

Kansas’ US Senate election wasn’t on the national radar as competitive at the start of the year. Why would it be? Kansans have not sent a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. But Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, won a crowded primary and has made the race one to watch this year. While Kansas typically leans right, voters in the state have shown frustration with Republican senator Roger Marshall over inaccessibility and his alignment with Trump, as they struggle to afford fuel and groceries, and grapple with sustained economic instability. Plus, Marshall, who practiced medicine for 25 years, was revealed to have sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them. Enter Hamilton, who frequently calls for bipartisan politics that put Kansans first, even if that means standing up to Trump.

Democratic US senator from Georgia

Ossoff, the youngest US senator at 39, is seeking a second term in what should have been a tight race in Georgia, the southern swing state. Polls are suggesting it will not be a close-run thing. The Democrat’s political glow-up and savvy speaking skills, captured in video clips meant to grab voter attention online, have made his reelection seem all but inevitable – and given rise to near-constant murmurs that he’ll run for president in 2028, with regular comparisons to Barack Obama, in tone and in youthfulness. The pair rallied together in Georgia last week. He has accused his opponent, Mike Collins, a Republican congressman, of being aligned with white supremacists – which Collins has vehemently denied.

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Texas

Could Texas finally flip – and could it be a theological Democrat – who does it? James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker, has been generating buzz – and raising record-breaking sums – in his run for the US Senate. Having fended off the firebrand Democratic congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, he now faces the state’s beleaguered Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, in the general election. With Trump’s backing, Paxton beat incumbent US senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary. The nomination of Paxton – who has faced a host of fraud and misconduct scandals during his time in office – has prompted Republicans to drop tens of millions of dollars to defend a seat they typically win with a clear margin. Talarico, dubbed “Talafreako” by Trump and his allies, has sought to win over independents and Republicans in the red state by appealing to their faith and speaking against corruption in politics.

Republican representative in Ohio

Ohio’s seventh congressional district wouldn’t ordinarily be competitive; Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024. But damaging allegations surrounding Max Miller, the embattled Republican incumbent, have given Democrats hope that they might flip the red seat. The 37-year-old Republican, who worked on Trump’s first presidential campaign, was elected to the seat in 2022. His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who is the daughter of Republican US senator Bernie Moreno, has alleged Miller physically abused her and their daughter, which he denied. Another of Miller’s ex-partners, former Trump press secretary Stephanie Grisham, has also accused Miller of physical abuse. He denied that allegation, too. The claims have featured heavily in ads against Miller in the district. Brian Poindexter, the Democratic challenger, is a union ironworker focused on addressing the cost of living.

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Alaska

Mary Peltola is one of the few prominent Democrats who were deemed to pose a potential threat to incumbent Republican Dan S Sullivan. She entered the race hoping to capitalize on Alaska’s recent independent streak and broad anti-Trump feelings. But in the final stretch, she faced allegations of mistreating staff by using slurs and shoving one aide – which her campaign downplayed, attributing Peltola’s behavior to stress. Her campaign also faced accusations of ballot stacking by recruiting another candidate named Dan J Sullivan to run in the state’s open primary. The New York Times reported that Peltola’s staff worked with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to add another Dan Sullivan to the ballot, thereby drawing votes away from the Republican senator. Peltola has said she knew nothing of the plan. Her campaign also denied recruiting candidates into the race.

Democratic nominee for US Senate in Florida

Marco Rubio’s elevation from the Senate to Trump’s secretary of state in 2025 left an open seat in Florida, which was filled by Republican Ashley Moody. Now, in the race for a full term, Moody faces Angie Nixon – a progressive and democratic socialist – who staged a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. While the Florida race isn’t seen as super competitive, or a likely win for Democrats, the small business owner and state lawmaker has grabbed attention and seen prominent figures on the left, including congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, campaigning for her. Progressives hope that Nixon can make the case that their candidates – and not just moderates – can have broad appeal in red states like Florida. Moody was the state’s attorney general before her appointment to the US Senate.

Republican US senator in South Carolina

Darline Graham had minimal involvement in politics and had never run for or held public office until this year, when she was appointed to the US Senate seat in South Carolina after her brother’s death. Lindsey Graham served the state in Washington, first in the House and then in the Senate, for decades. She decided – after encouragement from Trump – to seek a full term, and won the Republican primary. But Darline Graham’s inexperience, both in office and with policy itself, has come into sharp focus. Voter frustration with political dynasties have also made the race in this typically red state a toss-up, according to polls. Dr Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, is running against Graham after previously making a run for the US House of Representatives in 2022.

Republican US representative in Arizona

Juan Ciscomani, a 44-year-old Latino Republican congressman and former gubernatorial adviser, has faced close races for his US House seat in each election, narrowly beating out his Democrat opponent in 2022 and 2024 in the toss-up sixth congressional district in southern Arizona. Ciscomani, who was born in Sonora, Mexico and raised in Tucson, has sought to distance himself from Trump. His reelection campaign is a test of whether Latinos – some of whom swung toward Trump in 2024 and helped deliver his second term – will stick with the president, or side with Democrats, especially after Trump’s aggressive deportation scheme. JoAnna Mendoza, a US Marine Corps veteran and the Democratic challenger, has emphasized her local roots and called out Ciscomani for largely voting with Trump’s agenda.

Democratic nominee for US House in New Jersey

Rebecca Bennett’s odds of winning this toss-up seat increased when her opponent, the incumbent Republican Tom Kean Jr, disappeared for months from his public office. Kean, 58, was gone for more than three months from his job representing the seventh congressional district. He and his office declined to explain why until he returned, when he told people he had been hospitalized for depression. Before his prolonged absence, Bennett had flown under the radar. As New York Magazine put it: “Tom Kean Jr. needed to vanish to become interesting.” Bennett, a 39-year-old moderate Democrat and former navy helicopter pilot and aircraft commander, hopes to win over voters who are frustrated with Kean’s absence and Trump’s agenda. The district is known for split-ticket voting, whereby voters back candidates from different parties when electing figures to multiple offices in the same election. Bennett, a mother of two, has talked about how affordability concerns affect her household as well, including the cost of childcare.

Midterm elections 2026: how are votes counted and when will we know the results?

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:45 GMT

Everything you need to know about how winners are called, how states count ballots and Trump’s election denialism

US politics live – latest updates

There’s no simple answer as to when US voters will know the results of the midterms.

Elections are managed locally throughout the US, and it’s different in each state. Sometimes, if a race isn’t close, there’s a near-instantaneous sense of who won. In more contested races, it can take many hours, days or even weeks.

This year, all 435 members of the House of Representatives are up for re-election, and 35 Senate seats are up for grabs. The governor’s offices of 36 states are on the ballot, as well as countless other statewide and legislative races. That’s not to mention local councils and school boards.

The lag between voting and knowing results can lead to an information vacuum and uncertainty that partisan actors may exploit to spread lies about stolen elections. Donald Trump, who has denied the results of his 2020 loss and other elections when he hasn’t liked the results, has tried to assert federal control over elections, which the courts have rebuffed. But election officials are on guard for potential interference in election processes this year.

Here’s what you need to know about how votes are tabulated and when we may expect to know the results.

US voters cast ballots in person during early voting or on election day, and many millions also vote by mail. Some states send out mail ballots to all voters, while others have systems in place where a voter can request a mail ballot.

Some states will count ballots sent by mail for days after election day so long as they are postmarked by election day, a practice recently upheld by the US supreme court.

Paper ballots are typically tabulated by machines, with partial hand counts and audits checking those results for accuracy. Results are often uploaded in batches. In some places, mail ballots that arrive on election day are tabulated in advance then released soon after polls close, usually about an hour after closure.

There are also curing periods, where voters who need to provide additional information or verify the accuracy of their signature on a mail ballot have an opportunity to make sure their votes are counted. These ballots often are the last ones tabulated. Tabulation can take longer in places that are more populous or that have rules that allow for broader voting access, like universal mail voting or curing periods. It may also seem like it takes longer in closely watched races, but this is often a factor of the closeness of the race and importance of each ballot.

In 2024, MIT’s Election Data and Science Lab notes, even the slowest-counting states had tabulated a majority of their votes within about eight hours. All but California had counted more than 75% of votes after two days.

Results of a race are not considered final until they are canvassed and certified by local authorities, though winners are often clear well before these final deadlines.

If races fall within a very narrow margin, usually a fraction of a percent, they could trigger an automatic recount under state or local laws. These recounts can substantially delay results. News outlets usually do not call races if they are within the automatic recount margin.

Unlike a presidential year, there is no electoral college in the midterms, so no need to refresh your memory on that element until 2028.

News organizations, most notably the Associated Press, predict a winner based on early, unofficial results. These race calls do not impede official election processes – ballots will still all be counted and certified, even if winners are called well before all ballots are counted.

Candidates often wait for a race call by the AP and other organizations before declaring victory. In some instances, if races are closer or if they don’t trust results, candidates may not concede after a media race call.

The AP has said it doesn’t call races unless it is “highly confident of the outcome”. Its research team analyzes local rules and procedures, past races and ballot return patterns. Some of these race calls come soon after results roll in, usually in races that are in strongly partisan districts or without meaningful opposition.

In 2024, the presidential race was called by the early morning hours of the next day. But, the MIT Election Data and Science Lab notes, the last US House race in 2024 wasn’t called until 3 December.

As more ballots are counted, a candidate may gain or lose the lead in any given race. This is a function of ballots being counted, not some sort of nefariousness.

Trump and his allies have at various points claimed, without evidence, that elections officials have “found” ballots or injected fake votes into the tabulation process during overnight hours to flip winners.

These flips are sometimes called a “red mirage” or “blue shift” – a Republican candidate leads initially, then loses the lead. Mail voting patterns, which can impact lead-shifting as votes are counted, are not the same in each place, and in recent years, they have changed based on perceptions of whether mail voting is safe and accurate.

Republican voters have increasingly distrusted election results, led by Trump and his rampant election denialism.

This year, Democratic and independent voters have expressed fears that Trump could interfere with election processes, tabulation or certification. When Trump tried to pressure elections officials to overturn results in 2020, he was unsuccessful – now, though, there are more Trump loyalists in positions of power than in 2020.

Elections officials across the country have maintained that there are enough checks and balances in place to prevent efforts to overturn results, seize ballots or otherwise interfere with elections. Courts have routinely stopped these efforts in the past.

Midterm elections 2026: what time do the polls close today?

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:00:45 GMT

Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when polls close around the US, and some of the key races taking place

US politics live – latest updates

In the 2026 US midterm cycle, there are 35 Senate seats up for election, 36 governors’ races and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives up for grabs. There are also several ballot measures across the country on issues ranging from election administration to abortion access.

Democrats are looking to reclaim control of both chambers of Congress. They’ll need to gain four seats in the Senate to secure a 51-seat majority, and win at least 218 seats to take back the House.

Republicans are fighting hard to maintain their bicameral majority despite mounting national headwinds. They’re contending with a number of unpopular Trump administration policies: an affordability crisis stemming from the Iran war; a deadly immigration crackdown that has seen two American citizens killed by federal agents; a sweeping trade war; and Donald Trump’s own record-low polling.

Already, more than 56 million Americans have cast their early ballots, with millions more expected to vote on 3 November. Here’s an hour-by-hour rundown of when the polls close, and a look at some of the key races we’re watching in each state.

The majority of polls in Indiana and Kentucky will close at this time. But because parts of both states are also in the central time zone, some polling places will remain open until 7pm ET.

The next round of poll closings comes in most of Florida, Georgia, most of New Hampshire, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia.

We’re keeping a close eye on Senate races in several of these states. In Florida, progressive Democrat Angie Nixon is hoping to pull off an upset and unseat Republican incumbent Ashley Moody in one of two special elections this cycle.

Meanwhile in Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democrat senator in his first term, is fending off a challenge from the Trump-endorsed congressman Mike Collins.

In South Carolina, Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, is seeking a full term after being appointed by the state’s governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term after his death in July. She faces pediatrician and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews.

And in New Hampshire, Republicans are eyeing an opportunity to flip an open Senate seat, with former GOP senator John Sununu challenging congressman Chris Pappas in a race that has become increasingly concerning for Democrats in the campaign’s final stretch.

The remaining polling places open in Indiana and Kentucky will also close at 7pm ET.

North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia will all close their polls at 7.30pm ET.

In North Carolina, the open Senate seat is a key pickup opportunity for Democrats, with the state’s former governor, Roy Cooper, facing off against Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee.

And in Ohio, we’ll have the second special Senate election of the 2026 midterms, with former Senator Sherrod Brown seeking a comeback after losing his 2024 race. Brown is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a contest centered in part on the fight over data centers in the state.

We’ll see a flood of poll closings at 8pm ET. These include Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, DC, Illinois, most of Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, most of Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, most of North Dakota, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, most of South Dakota, Tennessee and most of Texas.

A number of marquee Senate races fall into this wave, including the battle for Michigan’s open Senate seat between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican congressman Mike Rogers. Holding the Great Lakes state is vital for Democrats, but the race is expected to be close. El-Sayed is leading in many of the recent polls, but is still within the margin of error.

In Maine, we’ll be watching to see whether progressive Troy Jackson can unseat five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.

And in Texas, Democrats are betting on James Talarico, the state lawmaker who has surged in the polls, to defeat Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican attorney general. A Democratic victory would mark the party’s first statewide win in more than 30 years.

Finally, Kansas has emerged as a late-breaking battleground, with Adam Hamilton seeking to unseat Republican Roger Marshall and become the state’s first Democratic senator in nearly a century.

There are also several competitive down-ballot House races in Michigan, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, where Democrats are hoping to flip swing seats won by Republicans in 2024.

At 8.30pm ET, Arkansas’ polls will close.

In Arizona, there are several competitive contests, including the race for the sixth congressional district, where Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani faces Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a former US marine.

The state’s race for governor is also one we’re watching. Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs is seeking a second term, but first must beat congressman Andy Biggs, who won the president’s endorsement in the Republican primary.

In Iowa, the neck-and-neck race for the open Senate seat pits Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson against Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek.

The Hawkeye state’s gubernatorial race is also shaping up to be competitive, with Democratic state auditor Rob Sand facing Republican nominee Zach Lahn.

At 9pm ET, polls will also close in Louisiana, Colorado, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Any remaining polling places in North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas will close at this time as well.

At 10pm ET, we’ll see almost all polls close in Idaho, Montana, Nevada and Utah.

One of the more under-the-radar gubernatorial races we’re watching is in Nevada, where Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford is hoping to unseat Republican governor Joe Lombardo in the Sun Belt battleground that Trump won in 2024.

Many polling places in one Oregon county will also close at 10pm ET.

At 11pm ET, we’ll see polls close in California, where former health secretary Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, is facing Republican Steve Hilton, a former adviser to British prime minister David Cameron, in the race for governor.

Most polls will also close in Oregon, along with all polls in Washington state.

In Washington, two-term Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who has frequently broken with her party on key issues, is hoping to hold on to her seat in a district that Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections.

Closing out the night will be Alaska and Hawaii, where most polling places will wrap up voting by midnight ET.

Alaska is also one of Democrats’ key pickup opportunities. Former congresswoman Mary Peltola has led Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan in recent polls as frustration with the Trump administration has grown and voters contend with soaring energy prices in the wake of the Iran war.

The race has drawn scrutiny from the Trump administration and the president himself, who have accused Peltola and Democrats of recruiting a namesake candidate to siphon votes from Sullivan. The justice department even sought to delay certification if the Trump-backed Sullivan lost, though a federal judge recently rejected that effort. Peltola’s campaign denied recruiting Dan J Sullivan, but a recent New York Times report suggested otherwise.

Champagne, cocaine and some very long walks: when pedestrianism ruled the sporting world

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:30:43 GMT

Crowds once flocked to see ambling athletes pull off amazing feats of stamina. Edward Payson Weston was chief among them

More than $1.4bn has been staked on prediction markets for this week’s US midterm elections, according to CNN.

Though a lot of people are about to win – or lose – a lot of money, it’s hard to imagine any wagers as consequential as the election bet that birthed a sporting craze spearheaded by a chancer who walked and talked his way into becoming one of the greatest athletic stars of the 19th century.

Before ultrarunning, there was ultrawalking: pedestrianism. The Victorian-era fad started in the US with laddish banter that got out of hand. A 21-year-old door-to-door bookseller named Edward Payson Weston made a wager with a friend that if Abraham Lincoln were elected president in 1860, Weston would walk 478 miles from the Massachusetts state capitol in Boston to the US Capitol in Washington. In less than 10 days.

“It was simply a banter between ourselves while dining together one day, and I do not suppose that either of us at that time had the remotest idea of ever attempting such a task,” Weston wrote in his 1862 account, The Pedestrian’s Adventures.

Born in Providence, Rhode Island, Weston was sacked from his job with a traveling circus because he was unable to perform as he recovered from being struck by lightning. He then worked as a copy boy for the New York Herald and discovered he had “great locomotive powers” while rushing across Manhattan. A slim 5ft 7in, he had average speed but exceptional stamina. The New York Times would later describe his “elastic, swinging stride and legs that never seemed to tire”.

Lincoln won the presidential election on 6 November 1860. On Christmas Day, Weston decided to stick to his word. Seeking to monetize his side hustle (as he put it, “I bethought myself to devise some means to defray my expenses”), he assembled a support team to accompany him in a horse-drawn carriage and secured sponsors who would pay him to deliver circulars to homes he passed on his route.

He set off on 22 February. His media blitz seemed to have backfired when he arrived in front of a crowd at the Massachusetts state house to start his walk to Washington: he was accosted by a constable who arrested him for an unpaid debt.

After negotiating his way out of trouble, Weston arrived in Washington on 4 March, narrowly missing his 10-day goal by a few hours after taking a wrong turn. That night he attended Lincoln’s inauguration ball. A couple of days later a member of Congress introduced him to the president, “who seemed much surprised that he should possess such great powers of endurance” and offered to pay his fare home. (Weston refused, insisting he would walk back.)

So began the long career of a man dubbed the “Wily Wobbler” for his distinctive gait, albeit that it was soon interrupted by the civil war. Weston put his ability to traverse great distances to use as a Union spy and dispatch-bearer. After the war, thanks in large part to Weston’s feats and celebrity status, pedestrianism became one of the most popular spectator sports of the remainder of the 19th century, with grueling, torturous events held in venues including Madison Square Garden in New York and the Oval in London.

The phenomenon has unsurprisingly captured the attention of several chroniclers, including Nick Harris, Helen Harris and Paul Marshall, who wrote a biography of Weston, A Man in a Hurry, in 2012. The history of pedestrianism teems with bizarre incidents and exceptional athletic achievements. Its culture presaged today’s commercialized, hype-driven and detail-obsessed sporting landscape.

This year is the 150th anniversary of Weston’s first British tour, which stoked transatlantic rivalries. A report in the Times in December 1876 describes Weston seeking to walk 505 miles in six days in a contest that started at midnight and was billed as Weston “against the world”. Three Englishmen were hired as pacers “to give a certain amount of zest to the affair”, each walking for 48 hours and incentivized with rewards of up to £60 (the equivalent today of £6,250, or $8,400). The newspaper reported Weston’s early split times down to the second: “Ten miles, 1h.53min. 50sec. ; 20 miles, 3h. 50min. 50 sec.” and so on. Even his pit stop was timed precisely: “Weston made but one stoppage, of 18min, 10sec, during which time his head and feet were bathed.”

Another report describes Weston consuming beef tea and gruel during a walk of 55 miles in 12 hours around Trent Bridge cricket ground in Nottingham. Ever the showman, he walked backwards for half a mile and “[accompanied] the band for a time on his cornet”.

Weston treated pain by dousing his feet with whiskey and lashed his legs with a riding whip until he bled as he tried to stay awake during an 1870 attempt to walk 112 miles in 24 hours. His body was a source of fascination to early sports scientists as he seemingly pushed the limits of human endurance. During a walk in Britain in 1884, doctors examined his pulse and breathing rates, tracked his food and drink intake and took samples of his urine and feces. Weston was even at the center of a debate over performance-enhancing drugs after it emerged that he chewed coca leaves during one race, thereby ingesting traces of cocaine. Some walkers experimented with other actual or presumed stimulants, including champagne. But Weston abstained from alcohol before and during races, making him a role model for the temperance movement.

What pedestrianism lacked was a governing body. While one of its legacies is Olympic race walking, introduced as a standalone event for men at the 1908 London Games, the International Olympic Committee was not founded until 1894. Hucksters and opportunists including PT Barnum filled the void by staging and marketing races and settling rules.

Events were often highly lucrative. The leading British promoter, Sir John Dugdale Astley, an MP and retired lieutenant colonel, inaugurated a “world championship” in 1878 with a prize for whoever could walk the farthest over six days. The winner received the Astley Belt and £500, the equivalent today of £54,000 or $72,000 in 2026. The first was won by Weston’s great rival, an Irish-American, Daniel O’Leary, who walked 520 miles around a track at the Agricultural Hall in Islington, north London (now the Business Design Centre).

As recounted in a New York Times article from 1879, a British walker who traveled to the US, Henry “Blower” Brown, gloomily watched a crowd of 3,000 hail Weston at Madison Square Garden and accused the American of deviously dissuading him from entering a money-spinning race. “[Brown] is short and stout, and has the face of the English prize-fighter,” the writer observed. “He sat in his box last night and drank lager, staring at the great throng which had assembled to greet his rival.” The article adds: “The Times reporter attempted to talk with him, but found that he had no ideas worth communicating to the public. ‘Blower’ Brown is a walker, and nothing else. His talents lie entirely in his legs.”

The surge in betting on sports and politics in the present-day US is throwing up a range of legal and ethical concerns that echo the challenges faced by pedestrianism, which was hugely attractive to gamblers but vulnerable to race-fixing. As the author Matthew Algeo pointed out to NPR, there were many ways to manipulate contests given that spectators could wager on a variety of outcomes within races, such as who would be the first walker to drop out or the first to reach 100 miles.

During one high-profile, high-stakes walk around a Bradford pub in 1864, a leading British female pedestrian, Emma Sharp, walked 1,000 miles in 1,000 hours. As she approached her target, gamblers who had bet against her reportedly tried to scupper her attempt in various ways, from trying to trip her up to hurling burning embers at her feet and attacking her with chloroform. In response she was said to have armed herself with a pistol that she used to fire warning shots.

Pedestrianism declined in the 1890s as it fell victim to shorter and more watchable pastimes, such as bicycling and baseball. But the closing years of Weston’s life were no less colorful than his youth. In 1909, on his 70th birthday, he embarked on a walk from New York to San Francisco, aiming to complete the challenge in just 100 days. The public interest was so great that he chronicled his exploits in a series of dispatches for the New York Times, and schoolchildren were let out early to cheer him on. He arrived a little later than planned, having covered 3,895 miles in 104 active days (122 days including rest periods).

Weston remained remarkably vigorous into his mid-80s. In 1924, aged 85, he was reported to have fought off intruders who shot him in the leg at his home on a farm near the Hudson River in New York state. Despite all the rewards and endorsements he collected during his career – including a Weston sock brand – the New York Times reported that, towards the end of his life, he was living off a $150-a-month trust fund and had long ago separated from his wife. His demise was poignantly cruel: he was left wheelchair- and ultimately bed-bound after being struck by a taxi in Manhattan while walking to church in 1927 and died two years later at 90.

From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 08:00:42 GMT

Around the world, virtues such as compassion and kindness are gathering dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted church

Towards the end of the summer, the Tory-Reform defector Robert Jenrick authored an op-ed piece for the Daily Telegraph about the seemingly impossible economics of rising benefits bills because of mental ill-health. In his capacity as Reform’s Treasury spokesman, his task was to big up its plans to cut 25% of so-called welfare spending by 2030, and thereby tackle what he called the state’s “suicidal empathy”.

Straight away, I wondered where this most opportunistic politician had borrowed that phrase from, and instantly found out: a book with the same title, published this year by the Canadian academic Gad Saad, whom the dust jacket describes as having particular expertise in “the use of evolutionary psychology in marketing and consumer behaviour”. It comes with an endorsement from Elon Musk. “Western civilisation is doomed unless the core weakness of suicidal empathy is recognised and actions are taken that are hard but necessary for survival,” says the world’s richest man. “All of Gad’s books, including this one, are great.”

Unfortunately, Suicidal Empathy is not great. It is, in fact, a baggy mess, glueing together absurd straw men (“suicidal empathy can cause people to care more about rapists and other felons than their victims”) to familiar arguments about immigration, Covid lockdowns and whether the word “imbecile” is offensive. One of its most head-turning claims is that the west’s supposed embrace of degenerate woke-ism is largely traceable to the fact that “women are much more likely to succumb to such emotional and ideological capture”. At a push, its most useful function is as a meandering guide to the soup of ideas simmering in the minds of hardcore Maga voters as they prepared for this week’s midterms.

There is a huge amount of this stuff around, crystallising the philosophical core of Trumpism and its adherent movements across the world – roughly, the idea that might is right and compassion is for wimps. We are now well beyond the culture wars and the US right’s long history of (to put it politely) Christian revisionism, and into the very serious prospect of a decisive western moral counter-revolution that may already be under way. That’s certainly the intention of the slew of voices responsible for podcasts, social media posts and other Maga potboilers – witness 2024’s Toxic Empathy: How Progressives Exploit Christian Compassion, by the Christian podcaster Allie Beth Stuckey, or last year’s The Sin of Empathy: Compassion and its Counterfeits, by the rightwing pastor Joe Rigney.

But here’s the crucial thing: the same moral push is also supported by alarming numbers of regular people. According to polling by the Public Religion Research Institute, while 84% of registered US Democrats support the proposition that empathy helps build a healthy society, only 54% of Republicans agree. Perhaps most strikingly, to quote from the survey’s accompanying blurb: “White evangelical Protestants are the only religious group in which a majority does not agree that empathy is a foundational moral value (42%). Instead, a majority (54%) say empathy can be dangerous.”

Much the same seems to be true of that possible Trump successor, JD Vance – a Catholic convert who now has the rare distinction of having locked horns with two popes. In April, Leo XIV plainly decried the US’s attacks on Iran, insisting: “Anyone who is a disciple of Christ, the Prince of Peace, is never on the side of those who once wielded the sword and today drop bombs.” Vance’s response? “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology.” Only a few months before, the vice-president insisted his “old-school” notion of Christian compassion descended in priority from “your family”, “your neighbor” and “your community” to “your fellow citizens in your own country”. Then and only then, he said, could you “focus [sic] and prioritize the rest of the world”.

Soon after, our era’s most pre-eminent moral philosopher was interviewed by the podcaster Joe Rogan. “The fundamental weakness of western civilisation,” said Musk, “is empathy, the empathy exploit.” Progressives, he said, have set themselves on “exploiting a bug in western civilisation, which is the empathy response”.

At that point, I went straight back to one of my favourite modern books: the classicist and historian Tom Holland’s bestseller Dominion, that brilliant history of Christianity and its global impact that illuminates how an emphasis on what we now call empathy (the word was only created in 1908, as the English translation of the German “Einfühlung”, or “in-feeling”) was one of that religion’s philosophical revolutions.

“Across the Roman world,” Holland writes, “wailing at the sides of roads or on rubbish tips, babies abandoned by their parents were a common sight.” Such everyday barbarism was also reflected in official attitudes to poor, disabled and infirm people – until a moral up-ending began with Rome’s conversion to Christianity under Constantine. As Holland writes: “Every week in churches across the Roman world, collections for orphans and widows, for the imprisoned, and the shipwrecked and the sick had been raised … Entire systems of social security had begun to emerge.” But there was an additional element of this sea change – which, in a modern context, stands in sharp contrast to everything from ICE detention camps to Musk’s vandalism of USAID and the 700,000 deaths it is reckoned to have already caused. As Holland puts it, “divine love for the outcast and derelict demanded that mortals love them too”.

No one would claim Christian countries and institutions stuck to those ideas in the centuries that followed, but the modern US is surely now moral light years away. And there is a British story here, too, bound up with the changes brought to our politics by Margaret Thatcher – who was raised as a strict Methodist, and occasionally blurted out quite remarkable opinions about Christian teaching and questions of morality: in January 1980, for example, she claimed that “no one would remember the Good Samaritan if he’d only had good intentions; he had money as well”.

In this and so many other respects, she was way ahead of her time, opening the path to the kind of moral contortions we hear not just from Jenrick, but both his new comrades in Reform and his former Tory colleagues. Some have gone even further: let migrants drown, they say, while others accuse the lifeboat service – the lifeboat service! – of complicity in a supposed invasion of untouchables, barely pausing for breath before they mourn the decline of “Judeo-Christian culture”. In the States, a proper Republican drubbing on Tuesday might give the anti-empaths the kind of shock they deserve, but Musk’s power and influence alone shows that it will take a lot more than a single round of election results to really push them back. Meanwhile, all over the world, compassion, kindness and other such virtues gather a thick layer of dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted church.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist
