‘I perfected deception’: My secret life as a relapsed alcoholic

The Guardian Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:00:38 GMT

Everyone knew about my years of addiction, the dangers I had put myself in. The second time around, after 11 years sober, not even my husband knew

I am finding it very hard to write about my return to drinking. This is unexpected, given that I spent more than 10 years identifying as an alcoholic and narrating, from the podiums of church basements, the most shameful and unflattering moments of my life. The story of how you initially fell into addiction is comparatively easy to tell, because it’s widely understood that nobody chooses to become an addict, that it’s something that sneaks up on you and takes hold gradually, usually when you are too young to know better, and that quitting is an uphill battle against denial and the difficult work of coming to admit to yourself that there is a problem.

It’s much harder to tell the story of how you convinced yourself to return to a habit that you had already pushed to its limit, a habit from which you’d been free for more than a decade.

I was not under the delusion that my drinking was contextual, that my 20s had been a particularly dark time, and that things would be different in my late 30s. People had suggested this over the years – people who were not addicts themselves and who saw a commitment to lifelong abstinence as a rather extreme response to the ordinary rough patches that people experience, especially in their youth, especially when there has been a disruptive life event, like the loss of my Christian faith.

People who are not addicts seem to put a lot of stock in context, perhaps because their own drinking fluctuates according to the ups and downs of life, and because they experience alcohol as a wave of relaxation or mild euphoria that softens the world’s rough edges, not as a bolt of religious rapture that makes you want to sell all your possessions and hole up in a cave with your one precious pearl, which is how it is for those of us who were born with this disease.

So how did I convince myself to return to drinking? For a long time, I did not even understand that there was an argument taking place. There was only the hypothetical, the mental game I played to pass the time, the idle fantasies. Each bar I passed became part of the game. It got a silent vote of yes or no, depending on whether I could see myself drinking there or not. I decided I could not sit at a bar – it had to be a table. And I could not order the drink, which is to say that I could not audibly request it. This was something I only understood the first time I allowed myself to imagine the scenario in detail. I could not say the words aloud. I could not hear myself say them. It could only happen if there was a deli case next to the register, or, as I’d once glimpsed, rushing through an unfamiliar airport to make a connecting flight, self-serve taps where you could pay at an automated station.

At some point, these hypotheticals bled into planning, but the threshold between those two mental states was so subtle I did not recognise it until I’d passed over. And even then, I failed to see it as a real threat. The hypothetical was a firmly contained grammatical structure, one that was relegated to the mind, which is, as everyone knows, unreal.

Wasn’t this what I’d come to believe? I’d recently published a book about AI and human consciousness and had spent that year speaking on panels with people who insisted that our minds were fundamentally computational and determined, conclusions that were not so different, on their surface, from the meditation lectures I’d been listening to about the illusory nature of the self. It occurred to me that the whole notion of “sobriety” was a narrative construct I’d been imbuing for years with reality and substance, as though it were a concrete facet of my identity, as though there were a “self” to be sober.

This line of thinking, I can see now, rested on a crucial (and perhaps deliberate) misapprehension of these teachings. The point of recognising the “unreality” of thoughts was to avoid getting caught up in their seductive logic. I had drawn from the lectures the inverse conclusion: that if my thoughts were not real, then they could not possibly hurt me or have any effect on the real world. And if selfhood was just a story, then I could tell that story however I liked.

I was in Helsinki for work that December – a month that is, at that latitude, almost entirely swallowed by darkness. It was 15 below zero most mornings, and my eyes watered so constantly from the cold that I now remember the city as a blur of light: candles flickering in the windows of oyster bars, the green pulse of mastheads gliding into the harbour. In the mornings, magnificent plumes of pink smoke billowed out of chimneys, and during the slender hours of daylight, all the buildings were cast in a rose-coloured light that seemed to belong to both dawn and dusk. The Christmas market was set up in the middle of town, and many of the tents sold cups of glögi, the traditional mulled wine, in large metal vats.

I was doing some shopping on my last night, wandering from booth to booth, encased in my parka, looking at the wooden nativities, the long taper candles, the meat pastries. Some of the tents offered glögi in both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties. I was very cold. I reached for my wallet, approached one of the vendors and ordered a glass of the non-alcoholic kind. The woman behind the table did not hear me, or did not understand my pronunciation. “Which one?” she asked in English. She picked up the small chalkboard sign on which the two alternatives were listed, and when I pointed, I found my finger gravitating, without hesitation, towards the other option. It was a split-second decision, a reckless act.

That’s how it felt as I paid for the drink and took it, my heart pounding.

I told myself it was a misunderstanding. I walked towards the bin to throw it away, but before I did, I took off the lid and drank half of it, maybe more. Then I left the market and walked two blocks to a restaurant. It was there, at the entrance to the restaurant, that I felt it, though it was not euphoria or religious rapture. It wasn’t even pleasant. I felt blurry and slightly confused. I ate, and the fogginess subsided, then turned into an awful depression.

I walked back to the hotel in the cold, consumed with a Sunday-evening emptiness that I had not felt in years. It would go away if I drank more, I thought. But the strangest thing was that I did not want more. I felt precisely the way I’d heard “normal” drinkers describe feeling after a single drink: tired, sedated, eager to reclaim their clarity of mind with a coffee or a glass of water. Eleven years had passed. All my cells had since replaced themselves. Maybe it was in fact unreasonable to think I would respond the way I had in my 20s, when I was lost and miserable. I had lived for 11 years in fear of that supposed inevitability, which some part of me must have known was not the truth, but one of the many necessary fictions on which I’d built my new life.

I did not plan to drink again after that night. I had no desire to do so, and I had given up looking for the deli kiosks and self-serve taps at airports. But then, quite suddenly, a new loophole appeared, one that fate itself supplied: QR codes. Seemingly overnight, they were bolted to every table and printed on the backs of menus, initiating the miracle of contactless service that allowed you to order without speaking your sin aloud.

I was flying out of Nashville one morning, a brilliantly sunny February day that felt like spring. I’d arrived at the airport three hours before my flight and found myself, immediately after passing security, at a restaurant with QR codes on the table. A seating area below some skylights. Pop music from the previous decade over the speakers. I sat at the table and ordered a burger and a glass of white wine. The first one went straight to my head. I ordered a second before my food arrived. That was when it happened. Then or just after I’d started the third.

When I tell this story at meetings, I don’t linger on this moment, but instead flash forward several hours to the layover at O’Hare, where I switched to vodka and ended up on my knees in the women’s bathroom, vomiting into a toilet that kept flushing automatically because my head was triggering the sensor. In meetings, I talk about how I almost missed my connecting flight, and I recall the waves of shame, relief and disappointment I felt later that night, when my husband picked me up from the airport and it became clear that he did not suspect anything.

I do not talk about that moment in Nashville, finishing my second or beginning my third, when I noticed for the first time the late-morning light that fell from the skylights, purely and simply, on to the surface of my table; the warmth that came down and lifted me out of my life, out of time, and placed me in a chamber where I could see everything from a position of cosmic indifference, a perspective that captures how life must look from the vantage of eternity, where it’s possible to see how the totality of a person’s temptations, digressions and errors contribute to the compositional beauty that makes up a life. I thought about all the rules I’d made and almost laughed at how silly and stupid they were, how they belonged to the fearful, small-minded part of myself who was deluded about what really mattered, and for whom I felt enormous compassion, the way you do for a child, because even the delusions were beautiful and belonged to the expansive order of the composition.

I do not talk about this moment at meetings because I would be guilty of romanticising and elevating an act of reckless self-destruction – and also, more importantly, because words are but resounding gongs and clanging cymbals, because it is impossible to describe in language that singularity where time dissolves, and all utterance fades into light, and which entirely consumed me that morning as I sat alone, dumbstruck in the winter sunlight, wondering how on earth I had ever consented to give this up.

The following nine months were, objectively speaking, the most boring period of my entire history with alcohol. They were also the purest and most perfect. There was nothing standing between myself and the bottomless freefall of bliss. I was not trying to prove anything. I was no longer under the delusion that I could control it; the only objective was to contain it. The experience was very nearly ascetic. I limited myself to airports and hotel rooms. I never spoke to anyone, except to request the cheque or to ask, at the hotel desk, where the ice machine was, though even these small transactions were minimised by the digital interfaces that had suddenly gone up everywhere, and which appeared to have been designed specifically for people in my position, people who had slipped between the cracks of their lives and were entirely content to remain in the cracks, unobserved by the world of conscience and daylight.

I did speak to my husband, on the phone and sometimes in person, on the days when I came home not yet entirely clear. These conversations caused a great deal of anxiety, though the anxiety did not arrive until the next day, an anvil of terror and guilt as soon as I woke up, because in the moment I had been floating 10,000 miles above my body.

I had spent a decade of my life – a formative decade, the first of adulthood – perfecting the art of dissemblance, and I fell back into the groove of these tactics through sheer muscle memory. It was like riding a bicycle. Arriving home an hour before he returned, I knew instinctively to get into the bath – an old trick, one that offered a rationale for flushed cheeks, plus the tub created a barrier, as did the fragrant suds, to the smell of alcohol leaving the pores.

Each binge was a controlled explosion, safely contained from the rest of my life. I reasoned they were hurting no one, and it’s true that for a while there were few consequences. Or perhaps I am cursed with “euphoric recall” – the inability to remember the lows with the same vivid resolution as the highs. I do remember the vomiting, both during and after.

It made a difference, whether it was during or after. During was not entirely unpleasant: you kneeled and opened your mouth and your body took it from there – there was nothing to it. And you always felt better afterwards, empty and slightly more sober, ready to drink more. It was a cleansing that literalised the central promise of the intoxicated mind: that every error could be undone, that all the tapes could be reversed, that all would be well.

After was a different story. The body still took over, but it was with churning, mechanical violence – or perhaps the problem was that the mind on those wretched mornings was not willing to play along, was not able to let go and surrender to the process. You tasted everything coming up, there was no way to avoid it, and it was not the blameless liquid that had escaped so easily the night before, but all the filth that had festered in your stomach for hours, the shame of whatever you had eaten and forgotten you had eaten before passing out. The clear afterbirth that followed, pure stomach acid that burned the back of your throat and tasted like death itself, acid you had to cough to get out.

And that was not even the end of it, because there was also the empty heaving, the eternity during which you sat on the cold tile floor, praying it was over, occasionally spitting fire into a wad of toilet paper, conscious the whole time of how close you were to death, grateful only that you did not see any bile.

There was so much to be grateful for during those months. I had forgotten about this, how any period of dissolution brings you into such close proximity to the gratuitous abundance of human kindness. I had experienced it throughout my 20s: the cab driver who picked me up when I was passed out on a kerb, drove me to the address on my licence, carried me up the stairs to my apartment and laid me on the couch, where he left me unharmed. The pharmacist who could have reported me for trying to fill an expired script (the date changed by one number), and who instead saw that I was shaking with withdrawal and told me to meet her outside, where she slipped me two pills and the number of a local detox centre. The woman who stopped at my table in the rehab cafeteria, where I was sitting alone, sobbing, and told me it would get better, her voice so full of calm authority that I assumed she was a doctor or a therapist, or perhaps an angel, and whom I discovered later was a patient who’d been admitted only three days before me.

The dangers this time around were not as extreme, but I was still frequently the recipient of baffling acts of compassion. The woman at the airport bar who paid my tab when I realised I was about to miss my flight. The flight attendant who brought me aspirin when I was vomiting in the aeroplane toilet. The librarian who was so entirely forgiving when I cancelled the virtual panel she had organised on the morning it was supposed to take place, and who may or may not have bought my line about a stomach virus.

These were not heroic acts, but the kindness was so entirely undeserved – in fact, the opposite of what I deserved – that it felt like grace in its most intense form, the grace of the reformers, unmerited favour “given to the most undeserving and unworthy”, as Luther said. We should all pity those perpetually capable, functioning adults who have never experienced this grace, which is among the rare miracles of this life.

One afternoon, as I was boarding a flight, I received a voicemail from the teenage son of one of my mother’s friends. I had not spoken to this kid – I still thought of him as a kid, though he was now 18 – for several years, but I’d heard through the family grapevine that he had just completed his second or third stint in rehab. His voice in the message was sullen and compulsory; it was clear that his mother had given him my number and urged him to call. But when I called him back, soon after arriving on the east coast and checking into my hotel, I was surprised to hear real desperation in his voice.

He’d been sent to rehab this last time, he said, after an overdose that may or may not have been a suicide attempt – he was not totally sure himself – and had been thrown out of the institution for smuggling in pills. He was now back at home with his mum, trying to go to recovery meetings. There were lots of people his age who were excited about sobriety, but he did not feel that way. He said that he could not picture his life without drugs and alcohol, that it was the most depressing thing he could imagine. There was an exhaustion in his voice that seemed to belong to someone much older, not a child who had his whole life ahead of him.

I listened for a long time and then said everything I knew to say: I told him that I loved alcohol more than anything, more than any person or thing, more than God. I said the thing about addiction is that it demands everything; no sacrifice is ever enough. I said that he could have this one luminous thing, or he could have everything else, which is to say every experience, every possibility, all the ups and downs that make up a life. I said these things and meant them. I truly believed, as I sat there on the floor of my hotel room, looking out at the freezing rain, that his life would be better if he could stay on the right side of that equation, just as mine had been better for doing so. I also, at the same time, believed that if I wanted to choose the single luminous object over a rich and full life, it was my business.

He asked how long I had been sober.

Eleven years, I said.

How hard it was during that year to say that number out loud! My whole life had become a lie, though so long as I remained in the realm of language and narrative, as opposed to the inflexible mathematics of time, it was easy to believe that nothing had changed. The story of my life was one I had been telling for more than a decade, and I believed it was strong enough to sustain private infractions. Or perhaps the point of the infractions was to discover how much the story could sustain. As far as everyone in my life was concerned, including even my husband and my closest friends, I was the same person I had always been – a person who could be counted on to keep an extra set of keys to your house, or to be named the godmother to your child, or to offer wise counsel to a kid who’d just got out of rehab.

I don’t pretend to remember exactly what I was thinking during this time, or all the convoluted ways I rationalised my actions to myself, but I do remember the fundamental inability to buy into the reality of my secret life, and the inarticulate conviction that so long as the official version of my life continued without hiccup, that was what counted. I felt like a marine crustacean whose shell remained on shore, a solid proxy for its being, while the animal inside slithered off into the sea.

This is an edited extract from Will and Attention, published by Little, Brown. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com

Google Will Turn Off Search for Schools That Reject A. I.

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Google is making it easier to restrict its A. I. tools for students. But schools that block A. I. entirely will lose student access to Google’s search engine.

By Dana Goldstein and Natasha Singer

Google announced Tuesday that early next year it would turn off artificial intelligence tools in its popular software for K-12 students, unless school administrators explicitly choose to make such tools available.

Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A. I.

But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A. I. entirely will also lose access to Google search.

A. I. features are now a standard part of Google’s commercially available search engine. “Search and A. I. are deeply integrated,” said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A. I., he added, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google is by far the dominant technology player in K-12 classrooms. Google’s suite of education apps — including Gmail, Docs and an assignment platform called Classroom — is ubiquitous. Google Chromebooks, low-cost laptops, are the most widely issued student devices in U. S. schools. And Google is synonymous with internet search, a crucial tool for students across the globe.

The company’s new strategy underscores Google’s powerful role in American education. If school leaders want continued student access to search within the company’s ecosystem, they will be forced to embrace Google’s A. I.

Lina Khan, a former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said in a statement that Google was using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its A. I. She added that multiple courts had found the tech giant liable for violating antitrust laws.

“This latest move shows it remains unchastened,” Ms. Khan said of Google’s new A. I. changes for schools. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools,” she added, “Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

In recent months, Google has been promoting its Gemini chatbot as a valuable educational tool, saying it can aid teachers in planning lessons and serve as a personalized tutor for students. A new student feature within Gemini, Guided Learning, is supposed to make it harder for students to use A. I. to cheat.

“We’re evolving our approach,” said Mr. Phillips. He promised tools that would “support the productive struggle” of learning and tamp down on students turning to A. I. for easy answers.

In August, Google turned on A. I. features as the default option inside its Classroom app for K-12 schools that had allowed students separate access to the company’s Gemini chatbot. The move upset some school leaders, who felt schools should be able to decide how and when students used Google’s A. I.

Google’s August change will now be reversed.

Parent activists have been pushing back against the use of A. I. in schools, and against screen time more generally. While A. I. chatbots can be useful tools for research and coding, they can also easily be used to cheat on school assignments and can provide false information. Research shows chatbots can also hinder critical thinking and ensnare adolescents in emotional dependency.

Last week, New York State passed a chatbot safety law that would prohibit companies from providing a variety of A. I. features for minors. And in September, the nation’s two largest school districts, in New York City and Los Angeles — both Google clients — broadly restricted student access to generative artificial intelligence on school devices.

In response to Google’s Tuesday announcement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City wrote on social media, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margin of Big Tech.”

Officials in the Los Angeles Unified School District have said that they were hoping students would be able to conduct Google searches with A. I. overviews turned off. The overviews are A. I.-generated summaries that appear at the top of searches. They can dissuade students from seeking out multiple sources of information.

On Monday, Google executives said that for districts that do allow A. I., there will be two options for search inside school-issued accounts, beginning in early 2027. One option will be search with A. I. overviews and A. I. chats turned on, similar to the current consumer experience. The other will be search using Guided Learning, the student feature within Google’s Gemini chatbot.

Guided Learning is intended to guide students through a topic step-by-step without providing them with answers that could short-circuit learning. It is supposed to offer an experience modeled on one-to-one tutoring.

The consumer version of Guided Learning is already available within Gemini, and can enable cheating. In a reporter’s test, it produced a detailed essay in response to an Advanced Placement history prompt.

There are greater restrictions in the school version that is currently being piloted, according to Brit Mennuti, product lead for Google Classroom. She said teachers would be able to review students’ chatbot transcripts, among other capabilities.

Kelly Clancy is a New York City public school parent and leader in groups calling for an A. I. moratorium in schools.

She said her seventh-grade son used Google search daily to complete assignments, such as a recent earth science project that required him to learn about lab safety.

“We have to go back to the drawing board on how we are teaching kids to research,” she said, suggesting that students could use alternatives such as physical libraries or competing search engines that allow more control over A. I.

Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, said Google’s decision could further energize the anti-tech movement percolating among parents and educators.

“This is a particularly clear example of the tech industry going out of its way to force A. I. on us all — even if we have said we don’t want it,” he said.

Dana Goldstein covers education for The Times.

Natasha Singer has covered tech in schools for The Times for more than decade. She is currently focused on the groundswell of parent concern about school laptops and A. I. chatbots.

Justices Seem Likely to Side With Colorado Catholic Schools Seeking Public Money

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The Supreme Court considered whether Catholic preschools in Colorado that decline to enroll families with gay and transgender parents can participate in a state program.

By Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Littleton, Colo., and Washington

The hallways of the St. Mary Catholic Parish school are decorated with Adam-and-Eve-themed apple prints and a colorful mural depicting Jesus’ life as a child. Inside the preschool classroom is a prayer table with a rosary and puzzle pieces shaped like the symbols of Catholicism.

Parents who send their 4-year-olds to the school a few miles south of Denver feel strongly about educating their children in the Catholic faith — but they also say the state of Colorado should pay for it.

And that has led to a clash that reached the Supreme Court on Tuesday. The conservative-dominated bench has issued a series of recent decisions expanding the role of religion in public life, a signature project of the court led by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.

After more than two hours of oral argument on Tuesday, the majority seemed likely to continue that trend, with several conservative justices asking skeptical questions of Colorado — and the three liberal justices appearing to side with the state.

At issue is a Colorado program that allows private preschools to get taxpayer funding, but those preschools are required to provide children an “equal opportunity” to enroll, including the children of gay and transgender parents. The Archdiocese of Denver argues that the requirement is at odds with its religious mission — and its members’ First Amendment rights.

The archdiocese, parish and parents sued Colorado, setting up the latest battle at the Supreme Court testing whether religious objections can override government prohibitions against discrimination.

Religious groups almost always prevail before the current Supreme Court. In 2021, the court ruled unanimously that a Catholic social services agency in Philadelphia could defy city rules and refuse to work with same-sex couples who apply to take in foster children. The next year, in a case from Maine, the court said that states that choose to subsidize private schools may not exclude or discriminate against religious ones.

In the Colorado case, however, lower courts have said the state “welcomed and actively solicited” the participation of faith-based preschools after voters approved a universal prekindergarten program in 2020. The state pays for at least 15 hours of free preschool each week at any public or private preschool, including religious ones, provided it meets the program’s requirements, including the nondiscrimination agreement.

In 2023, the archdiocese directed its preschools not to register, arguing the requirements ran counter to its views on sexuality and gender identity. Teachers, other staff members and parents at its schools sign a “statement of community beliefs” that acknowledges that the archdiocese does not recognize same-sex relationships or transgender status. Enrolling children of gay and transgender parents, according to school officials, would “likely lead to intractable conflicts.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who is often in the majority, and Justice Neil M. Gorsuch suggested on Tuesday that even if Colorado’s program was technically open to Catholic schools, the state should have anticipated that the nondiscrimination requirement would preclude their participation.

What is the difference, Justice Barrett asked, between setting up a program that overtly excluded religious schools and “choosing to impose a condition that you know” certain Catholic schools “will be unable to agree to?”

Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, who is also often a critical vote, asked what harm it would be to grant an exemption to the Catholic schools when plenty of other schools would accept families with gay and transgender parents.

Why not “avoid the clash,” he asked.

In response, Helen Norton, the state’s lawyer, said Colorado had an interest in “ensuring that its public funds go to schools that ensure equal opportunity.” She added that “families are harmed when they’re turned away” from publicly funded schools they choose.

According to the lawsuit, Colorado is excluding hundreds of families across 34 preschools overseen by the archdiocese. As a result, the archbishop of Denver said last week that enrollment is down 20 percent and two preschools have closed, as parents have withdrawn their children and enrolled them in schools that get public funding.

One couple who joined the suit, Dan and Lisa Sheley, met as students at a Catholic college and say they now want their seven children to be steeped in their faith and values both at home and at school, where Lisa works. Because of the state’s policy, the Sheleys said, they have missed out so far on at least $18,000 in tuition assistance. They expect to lose thousands more when another child becomes eligible for the program.

In an interview, Lisa Sheley said the couple voted for the program believing it would be universal. Now, she said, they’ve discovered “it is not universal because we’re being discriminated against and not allowed to participate.”

The school is being represented by lawyers from the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a religious legal organization. They told the justices in court filings that the government cannot condition access to a public benefit on a recipient’s abandoning their religious beliefs.

“Catholic schools wanted to be a part of it, and Colorado wanted them to be a part of it, but when push came to shove, we couldn’t compromise what we believe,” said Nick Reaves, the lawyer representing the school, parents and archdiocese before the court on Tuesday.

Jared Polis, Colorado’s Democratic governor, said in a statement that state officials intentionally included faith-based groups when they created the program. At least 79 faith-based providers participated in the last school year, serving at least 2,052 students and receiving more than $9.5 million in payments.

In court filings, Colorado’s lawyers argued that the anti-discrimination requirements do not infringe on the schools’ religious beliefs because those schools are free to teach whatever they would like about sex, marriage, gender and family. They need only refrain from excluding children from enrolling “simply because their parents are gay.”

The state also noted that the requirements apply equally to all participating preschools — public, private, secular and religious.

All three liberal justices seemed to embrace the state’s claims and said the Catholic schools were seeking to be treated differently or better than other participating programs and in a way that would discriminate against families with gay and transgender parents.

“Your schools want to discriminate by exclusion,” said Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. “Nobody else is allowed to do that.”

Both Justices Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor asked why the same line of reasoning would not allow schools to turn away children based on race or ethnicity because of a religious belief.

Scott Skinner-Thompson, a law professor at the University of Colorado who specializes in civil rights and constitutional law, said states have long had the power to impose conditions on recipients of taxpayer funds, such as committing to comply with nondiscrimination requirements.

“St. Mary’s is saying that’s not tenable with our faith position. That’s fine. It’s a simple choice not to take the money,” he said. “The state is trying to balance protecting L. G. B. T. Q. families and preserving religious liberty.”

After a three-day trial, a federal judge said in 2024 that while states may not decline to fund religious schools, states “are not obligated to subsidize discrimination using taxpayer dollars, even when that discrimination is based on religious beliefs.”

A unanimous panel of the U. S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld that decision last year, citing an important Supreme Court precedent limiting First Amendment protections for religious practices.

The 1990 decision, Employment Division v. Smith, said laws that apply neutrally and across the board, without singling out religion, typically do not violate the First Amendment’s protection of the free exercise of religion.

That decision is unpopular among many conservative Christians, who say it does not offer adequate protection to religion. Three justices — Clarence Thomas, Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Justice Gorsuch — have called for overturning that precedent, with Justice Alito writing in 2021 that it “threatens a fundamental freedom.”

Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett expressed hesitation in the same case about the implications of overruling the Smith decision and what would replace it. The court did not directly address the question of whether to overturn it in Tuesday’s argument.

In the court’s 2021 decision in the foster care case from Philadelphia, Chief Justice Roberts said the city’s policies had not met the requirement set out in Smith that laws must be “neutral and generally applicable” because city officials were permitted to make certain exceptions.

Lawyers for the Catholic school in Colorado, backed by the Trump administration, relied on that line of reasoning and asserted that the state has granted exceptions to its requirement — but for secular reasons and not religious ones.

The appeals court was unpersuaded that the exceptions the state has so far allowed, which include letting some schools give preferences to low-income families or children with disabilities, are parallel to what the church has requested.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

Flouting Consumer Law, Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A law to end surprise medical bills has generated millions of high-dollar payouts for doctors. Health plans are now fighting back by frequently withholding money.

By Margot Sanger-Katz and Sarah Kliff

The authors are covering the implementation of the No Surprises Act. They welcome tips at nytimes. com/tips.

Over the past two years, Flight for Life has airlifted car crash victims, premature babies and adults struggling to breathe to hospitals across southeastern Wisconsin.

Anthem, the major health insurer, covered dozens of those patients, but it has refused to pay $2.1 million it owes the company for their helicopter rides.

The amounts due for each emergency medical flight range from $9,382 to $62,373. Anthem has historically paid its bills, but late last year it suddenly stopped.

“It was like a faucet they just shut off,” said Flight for Life’s executive director, Leif Erickson.

The insurer’s willful nonpayment is the latest in a cascade of unintended consequences brought about by a widely supported law that was intended to protect patients from surprise medical bills.

The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for arbitrators to decide appropriate levels of reimbursement, and it has already triggered millions of disputes between medical care providers and insurers. Doctors have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning arbitration settlements that sometimes far exceeded the usual insurer rates.

Now, fed up with what they consider unfair outcomes, insurers are fighting back by refusing to pay.

The law, the No Surprises Act, was enacted with a large bipartisan majority to ensure patients never got excessive bills in situations, like emergencies, where they could not pick their doctors.

The arbitration system set up by the law was supposed to resolve billing disputes when health care providers and insurers could not agree on a price: An arbitrator reviews a proposed dollar amount from each side and decides which one is most reasonable. Insurers are required to pay that amount within 30 days, and billing patients for anything beyond that is prohibited.

Lawmakers expected the system to be used rarely and to produce reasonable payments. Instead, doctors and other health care providers have been swamping arbitrators with millions of claims, often for amounts that far exceed what is customarily paid for a service. And they have won the vast majority of their cases — sometimes receiving sums such as $440,000 for a breast reduction, $73,000 for an ankle X-ray, or $125,000 for assisting on prostate surgery.

Insurers have sued doctors and lobbied Congress to change the law, contending that the large awards and lopsided results are driving up health insurance premiums.

But with Washington moving slowly, they have adopted the strategy of simply declining to pay.

Nearly 30 percent of arbitration awards has gone unpaid since 2024, according to an analysis of 400,000 such awards provided by a major medical billing firm that The New York Times reviewed.

Anthem’s nonpayment rate was the highest by far, at 74 percent, but other large insurers, including Cigna, UnitedHealthcare and Aetna, have also declined to pay a significant portion.

Share of cases where the insurer did not pay the arbitration award, according to data from HaloMD, a medical billing firm

Note: Analysis of 409,102 cases from January 2024 to July 2026. Only includes cases in which payments to doctors could be reliably tracked.

Source: HaloMD.

By The New York Times

The standoff has created dysfunction and lawlessness in a system that a growing number of lawmakers and administration officials say needs to be changed.

“The providers are succeeding in what feel like egregious award levels, and then the insurers are also doing some of this egregious behavior by not paying,” said Katie Keith, the director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law. “But there’s not accountability on either side.”

Health plans, including Anthem, criticize HaloMD, the company that provided The Times with payment data, for using business tactics that exploit the arbitration system and result in large payouts. Only one of the major insurers The Times contacted disputed the accuracy of the data. A Cigna spokeswoman said that a significantly smaller share went unpaid in 2026 than what the Halo data showed.

Most large health insurers told The Times it is their policy not to pay awards if they believe the claim should never have qualified for the arbitration process, even when the arbitrator determined it to be eligible.

In the case of Flight for Life, Anthem says it will not pay because it believes the medevac service violated the arbitration system’s complex procedural rules, an assessment Flight for Life disputes.

Ariel Bayewitz, vice president of health economics at Elevance Health, Anthem’s parent company, said that the company “believes strongly” in paying eligible awards on time. But, he said, Anthem estimates that most claims that have moved through the arbitration system should have been found ineligible, because they either didn’t follow the rules or were for situations not covered under the consumer protection law.

“More providers are submitting ineligible cases because ineligible cases aren’t being dismissed like they should be,” he said.

Smaller health plans also have been withholding payments in cases where they think the award is unreasonable. Some even have form letters they send to doctors whose awards they won’t pay.

“The determination is not merely high; it is legally defective,” says one such letter, from the New York insurer EmblemHealth, declining to pay an award 99 times its usual rate for a breast reconstruction.

“Recently, we have observed a significant increase in very high-dollar claims, which we are actively reviewing and challenging as appropriate,” said Alex Gomez, a spokesman for the plan.

A spokeswoman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the arbitration system, said the law always requires insurers to pay arbitration awards.

Doctors and air ambulance companies have turned to the courts, filing hundreds of lawsuits to enforce the arbitrators’ decisions, but three federal appeals courts have ruled that the No Surprises Act does not include a right to sue.

Stephen Ware, a professor of law at the University of Kansas, said that unlike most arbitration situations, the No Surprises Act does not explain how a ruling can be enforced. One appeals court decision suggested that the government could sue to force insurers to pay. So far, the Trump administration has not exercised such power.

Doctors have said that the nonpayments make it hard to manage their practices. Some who have built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts have taken on debts to stay afloat.

Dr. Jennifer Raley, a managing partner at Wake Emergency Physicians in North Carolina, said her practice had $1.2 million in outstanding awards. It won 1,032 arbitration cases in 2025, with an average award around four times what insurers typically pay.

In January, it had to take out a line of credit to make payroll.

“We just want to get paid what we need to pay the people who saw the patients,” she said. PHI, a national air ambulance company, recently closed a base in Red Bluff, Calif., a small city between Sacramento and the Oregon border.

In an interview, PHI’s chief executive, Scott McCarty, cited $16.3 million in outstanding payments from Anthem as the cause of the closure.

“The insurance companies cannot unilaterally decide to breach a federal law if they don’t like the end result,” Mr. McCarty said. “That’s essentially what they are doing.”

Anthem spokeswoman Janey Kiryluik said that the insurer was “actively trying to bring PHI Air Medical into our network,” but that the medevac company had requested unreasonably high rates. She said that, in arbitration, it typically requests $56,000 per flight.

Dr. Brian McHugh, a neurosurgeon from Long Island, N. Y., has repeatedly received letters from Anthem challenging his awards on the grounds they are too expensive. Dr. McHugh often wins arbitration awards that are 40 times higher than what Anthem typically pays, according to federal data.

He said other doctors at his practice had stopped seeing Anthem patients.

Ms. Kiryluik said the insurer does not use a financial threshold as a “basis for holding payment,” and that it no longer uses the letter Dr. McHugh received.

Anthem, like all major insurers, supported the No Surprises Act when Congress was writing the legislation during the first Trump administration. But over the last six years, the company’s executives have soured on the law’s arbitration system, saying that it encourages abusive billing. Many of the high awards have been for scheduled procedures, not the emergency care the law was written to address.

Anthem defends its nonpayment policies as intentional. In a 13-page report, it estimated that 60 percent of its cases that arbitrators had decided should never have qualified. This year, it has not paid 83 percent of arbitration claims, according to the HaloMD data, a substantial jump from previous years.

The Labor Department, which oversees large employer health plans, is investigating Anthem’s failure to pay arbitration awards, according to documents The Times obtained. Ms. Kiryluik, the Anthem spokeswoman, said the plan was cooperating with the investigation.

The 400,000 claims that HaloMD shared with The Times make up around two-thirds of the total arbitration cases it has won since 2024. The data set only includes cases for which HaloMD could reliably track payments to doctors.

Anthem and other insurers contend that HaloMD is part of the problem. They say Halo typically submits unreasonably high bids to arbitration, sometimes winning 113 times typical insurer payments. The company has also been accused of filing a high volume of ineligible claims. Five insurers have sued Halo, accusing it of fraudulent behavior. Three of them, including one from Anthem, have been dismissed in federal court, on the grounds that courts can’t review the arbitrators’ decisions.

HaloMD spokesman Patrick Velliky said that the insurers’ lawsuits were “an attempt to intimidate physicians and clinicians out of seeking fair and sustainable reimbursement.”

The law set up a series of deadlines and procedures that doctors need to follow. They limited access to the system to certain situations. Cases where the patient has a government plan, like Medicare or Medicaid, are not eligible. Nor are situations where the doctor already has a contract with the health plan.

Insurers say they sometimes see doctors winning two times for the same care — first in a state-level system to resolve medical billing disputes, and then again through federal arbitration.

“We’re not going to pay it twice,” said Josh Goldberg, executive director of heath policy at Health Care Service Corporation, which covers 27 million people through six Blue Cross affiliates. “This is just a situation where we’re a little bit between a rock and a hard place.”

The insurer is “not the final decider,” said Ms. Keith. She described Anthem’s strategy as “high-risk” because it flouts binding arbitration decisions.

But insurers expressed frustration that the system incentivizes arbitrators to find claims eligible. They get paid a flat fee for each dispute they resolve. If they rule a case is ineligible, they earn nothing.

The No Surprises Act gives the Trump administration authority to fine health insurers $100 for each day they do not pay an arbitration award. So far, it has not issued a single penalty.

Doctors have submitted hundreds of complaints about unpaid awards to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversee the system. Those that The Times spoke with said they had rarely received a response.

“There has to be some enforcement,” said Thomas LaGreca, a partner at Callagy Law, which files claims for providers. He estimates that 27 percent of clients claims remain unpaid six months after arbitration decisions. Health plans also said that C. M. S. had failed to respond to thousands of complaints about the large number of ineligible claims.

Spokespeople for both C. M. S. and the Labor Department declined to respond to questions about why they had not issued penalties to enforce the No Surprises Act.

A Trump administration spokesman told The Times in July that “the system is being gamed” by doctors and that the government was “actively working to clean it up.” The administration has not yet announced any policy changes.

Congress has recently taken a greater interest in reform, with one Senate committee hosting round table meetings and a top House Democrat introducing new legislation.

“There are problems on both sides, and I’ll readily admit that,” Representative Greg Murphy, Republican of North Carolina, said in an interview.

But Mr. Murphy, who worked as a urologist before running for office, said he believed that the “majority of abuses” had been committed by insurers who do not pay awards. He has introduced legislation that would stiffen penalties for nonpayment.

“I ran a small business,” he said. “If I don’t have income, guess what happens to the business? It dies.”

Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, chairs the Senate Health Committee and was an architect of the No Surprises Act. He has told those involved in the process that he views fixing its problems before he leaves office in January as a legacy project.

Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey, was also an author of the original law. He has a different idea: abolishing the complex arbitration system altogether. Last month, he introduced a bill that would resolve billing disputes by setting a flat payment for doctors at the level insurers typically pay.

Mr. Pallone has been skeptical of arbitration supporting it as part of a compromise to get the surprise billing ban passed. He said the reality was even more chaotic than he had predicted. “We have the proof with the facts that shows that this arbitration system is out of hand,” he said.

Margot Sanger-Katz is a reporter covering health care policy and public health for the Upshot section of The Times.

Sarah Kliff is an investigative health care reporter for The Times.

Poland Beefs Up Security at Border With Russia

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there had been “disturbing movement” in Kaliningrad, a Russian region just north of Poland.

By Andrew Higgins

Reporting from Warsaw

Poland has launched a “special operation” involving counterterrorism police, intelligence officers and beefed-up border security on its northern frontier with Russia, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, calling it a response to “disturbing movement” that could be preparation for “armed incursions.”

Mr. Tusk, speaking in Warsaw, said the late-night movement just across the border in Kaliningrad — a Russian region sandwiched between Poland, the Baltic Sea and Lithuania — involved unidentified people carrying flashlights, whose intentions were not clear.

He said Poland had received warnings from allied intelligence services of possible “acts of sabotage or more serious provocations on the border with the Russian Federation.” Mr. Tusk added that “more precise information,” received recently, indicated that “events could occur in the first half of November, including armed incursions” into Polish territory.

“It’s not a coincidence that this tension, provoked by the Russians, is occurring today,” Mr. Tusk said, citing “global uncertainty and confusion” over the midterm elections in the United States and a “sense of conflict and instability” in Poland because of a bitter political dispute over its constitutional court.

European governments have been frazzled in recent months by a spate of sabotage operations that officials have blamed on Russia, including a failed drone attack on a German airport. There have also been warnings, citing intelligence reports, that Russia could be planning some kind of military incursion or provocation along NATO’s eastern flank.

An airport outside of Warsaw shut down briefly on Tuesday after a bomb threat was directed at a flight from London, one of two Warsaw-bound flights that were targeted in what appeared to be hoax threats. Several other flights in Europe were also subjected to bomb threats. All landed safely, and the threats were being investigated.

Some of Mr. Tusk’s political opponents accused him of using border tensions to distract attention from an effort by government-backed judges on the Constitutional Tribunal to unseat its chief justice, a supporter of Poland’s former right-wing governing party, Law and Justice. Mr. Tusk’s government sent riot police to seal off the court on Friday.

President Karol Nawrocki, a foe of Mr. Tusk and a vocal supporter of the chief justice, barely mentioned Russia at a National Security Council meeting held on Tuesday to discuss defense issues, focusing instead on the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal.

While stating that “the aggressor,” a reference to Russia, “must be effectively deterred” even as it “operates below the threshold of war,” Mr. Nawrocki vowed to resist changes at the court and “stop this attempt to overturn the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland.”

Kaliningrad, formerly German land that was annexed by the Soviet Union after World War II, is Russia’s westernmost territory. As the headquarters of its Baltic Fleet and a major military garrison, it has long been viewed as a potential launchpad for military action.

Poland’s previous right-wing government, facing a tough election in 2023, warned that Russian mercenary fighters were mobilizing to seal off the so-called Suwalki Gap, which stretches from Kaliningrad to Belarus between Poland and Lithuania.

Once, closing the gap would have separated the three Baltic states, all members of NATO, from the rest of the military alliance. But Finland’s entry into NATO after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that. The mercenaries that the government warned about in 2023 never appeared.

Far more likely than an armed incursion from Kaliningrad into Poland, according to analysts, are small-scale provocations and sabotage operations aimed at destabilizing Mr. Tusk’s government, which Moscow reviles because of its strong support for Ukraine and the European Union.

Disorder on the frontier, according to this theory, could help turn Polish opinion against Ukraine and boost right-wing political forces that are hostile to the European Union, Ukrainian refugees and, in some cases, military support for Kyiv. Most of the weapons and ammunition that Ukraine receives from the West pass through Polish territory.

Instability on the border could also stoke further political tumult amid rising passions over the standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal. Mr. Tusk’s opponents accused him of staging a “coup d’état” after the deployment of riot police outside the court, where five new judges appointed by Parliament had supported a move to unseat the chief justice.

The right-wing opposition insists that those judges are impostors because Mr. Nawrocki, the president, refused to preside over their swearing-in ceremonies. The president has no veto power over judicial appointments, but does have ceremonial duties, something that Mr. Nawrocki has used to try to block the new judges.

On Tuesday, Mr. Tusk tied right-wing denunciations of his actions to a campaign of similar attacks by officials and state media outlets in Moscow, apparently hoping that the deep suspicion of Russia shared by nearly all Poles would help rally public opinion behind his efforts to break the judicial deadlock.

Urging his critics not to become “useful idiots,” Mr. Tusk said: “It’s invaluable today that Polish politicians don’t intentionally or foolishly serve the interests of Russia, which relies on destabilization, disregard for international law, deeming the European Union its main enemy, and so on.”

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting from Warsaw.

Andrew Higgins is the East and Central Europe bureau chief for The Times based in Warsaw.

Ken Burns: We Face Our Nation’s Fourth Great Crisis

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Ken Burns

Ken Burns is a documentary filmmaker. His last film was a series on the American Revolution.

There have been three great crises in American history: the Civil War, perhaps the defining event in our history after the Revolution itself, the Great Depression and World War II. These events tested our republic and our resolve in fundamental ways, but the center always held — elections took place, there was a peaceful transfer of power and the judiciary was still independent. Our core democratic institutions remained fundamentally strong, respected by the public and our leaders alike. The guardrails of our democracy held and were even strengthened as we emerged from each.

As we go to the polls today in this most consequential of midterm elections, we face our country’s fourth great crisis. Because of misinformation, which the current administration encourages, age-old fears and conspiracies have created a sense of us versus them that is fundamentally at odds with a healthy democratic society. Elections are in doubt, the highest court seems compromised, history has been distorted, books have been banned, and dictators have been coddled while our closest allies have been ridiculed and dismissed. People are rightly concerned whether our institutions are at a breaking point.

I’ve spent the better part of the past two years crisscrossing the country, discussing the release of our PBS series on the American Revolution. No matter where I went or to whom I spoke, people asked me the same questions: What did I learn about our complicated and fragile republic over the nearly 10 years it took to make the film? Can a country as divided as ours survive? What might our founders think of us today?

I think the founders would be hugely disappointed that so many members of the legislative branch have ceded so much power to the executive branch, which has filled that vacuum with corruption and assaults on the rule of law, even undermining the fundamental right to vote. John Adams, who insisted that a republic could not function without virtuous leaders, would be appalled at the prevailing vulgarity and incompetence.

From the start, the creation of the United States was unlikely. For most of human history, people had lived under authoritarian rule, but in the 13 former British colonies clinging to the Eastern Seaboard, people (white men) would create something new: citizens.

“All experience has shown,” Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence, “that mankind are more disposed to suffer, while evils are sufferable, than to right themselves by abolishing the forms to which they are accustomed.” Maintaining a democracy would be difficult, an active exercise that would simultaneously try to honor our individual freedoms (what each of us wants) and our collective freedoms (what we need).

George Washington’s great achievement was not just winning a war against overwhelming odds, but persuading 13 new states with different economies, religious beliefs and competing interests that they were now part of something new in which old animosities would yield to an individual, as well as collective, sense of union. There would be an “us,” with no “them.”

During the Constitutional Convention in the summer of 1787, delegates understood that in the many compromises they would strike, they also had to engineer defenses against the rise of a tyrant. In a letter to James Madison, Jefferson worried that a president who lost an election might “pretend false votes” and “hold possession of the reins of government.” Alexander Hamilton was also concerned that an “unprincipled” man would “mount the hobby horse of popularity” and “throw things in confusion.” “In a government like ours,” he wrote, no one is “above the law.”

Today, nearly six years after an angry mob stormed the Capitol to overturn the results of the 2020 election, election denial is still part of the current administration’s playbook. Only four of the 13 Republican candidates in highly competitive Senate races have said that they would accept the outcome of the upcoming elections unconditionally.

It hasn’t always been that way. During Watergate, as damning evidence accumulated, members of President Richard Nixon’s own party concluded that their obligation to the Constitution was greater than their obligation to him or the G. O. P. In August 1974, Republican congressional leaders went to the White House and told Nixon that his support in Congress had collapsed. He announced his resignation the next day.

Citizens today should remember that our democracy relies on an ongoing conversation between them and the past. At Gettysburg, only a few months after the largest battle ever fought on American soil, Abraham Lincoln asked the living to dedicate themselves to “a new birth of freedom,” recognizing that every generation must renew and expand on the promises first made in Philadelphia. Dwight Eisenhower, who knew better than most the terrible cost of war, reminded us in his farewell address that only “an alert and knowledgeable citizenry” could preserve liberty and security.

I’m optimistic that the American people recognize that our democratic institutions and sense of decency can bring us together.

We have come back from crises before. We were more divided than we are today during the Revolution, the Civil War, Reconstruction and Vietnam. For 250 years, our country has prevailed in fits and starts, forging achievements, however imperfect, related to race and equality in American life.

But given our divisions, as we vote we must each ask ourselves: What kind of leadership will see us through the current crisis? Why do we continue to support leaders who are invested in deepening our divides, who tap into conspiracy theories to frighten the public, deny facts and, to quote Alexander Hamilton, “throw things into confusion,” so that they “may ‘ride the storm and direct the whirlwind’”?

Most midterm elections are seen as referendums on the policies of the president. This one is no different. But there’s something more fundamental at stake here, beyond policy differences. This election is about the people — who are empowered to check our chief executive — and the candidates running for Congress, who either have sworn an oath to the Constitution or hope to do so. Whether they are prepared to honor their oath should matter enormously to everyone who values the idea of us — the idea of America.

The founders knew they had to reverse engineer against a potential tyrant. Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power to check the executive branch. Today’s election is, in many ways, about whether members have lived up to that responsibility or violated their oath of office.

Ken Burns is a documentary filmmaker. His last film was a series on the American Revolution.

Israeli Claims of Iranian Chemical Weapons Divide U. S. Officials

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Some administration officials suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to draw President Trump back into military action.

By Julian E. BarnesNatan OdenheimerEric SchmittAdam Rasgon and Dustin Volz

The reporters have been covering the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Israel has shared intelligence with the United States asserting that Iran is considering the use of chemical weapons against its adversaries, information met with alarm by some American officials and deep skepticism by others, according to U. S. and regional officials.

Some American officials see the Israeli intelligence as part of a pressure campaign by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government to persuade the Trump administration to return to major combat operations against Iran.

Other officials believe the threats should be taken seriously, given the recent array of warnings about Iran’s preparations to attack American interests.

Israel has shared some of the information with officials in Gulf countries. Several doubted that Iran was developing plans to use chemical weapons and believe Israel is trying to push the United States and its partners to return to a more intense phase of the war.

American claims about Iran’s chemical weapons, or its intent to build them, go back decades. In 2003, Iran acknowledged it had developed chemical capabilities during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s but said it later dismantled them.

In recent years, the United States has publicly asserted in its annual unclassified intelligence assessments that Iran “likely aims” to continue its research and development of chemical weapons.

Iran has publicly denied having chemical weapons and previously described such allegations as psychological war waged by Israel and Mr. Netanyahu.

All of the people interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity, given the secret nature of the Israeli intelligence, the sensitivity of Iranian planning and the classified American discussions.

After eight months of war, the United States and Iran are in something of a holding pattern, exploring the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough and preparing for renewed warfare.

The debate over the new intelligence shows how tense the moment is and the potential for grave miscalculation. U. S. officials have said the Trump administration has no intention of using a nuclear weapon, but Iranian officials are not so sure.

The Needle, our live forecast, returns tonight

We’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and House once enough votes have been reported.

Waiting for estimates

Waiting for estimates

Mr. Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival after he failed to secure a clear path to forming a government in elections last week. Some analysts believe that the veteran leader may be seeking to use a security emergency as leverage to compel opposition leaders to join him in a coalition.

In recent conversations with U. S. spy agencies and other officials over the past two weeks, Israeli officials have portrayed the chemical weapon threat as more urgent than Iran’s ambitions to develop a nuclear weapon.

The Home Front Command, the Israeli military unit responsible for emergency response and issuing guidance to civilians, is running drills across Israel this week but is not including chemical weapons preparation as a major part of the exercises.

The command has also not issued widespread reminders to its officers or the public regarding safety guidelines for such a possibility, according to two unit officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the news media. The Israeli military declined to comment.

In recent weeks, the U. S. military has built up a vast arsenal in the region, with naval ships, fighter planes and bombers ready to launch a relatively short campaign of intense strikes after the midterm elections, should President Trump authorize action.

At the same time U. S. and other diplomats are trying to forge an agreement with Iran which would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, address Tehran’s nuclear program and put off further military action. The buildup of forces could be intended as much to support that diplomatic push as it is to prepare for a return to war.

Iran has intensified attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, hoping to exert maximum economic pressure on the United States ahead of its elections on Tuesday.

The use of chemical weapons is a particularly fraught issue for Iran, one of a few countries that have suffered the effects of them. During the Iran-Iraq war, Saddam Hussein deployed chemical weapons, killing thousands and leading to decades of health problems among some 100,000 Iranian veterans and civilians, according to Iranian experts.

U. S. intelligence agencies have long tracked Iran’s development of chemical weapons, which are banned under international law. Israeli intelligence agencies have told U. S. counterparts that they believe Iran is moving rapidly to develop the technology to put such weapons on a missile or to sneak them into Israel or another country to use in an attack, according to American officials.

For some American officials, the talk of chemical weapons threats from Iran has evoked the flawed U. S. intelligence in 2002 about Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction. Iraq had largely abandoned or frozen its nuclear, chemical and biological programs by then, but U. S. intelligence agencies told President George W. Bush’s White House that their assessment that Iraq had such weapons was ironclad.

People briefed on the new intelligence had different views on how quickly — or effectively — Iran could deploy a chemical weapon. While mounting a chemical weapon on a ballistic missile is not difficult, ensuring that the weapon can effectively disperse a chemical agent is, according to weapons experts and U. S. officials. Smuggling a bomb across a border also poses challenges.

Using a drone to deliver a chemical weapon is also a possibility.

A regional official said Israel had presented Gulf countries with claims that Iran was working to make its chemical weapons operational. Israeli officials did not share evidence but briefed the officials on their assessments, which the official said Gulf governments found unserious.

The White House did not comment, but a U. S. official said Mr. Trump would keep America and its allies safe from any potential threat. The C. I. A. declined to comment.

A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu’s office said that “Israel closely tracks every threat posed by the Iranian terror regime and is prepared to deal with it.” A spokesman for Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return a request for comment.

While there is little debate in the U. S. intelligence community that Iran is developing chemical weapons, there is significant debate over whether its leaders would ever use those weapons, especially if not provoked by further attacks.

The U. S. director of national intelligence warned in 2024 that “Iran probably aims to continue research and development of chemical and biological agents for offensive purposes.”

Dana Stroul, the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration, said it had been known for more than two decades that Iran stockpiled components for chemical weapons but that Tehran has never deployed them.

But Iran might feel “existentially pressured and potentially crossed the line to direct offensive use of these unconventional weapons,” said Ms. Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The United States has monitored a variety of threats from Iran, as intelligence collection intensified after the discovery of an Iranian plot to attack a military base in Britain used by American warplanes.

On Oct. 23, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, sent Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser, a memo warning of the threat of Iranian attacks. U. S. diplomats and other personnel were then put on high alert.

U. S. agencies assess that the threat against Americans in the Middle East and several other countries is at its highest level since the war started in February, U. S. officials said.

U. S. Central Command has a plan to strike Iran beginning as early as Wednesday, after the U. S. midterm elections and when three aircraft carriers are in the region, according to U. S. officials.

The ideal conditions for the type of campaign the military has laid out will last only a short time. After early November, one of the aircraft carriers will need to return to its home port. Early November is also a period of moonless nights, the kind of deep darkness the U. S. military likes to use for its attacks.

Some Trump cabinet members have argued for more time to let a campaign of economic pressure work. They say a U. S. blockade and sanctions on the country will eventually bring down the Iranian government.

But some officials point out that Iran has been able to weather the pressure campaign and that there is little indication that the Iranian government will collapse without additional military attacks.

Stephanie Walker, a senior national security and intelligence official at the F. B. I., said last week that the Iranian threat to U. S. interests was “a top focus right now for the entirety of the U. S. government.”

Tehran’s goals, Ms. Walker said, included espionage, influence and cyberattacks. Iran-linked hackers targeted scores of water systems across the United States this summer, leading some counties to issue boil-water advisories.

Iran has also attempted to impersonate people online in order to dupe their associates into sharing access to sensitive information with them. Artificial intelligence has made this form of trickery far easier, “especially with vishing,” she said, referring to voice-based phishing attacks.

The war “changed Iran’s calculus for what they were willing to do here against us,” Ms. Walker said last week at a national security conference in Sea Island, Ga.

Reporting was contributed by Vivian Nereim and Tyler Pager in Palm Beach, Fla., Maggie Haberman in Washington and Ronen Bergman in Tel Aviv.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Trump Says U. S. to End $4 Billion in Aid to Israel in Favor of New Deal

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The president’s announcement on Election Day, which he said was part of an agreement reached months ago, was a sign of how quickly the politics surrounding Israel have shifted.

By David E. Sanger

President Trump said on Tuesday that the bulk of American aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year,” under an agreement reached with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu months ago. He described the Election Day declaration chiefly as a political effort to take a “bad talking point” away from the left wing of the Democratic Party.

“We were giving them 4 billion,” Mr. Trump told Brian Kilmeade of Fox News in a morning interview, just as polls were opening on the East Coast. “We are. But it gets cut off at the end of the year.”

Instead, he described a different agreement in which Israel would pay for weaponry from the United States. The move comes as Congress was already considering phasing out the aid and instead undertaking a far more integrated defense and technology partnership built around legally mandated defense industrial cooperation between the two nations. Such a partnership could be lucrative for Israel through joint projects with the Defense Department and American military contractors.

Mr. Netanyahu has spoken in recent months about moving away from the aid from the United States, but has not laid out a timetable. But the current memorandum of understanding with Israel does not expire until 2028; Mr. Trump seemed to suggest on Tuesday canceling it two years early, with Israel’s consent. Mr. Netanyahu’s office did not immediately comment on the president’s statement.

The timing of Mr. Trump’s statement was remarkable: Just as polls opened in the United States, a Republican president was walking away from what has become a mainstay of American foreign policy for decades.

His comments appeared to recognize that it would be extraordinarily difficult to get new aid packages through Congress, and perhaps impossible after Tuesday’s election. But he never actually mentioned Gaza or the rapid erosion of support for Israel in the United States in the three years since the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks.

“They don’t need it,” Mr. Trump said of the American aid, “and because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” he said, a reference to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for an open Senate seat in Michigan, who has been among the most openly critical of Israel.

“It’s a bad talking point,” Mr. Trump said. He went on to add “Israel’s our No. 1,” but a “thriving country.”

Mr. Netanyahu had his own reasons to get out of the arrangement: Control over aid to Israel has increasingly become a cudgel for those in Congress trying to compel Israeli government action. If Israel were to receive American armaments through more traditional military sales, or as part of a trade and technology agreement, the process could become less of a ritualized battle in Congress — though congressional oversight would not end.

But in Israel, his opposition pounced, and the issue quickly became a point of argument as Mr. Netanyahu struggles with Gadi Eisenkot to form a government after an inconclusive election in Israel last week.

Mr. Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party and Mr. Netanyahu’s main challenger for the premiership, said in a statement that “the fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger.

“We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”

Robert Jimison and Natan Odenheimer contributed reporting.

⁠⁩

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.
