House Republicans Accuse Top Psychology Group of Antisemitism

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A monthslong G. O. P. effort culminated in a scathing report about emails and other exchanges within the American Psychological Association.

By Christina Caron and Azeen Ghorayshi

Republicans are stepping up efforts to investigate what they say is broad antisemitism at the American Psychological Association, just weeks after a Department of Education committee recommended putting the brakes on the organization’s accrediting power.

House Republicans blamed the organization for “troubling leadership failures” that they say have alienated Jewish members and undermined confidence in the association’s ability to set standards within the field in a report released on Thursday. The report is the latest attempt to scrutinize the ideology of the A. P. A., the leading scientific and professional organization representing psychologists in the United States.

Wendi S. Williams, the A. P. A. president, flatly rejected the accusations, saying in a statement that the organization “unequivocally condemns antisemitism in all its forms.”

The A. P. A. has nearly 200,000 members and provides accreditation to more than 1,300 training programs, including doctoral internships and postdoctoral residencies.

Since taking control of the House in 2023, Republicans have held hearings on antisemitism aimed at academia and progressive institutions. Some critics have argued that the Trump administration has weaponized claims of antisemitism against these longstanding targets of conservatives.

The report, issued by the House Education and Workforce Committee, concluded that anti-Jewish sentiment “has manifested across the association’s resolutions, listservs, newsletters, publications, and conferences.” It cited “radical activist-academics” who have promoted ideology that “demonizes Israel, minimizes Hamas terrorism and portrays Jews as white oppressors.”

The committee, led by Representative Tim Walberg, Republican of Michigan, began investigating the A. P. A. in December. The report details emails sent to public listservs in the days after the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, as well as internal discussions among association leadership deliberating how to publicly respond.

“We don’t agree with the report,” Dr. Williams, the head of the A. P. A., said. She added, “Since these concerns were first brought to A. P. A.’s attention, A. P. A. has taken meaningful steps to ensure that Jewish members, like all members, can participate fully and safely in the organization and the profession.”

Proponents of the report applauded the confirmation of complaints long aired by some Jewish psychologists, while others argued that it purposely conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The report cited numerous excerpts from documents in concluding that the A. P. A. promoted a climate of antisemitism. These included listserv emails in the days after the Oct. 7 attack from some association members who argued that Hamas was “protecting civilians” and deserved “kudos.” It cited a newsletter in which the A. P. A.’s community psychology division described the attack using language like “uprising.” It detailed pushback against Jewish members who wanted to form an official ethnic subgroup — similar to existing groups for Arab, Asian American and Black psychologists — including arguments that Jews had “benefited from white privilege.”

The House Republicans’ report also criticized a revised A. P. A. resolution on antisemitism, approved in February, suggesting that the new language diluted the word’s meaning.

Some groups representing Jewish psychologists and Jewish Americans celebrated the report.

“This report confirms the extent of antisemitism within the A. P. A. as well as the failure of leadership within that association to deal with it,” said Kenneth L. Marcus, the chairman and chief executive of the Brandeis Center, a nonprofit focused on combating antisemitism. For years, he said, the Brandeis Center has “gotten reports of antisemitism from mental health professionals, from students of psychology and from patients.”

In June, after Mr. Marcus’s group filed a complaint accusing the A. P. A. of marginalizing Jewish and Israeli psychologists, the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights opened a federal civil rights investigation into the organization.

But the report also reflected bitter divides, including among the Jewish members of the A. P. A., over how to define antisemitism.

Roy J. Eidelson, who is Jewish and a former president of the A. P. A.’s Society for the Study of Peace, Conflict and Violence, said he disagreed with the report’s contention that antisemitism had spread throughout the organization.

Antisemitism is discrimination, prejudice and hostility toward Jews, he argued. “It is not criticism of Israel or Israel’s actions, and it is not support for Palestinian rights,” he said.

The report called Dr. Eidelson one of the association’s “most vocal antizionist members,” citing an essay he wrote about the “weaponization of antisemitism” and noting that it was praised in 2025 by the A. P. A. president at the time, Debra Kawahara.

Dr. Eidelson said the essay was intended to describe “false charges of antisemitism” used to discredit those who had criticized the attacks on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as genocidal acts. “It’s a real frustration to me and to many Jews like me,” he said.

A related fight unfolded over the A. P. A.’s 2026 change to its public position statement on antisemitism. Its 2007 resolution stated that antisemitism “may be asserted in the context of discourse regarding the actions of the Government of Israel.” The new resolution stated that “it is antisemitic to hold Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel; to require Jews to publicly condemn Israel; to assume that Jews are more loyal to Israel than to their home countries; and to deny Jews in Israel/Palestine the right to exist and flourish as Jews on the basis of legal equality.” It also added a definition of the “weaponization” of antisemitism: “the manipulative or bad faith invocation of accusations to silence legitimate criticism, scholarship, or activism.”

The House report contended that the new resolution “greenlights” antisemitism.

Jonah Rubin, the senior manager for campus organizing at Jewish Voice for Peace, a nonprofit representing anti-Zionist Jews, which wrote a letter to the A. P. A. supporting the resolution change, said congressional investigations into universities and the A. P. A. were “worsening antisemitism, not combating it effectively, and this committee doesn’t care.”

In September, the Education Department’s National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity recommended that the department suspend the association’s commission on accreditation for 12 months, citing a “pervasive culture of antisemitism.”

Aaron Joyce, the A. P. A.’s head of accreditation, said in a statement last month that suspending accreditation would have severe consequences, including reduced funding for many accredited psychology programs that would make it more difficult for students to meet state licensure requirements.

Christina Caron is a Times reporter covering mental health.

Azeen Ghorayshi is a Times science reporter.

Five Telltale Signs of a Democratic Blowout

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Kristen Soltis Anderson

Ms. Anderson, a contributing Opinion writer, is a Republican pollster and a moderator of Opinion’s series of focus groups.

By now, the contours of the 2026 midterm elections are pretty clear: President Trump’s approval rating has tanked, and winds are blowing in a Democratic direction. Democrats have higher voter enthusiasm, and we have the normal anti-incumbent vibes coupled with overall economic discontent. The question is: How strong are those winds? Here’s what I’ll be looking at on election night.

A Texas undervote? Over half a billion dollars has been spent in the Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. (In a sign of just how wild things have gotten, a couple of weeks ago I was served anti-Talarico TV ads while watching my Florida Gators defeat the Texas Longhorns in college football … while sitting on my couch in Washington.)

It’s one of the marquee contests this year, yet I wonder about the potential undervote: That’s when voters cast ballots but don’t make a selection in a particular race. Sometimes that happens when they don’t think they know enough about the candidates to make an informed decision, though that’s almost certainly not the case here — Texas voters probably know more about Mr. Paxton and Mr. Talarico than they ever wanted to.

But I keep thinking about our Times Opinion focus group of Texas Trump voters who said they didn’t plan to vote for the scandal-plagued Mr. Paxton. Some of them found something to like in Mr. Talarico, while others found him to be out of step with their values and said they wouldn’t vote for him either. In general, Mr. Talarico’s voters like him and want to vote for him. On the other hand, many of Mr. Paxton’s voters are not exactly excited for their guy. One thing Republicans are banking on is the idea that in the end, some of them will decide Mr. Paxton is the lesser of two evils and vote for him in spite of their reservations. If our focus group participants are any indication, I wouldn’t be surprised to see a noticeable number of Texans simply leaving the Senate race blank.

The pull of partisanship. Democrats’ path to Senate control requires picking up a couple of seats in places that voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 by double digits. To do that, they’ll have to overcome a trend that has grown stronger and stronger in recent Senate elections: partisanship.

In the not-too-distant past, it wasn’t abnormal for a state to vote one way at the presidential level and another for the Senate. Montana and West Virginia would back Republicans in presidential contests but then send Jon Tester and Joe Manchin to Washington. Rhode Island, Illinois and Massachusetts gave us Republican senators in Lincoln Chafee, Mark Kirk and Scott Brown. However, the phenomenon of states voting for a party’s presidential candidate by a double-digit margin while electing a senator of the other party has largely evaporated in the Trump era, Mr. Tester and Mr. Manchin notwithstanding.

In 2024, Kansas voted for Mr. Trump by a 16-point margin. Iowa went for Mr. Trump by 13. They’re both on this year’s Democratic wish list, a list that goes into deeply red terrain, including Texas, South Carolina and (checks notes) Mississippi. For Democrats to break through in some of these deep red states, they’ll have to overcome the magnetic pull of partisanship that has characterized Senate elections in recent years.

Ohio’s upscale suburbs. In 2004, Tim Russert’s famous whiteboard said it best: Ohio, Ohio, Ohio. The state’s pivotal role in that year’s presidential election confirmed its status as the ultimate bellwether state.

In the Trump era, Ohio has turned redder at the presidential level; in 2024, Mr. Trump won it by double digits — his largest margin there ever. But the wealthy suburban Delaware County, north of Columbus, has moved in the opposite direction. In 2004, George W. Bush beat John Kerry there by a ratio of two to one. However, this highly educated and fast-growing county gave the Republican Bernie Moreno only a slim 1.5-point margin in his 2024 Senate win.

Republicans have gained among rural and blue-collar voters, even while shedding support from upscale suburbanites. If Delaware County goes blue after decades as reliable G. O. P. turf, it will illustrate the limits of that strategy.

Florida’s Ninth Congressional District. Osceola County is a perennial favorite of mine to watch on election night, and not just because I basically grew up there. It’s a heavily Latino county that went from deep blue 10 years ago to narrowly preferring Mr. Trump in 2024.

Representative Darren Soto, a Democrat, has represented the area for nearly a decade, but this year’s mid-decade redistricting in Florida has put him in a much tougher district that now includes slices of rural Central Florida and some Republican-leaning chunks of the coast brimming with conservative retirees. Whether he can hang on will probably depend on whether a blue wave, powered in part by Latino voters swinging back to Democrats, materializes.

Revenge of the youngs. For years, I’ve been sounding the alarm about Republicans’ struggles with the millennial generation. Then Gen Z came along and, by and large, appeared even further left than millennials. In 2024, my prophecies of G. O. P. generational doom were put on hold, as Mr. Trump held his losses among voters 18 to 29 to a mere 11 points and among those 30 to 44 to just four.

I suspect, though, that 2026 will reveal 2024 as more of a blip than a durable rightward trend among young adults. Though early voting data isn’t a crystal ball, analysts at VoteHub are showing a missing young Republican effect emerging. Disillusionment with the status quo has transferred from a Democratic octogenarian president to a Republican octogenarian president.

Meanwhile, Democrats have elevated a number of rising millennial stars like Mr. Talarico, Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan this midterm cycle (called the Mr. Brightside caucus by one reporter). To Republicans’ dismay, this might be the year when the selfie vote strikes back.

Trump is truly a uniter. I went from being the only democrat in my family to all of us, from my parents to my aunt and uncles, being Democrats. And not wish washy democrats. Full on “never voting for the GOP again” democrats.

The mistake is interpreting every electoral swing as ideological change. Many voters are not moving left or right so much as becoming less willing to stay put. Political parties love to mistake victory for validation. Voters are saying something much simpler: you’re next. Watching from outside America, I find myself longing for something beyond victory for either side: the return of serious American leadership.

I have been burned by the American electorate to be anything other than anxious and stressed on Election Day, much less optimistic. A time traveler could show up and tell me there’s a blue wave and I wouldn’t believe them until we get into January and everyone elected is seated.

Kristen Soltis Anderson is the author of “The Selfie Vote: Where Millennials Are Leading America (and How Republicans Can Keep Up).”

Trump Effort to Prove Rampant Noncitizen Voting Leads to Few Charges So Far

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Just 236 people have been charged with voting-fraud-related offenses by the Trump administration, despite its unsubstantiated claims that fraud is widespread.

By Madeleine Ngo

The Department of Homeland Security has mounted an extraordinary campaign to hunt for illegal voters, devoting hundreds of federal agents to the task of poring over tens of thousands of voter records and knocking on the doors of people suspected of being noncitizens who unlawfully cast ballots.

But the crusade has so far resulted in the Trump administration’s charging only about 236 people with voting-fraud-related offenses across the country since the president took office, according to the Justice Department. That includes some noncitizens accused of registering to vote but not actually casting ballots.

The figure is a minuscule share of the more than 158 million ballots cast in the 2024 general election, and falls far short of the figures cited in July by Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, who claimed without evidence that more than 250,000 potential noncitizens were registered to vote in just four states alone.

The small number of charges has further undermined President Trump’s specious claims that voting by noncitizens is pervasive and tilting elections for Democrats, and raises questions about why the Homeland Security Department has dedicated vast resources to the effort ahead of the midterm election.

“This is about delegitimizing an election that they’re very worried about,” said David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department who runs the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to support election officials. “They’re trying to manufacture evidence and they’re failing.”

The administration’s campaign to scrutinize noncitizen voters has involved a close partnership between the Homeland Security Department and the Justice Department, which has led efforts to criminally charge noncitizens with illegal voting. The Homeland Security Department’s investigatory work has also been core to recent attempts by the Justice Department to intervene in the election.

The Homeland Security Department has defended its focus on the issue, saying that it would root out election fraud wherever it could be found and ramp up deportations of noncitizens who illegally voted or registered.

The Needle, our live forecast, returns tonight

We’ll turn on our real-time estimates of who will win the Senate and House once enough votes have been reported.

Waiting for estimates

Waiting for estimates

“D. H. S. is committed to ensuring fair, honest and accurate elections,” the department said in a statement. “D. H. S. is upholding the rule of law and protecting the integrity of American elections by removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U. S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders.”

Voting by noncitizens, who are barred by law from registering to vote or casting ballots, is exceptionally rare, according to multiple studies. Critics have said the Homeland Security Department’s aggressive efforts to investigate noncitizen voters instead appear to be aimed at intimidating voters and laying the groundwork to challenge the election results.

Immigration advocacy groups have also expressed fears for months that federal agents could turn up at polling places, though as of Tuesday morning, there were no signs of immigration authorities patrolling voting sites.

Tasking hundreds of officers with scouring state voter rolls and deploying agents to interview people at their homes to root out noncitizen voters is a remarkable use of the Homeland Security Department’s powers. The largest federal law enforcement agency, the department was created in the wake of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks to help protect the country from threats.

The Trump administration has leveraged at least four of its nine main agencies to promote investigations into noncitizen voters. That includes agencies that typically focus on deportations, border management, disaster relief, and immigration applications.

Federal agents who specialize in investigating national security threats and immigration benefit fraud have been diverted to finding noncitizens on the voter rolls. Homeland security agents who usually investigate crimes like child exploitation and illegal trade have also investigated more than 150 organizations that they say may be helping noncitizens illegally register to vote.

But the department’s efforts have so far resulted in a small number of charges and little evidence that voter fraud is rampant. The bulk of the 236 charges have been made in the last nine weeks alone, according to the Justice Department, a sign that the administration has dramatically ramped up prosecutions ahead of the midterms. The proportion actually convicted of an offense could end up even smaller.

Investigations into noncitizen voters have historically followed a pattern. State or federal election officials first report that hundreds or thousands of noncitizens may be on the voter rolls. But the figures often shrink to dozens after further investigation. Each inquiry ends with few, if any, prosecutions.

“The massive amount of resources that have been devoted to this operation have uncovered only tiny numbers of individuals who may have voted or registered to vote,” said Wendy R. Weiser, the vice president for democracy at the Brennan Center for Justice. “It’s just reinforcing what is known and actually raises questions as to what is the purpose of this operation.”

Some of the Trump administration’s claims of large numbers of noncitizens on the voter rolls in certain states have also unraveled. After homeland security officials claimed that nearly 16,000 people might be noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada, they sent to the state a list of 185 names that had “gone through a rigorous manual review process.” State officials later determined that all 185 were citizens.

Some of the Homeland Security Department’s efforts have faced legal setbacks. Last month, a federal judge in California restricted the department from carrying out field interviews in nine states as part of an effort to investigate noncitizen voters. In September, a federal judge ruled that the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which leads the federal response to disasters, could not withhold emergency preparedness grants from states that refuse to make changes to their election processes, including verifying voters’ citizenship.

But that has not deterred the department from pressing ahead with other investigations.

In late October, a group of officers with U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — an agency within the Homeland Security Department — were directed to review about 15,000 cases of people suspected of illegally registering to vote in California, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

The directive is a continuation of an earlier nationwide effort by the agency to examine voter records and federal databases to generate leads for ICE agents to further investigate potential cases of noncitizen voters. The agency’s investigation led immigration officers to identify more than 20,000 people the agency claimed illegally registered to vote in California, according to court documents.

The new effort underscores the Trump administration’s fixation on California, which the Justice Department recently sued to try to force the state to set aside ballots from the 20,000 people the administration suspects are “likely noncitizens.” In a court filing, data scientists analyzing that list of voters said they found that more than 40 percent of the people on the list do not appear on California’s voter rolls. The analysis also found that the list included thousands of people who appear to be citizens.

After a federal judge rejected the effort, the administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to require that California set aside the ballots. The court rejected the request just hours later.

In an October email reviewed by The Times, Paul Gleason, a homeland security official, told officials involved with the new effort that officers would be examining registered voters in California “with no evidence of actual voting.” It is illegal for noncitizens to falsely certify that they are citizens when registering to vote, even if they never ultimately cast a ballot. Some immigrants, though, have said that they inadvertently registered while obtaining or renewing driver’s licenses, pointing to voter laws that have made it easier for people to register to vote at motor vehicle agencies.

In a September email reviewed by the Times, Mr. Gleason said that immigration officers had already reviewed more than 150,000 cases and made over 66,000 referrals to ICE for further investigation as part of the nationwide effort to find noncitizen voters. Several former homeland security officials said in interviews that the number of referrals amounted to a massive workload for ICE agents tasked with following up on the leads.

Proponents of the administration praised it for investigating a problem they believe deserves more scrutiny. Kenneth T. Cuccinelli II, an acting deputy homeland security secretary during the first Trump administration, said he thought it was clearly appropriate for homeland security agents to investigate noncitizen voting and help secure elections.

“I realize that the extent or scope of the problem itself is debated,” Mr. Cuccinelli said in a recent interview. “But what can’t be debated is that the issue exists.”

But some former homeland security officials questioned why the department has devoted ample resources to the effort and tasked federal agents with investigating the rare issue of noncitizen voting.

“Should you be pulling special agents and federal criminal investigators off national security issues to focus on that? When I weigh out public safety threats, the answer is absolutely not,” said Eric Balliet, who worked at Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigations arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, for more than 20 years.

I’ve been talking to current and former Homeland Security officials for months about the administration’s effort to root out noncitizens who illegally voted. Created in the wake of the Sept. 11 attacks to protect the country from national security threats, the department has partially redirected agencies typically focused on deportations, border management, disaster relief and immigration applications toward investigating noncitizen voters. Yet those efforts have so far resulted in a small number of charges and little evidence that voter fraud is rampant.

Glenn Thrush, Amy Schoenfeld Walker and Seamus Hughes contributed reporting.

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.

Strike on Ukraine Humanitarian Hub Is Feared to Be Among War’s Deadliest

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Hours after the Russian attack, which killed at least 31 and left dozens missing, the United States said that peace talks with the two countries would resume after nine months.

By Siobhán O’Grady and Liubov Sholudko

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

A day after a Russian glide bomb attack killed at least 31 Ukrainians at a school distributing medicine and food, emergency workers braved armed Russian drones on Tuesday as they searched for dozens of people still missing, officials said.

It could take days to determine the exact toll: The threat of continued Russian strikes limits rescuers to short bursts of activity. But the attack was the deadliest against civilians in the southern Zaporizhzhia region during nearly five years of war, and could amount to one of the deadliest of the entire conflict.

Hours after the strike on Monday, the Trump administration’s peace envoy, Steve Witkoff, announced that talks among the United States, Russia and Ukraine would be held early next week in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates.

The meeting, the first since February involving all three countries, would address postwar security arrangements and steps toward peace, Mr. Witkoff said. The Russian and Ukrainian governments confirmed on Tuesday that they would send negotiators to Abu Dhabi.

But even as the Trump administration tries to restart peace talks, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said that Russia had made clear its intention to continue the war by striking the humanitarian hub in the village of Komyshuvakha on Monday.

Russia hit the village with at least nine glide bombs, each loaded with around 3,000 pounds of explosives, Ukrainian officials said. The attack served as a stark reminder of the limits of a rare local cease-fire in the neighboring Kherson region, which ended a day before.

That six-day truce allowed the evacuation of hundreds of civilians facing starvation in the besieged city of Oleshky, which Russia has occupied since 2022.

The school that was hit in the village of Komyshuvakha doubled as a bomb shelter. The attack trapped civilians and rescue workers inside.

At least two rescue workers and four police officers who arrived to treat the wounded after the first bomb landed were killed in the subsequent round of bombing, Ukraine’s emergency response services said. Russia has long used this tactic, known as a double tap, to target emergency workers responding to attacks.

On Tuesday, Russia continued to send armed drones over the village, Ukrainian officials said. About 50 people remained missing, they said.

“Every single hour, the rescue operations are being interrupted because of F. P. V. drone threats,” said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of Zaporizhzhia’s regional military administration, referring to first-person-view drones. “It’s a cynical thing to do.”

Residents had visited the school each week to receive humanitarian aid, Mr. Zelensky said on social media. “This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation or real justice,” he wrote.

The temporary cease-fire in the neighboring Kherson region lasted from Tuesday through Sunday. The evacuation operation in Oleshky raised hopes for further cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow to ensure the safety of civilians near the front line. It was the first truce of its kind since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

The deal, brokered in part by the American first lady, Melania Trump, offered “a moment when the next steps could have shown that a move towards peace was possible,” Mr. Zelensky wrote. But after the bombing of Komyshuvakha, he added, “Russia is sending a completely opposite signal — Russia is counting on further killings.”

Zaporizhzhia is one of four Ukrainian regions that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia claimed to have annexed in 2022, though his forces never managed to seize Zaporizhzhia’s regional capital, a city of the same name. The front line stretches across the region, and fierce fighting has continued for years, including around Komyshuvakha, where Russian drones have tormented civilians who stayed behind.

The school was built after the full-scale invasion with a reinforced concrete basement that was used as a shelter. But by the time the school was ready for class, the situation in Komyshuvakha had become grim. While the front line had not significantly shifted, drones could now fly much farther, leaving Komyshuvakha trapped in the middle of what is known as the “kill zone.”

Students attended the school for only a few months before officials evacuated all children from the area. Adults were urged to leave as well, but many hesitated for common reasons: They had animals to care for, or they feared being a burden in a new town away from their own land. Many of those who stayed were older or disabled.

Each Monday, they received aid from volunteers at the school. This week, when the first glide bomb struck the village, residents rushed to the school’s basement for shelter. But the heavier bombs that came next were designed to cause mass destruction, officials said.

The concrete could not withstand the impact, and many people hiding from the attack were buried underground.

Mr. Semikin rushed to the scene on Monday, stopping to take cover from Russian drones along the way, he said. A video he posted showed that little of the school remained. Behind him, smoke rose over piles of debris.

Siobhán O’Grady is a Ukraine correspondent for The Times, based in Kyiv.

What Caused a Jet to Dive Nose First Into the Ground?

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Florida Learjet Crash

Advertisement

Supported by

Ice, experts said, can change the shape of a plane’s wing, disrupting its aerodynamics.

By Alexander Nazaryan

Ice. Turbulence. Human error. Aviation experts believe that some combination of those factors caused a Learjet on its way to the Bahamas from Texas to crash on Sunday afternoon outside Palm Beach, Fla.

Nine people were killed in the crash, which left behind a bomb-like crater and questions that could take months to answer.

Images of the airplane hitting the ground, as well as audio of its terrifying last moments — recorded in exchanges between air traffic control and the 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras — have proliferated online, adding immediacy to the harrowing scene.

For now, the most basic of questions remains unanswered: What happened?

Federal officials cautioned that it was too early in the investigation to make a determination but that ice and the weather were “certainly a factor.”

On its way from Austin, Texas, at 35,000 feet, the two-engine Bombardier-made jet flew into a thunderstorm cell around 12:48 p. m.

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” Ms. Filgueiras told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center.

As moist storm air rises and cools, ice crystals form. “Anytime you get moisture up in that cold air, you can get icing conditions,” said Robert E. Joslin, a professor of practice in the department of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.

“Flying in icing conditions can present operational risks,” according to the National Transportation Safety Board. Ice can affect the airframe and engines, which can make it harder to maintain the plane’s path and speed and to remain level.

As little as a quarter-inch of ice on the edge of a wing can “cause sudden departure from controlled flight,” and ice accumulation on some equipment “can cause flight instruments to cease operating and can affect airspeed, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator indications,” according to the N. T. S. B.

“It sounds like the plane iced when they flew through the cell,” said Daniel Bubb, a former pilot who now teaches at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and is the deputy director of the Nevada Aerospace Hall of Fame. “They thought at first it was light to moderate icing. But then it sounds like it got really severe.”

Airplanes stay aloft according to Bernoulli’s principle. Wings are engineered so that air moves faster over the wing than beneath it. That creates a pressure differential that, in turn, creates lift. Ice changes the shape of the wing, disrupting the aerodynamic balance necessary for flight.

“The plane can become almost uncontrollable,” Dr. Bubb said. He said he believed that the plane might have stalled. “They couldn’t recover from it, and they crashed,” he said.

Dr. Joslin said that as the Learjet started to lose altitude, its aerodynamic burden would have become untenable. “When those airloads get excessive, it can also lead to structural failure, which can exacerbate the situation,” he said.

In addition, Dr. Joslin said, “ice accumulation on the cockpit windscreens can restrict the pilots’ view of the aircraft, which is critical as a backup for avoiding terrain collision, aircraft collision and adverse weather.”

As Ms. Filgueiras and her co-pilot were trying to maneuver their way out of an emergency, they could have been flying blind. Gregory A. Feith, a former senior N. T. S. B. investigator, said the crash reminded him of American Eagle Flight 4184, which he investigated in 1994 in Roselawn, Ind. That crash killed all 68 people onboard.

“It’s almost identical,” he said.

But even if ice was a factor, human error may also have played a role.

A Learjet 60 has three systems for de-icing: electric heaters in the forward edge of the wings and horizontal stabilizers; an inflatable rubber bladder that can expand to break up ice; and the ability to circulate warm exhaust over the wings.

But for any of the de-icing systems to work, “the pilots have to activate them,” said Mike McCormick, the former director of air traffic control at the Federal Aviation Administration and a professor at Embry-Riddle.

“So that’s going to be the big question,” he added. “Were the pilots aware of and were they informed that they were entering into weather conditions that would contribute to ice accumulations?"

Mr. Feith said that the Learjet most likely encountered “clear ice,” suspended water droplets that cover much more area than other types of ice encountered in flight. The pilots may have underestimated the damaging effect the ice had on the flight controls, Mr. Feith said. They then sought to deal with the turbulence by climbing, which may have caused a “violent pitchover,” he said, causing what’s known as a “tailplane stall.”

Investigators have not yet revealed whether any structural failure took place, but some social media users pointed out that the plane’s horizontal stabilizers appear to be missing in images from right before the jet hit the ground.

“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact,” Tom Chapman, a National Transportation Safety Board member, said at a news conference on Monday.

That could suggest an additional culprit — turbulence.

As the plane approached the storm cell, Ms. Filgueiras described “moderate turbulence,” with the Learjet experiencing changes in altitude of 600 to 700 feet, according to her exchanges with the flight control center in Miami.

“That’s a lot of displacement for a turbulence encounter,” said Patrick Smith, a pilot who writes about aviation at Ask the Pilot. Mr. Smith said that the horizontal stabilizers could have been “torn away by unusually strong turbulence or improper reaction to unusually strong turbulences,” though like the other experts interviewed for this article, he said it was too early to tell.

Dr. Bubb said there was one clear lesson amid the devastation.

“This, to me, is just a textbook example of exactly what we’re taught when we’re pilots, and that is, don’t fly through thunderstorms, because you just don’t know their severity,” he said.

Karoun Demirjian contributed reporting.

A Test for Israeli Democracy: Should Jews Ask Arabs to Join the Government?

The New York Times November 03, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Arab lawmakers give opponents of Benjamin Netanyahu a clear majority in the Parliament. But many Jewish lawmakers are trying to avoid relying on them.

By David M. Halbfinger and Natan Odenheimer

David Halbfinger reported from Jerusalem and Natan Odenheimer from Tel Aviv.

Israel’s democracy is facing a huge test after Arab political parties made historic gains in last week’s election.

And opponents of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are facing an enormous dilemma over whether Arab lawmakers should now be given a share of power in a new government.

Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents secured a clear majority in the Parliament by winning 67 out of 120 seats. But 19 of these were won by the Arab parties, and their inclusion in a governing coalition is seen as so problematic by many Israeli Jews that opposition leaders are putting themselves through contortions looking for ways to form a government that would not rely on Arab lawmakers.

The aversion to building a government with the two main Arab factions — the United Arab List, or Raam, and the Joint List, which comprises three smaller parties — is enormously frustrating to political activists who helped drive Arab turnout to a near-record high of 77 percent last week.

“Why is it so complicated? A vote of an Arab citizen of Israel should equal no less than the vote of a Jewish citizen,” said Alon-Lee Green, a founder of the Jewish-Arab organization Standing Together.

The efforts to sideline the Arab parties also fuel complaints among many Arab citizens, who represent about 20 percent of the country’s population, that Israeli Jews welcome their participation in the political process only up to the point where they might wield real power.

“This is the problem with Israeli democracy,” said Thabet Abu Rass, a longtime advocate for Arab-Jewish partnership. “It’s a democracy for Jews, but it’s a Jewish state for Arab citizens like me. We Arab citizens are entitled to the same rights, and would like to use them to dictate who’s going to lead the country.”

“But some Jews say no, democracy is for Jews only,” he said. This has become especially true since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, he said.

Indeed, welcoming the Arab parties into a new government, particularly at a time of conflict, is dismissed by many Jewish Israelis as unworkable, overly risky, and even unconscionable.

Few would deny that racism plays a part. But Israeli Jews also view the particular Arab parties — Raam, headed by Mansour Abbas, and the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen — with varying degrees of skepticism.

Mr. Abbas’s party has its roots in the Muslim Brotherhood movement, as does Hamas, a history that right-wing critics often highlight in denouncing him.

But Mr. Abbas was once the first lawmaker from an independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, and he has won many Jewish admirers by working with Jewish lawmakers. He has focused on domestic issues affecting Arab citizens, like violent crime and discriminatory housing policies, and devoted little attention to Israel’s policies in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Joint List’s members, by contrast, have focused more on Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in the occupied territories and have generally preferred to criticize government policy from the opposition. Some have denounced Israeli military actions, assailed Israel’s war in Gaza as genocide or referred to slain Palestinian militants as “martyrs.”

“Abbas managed to make himself more legitimate because he made it very clear he’s in politics to look after the domestic affairs of his own community,” said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group. “But you don’t hear the same music from the members of the Joint List.”

Mr. Plesner noted that even Mr. Abbas, when asked whether he supports toppling Hamas, deflects the question. “Any Zionist Israeli expects that any government would work toward toppling Hamas, because of what Hamas did and wants to do to Israel,” Mr. Plesner said.

Mr. Abbas and Mr. Jabareen bristle at such questions as demeaning and tantamount to demanding loyalty oaths. Both men have condemned the Oct. 7 attack, and Mr. Abbas has said that such violence has only harmed the Palestinian cause.

Before last week’s election, Arab parties never held more than 15 seats in Parliament. Until Mr. Abbas joined the governing coalition in 2021, Arab party leaders generally resisted taking part in governments and thus sharing in responsibility for Israel’s occupation and military actions.

But discriminatory policies, like the demolition of Arab citizens’ homes built without official permits, and soaring crime in Arab towns that Arab Israelis attribute to police negligence, have prodded lawmakers like Mr. Jabareen and others in the Joint List to vow to do all they can to drive Mr. Netanyahu’s government from power.

Discrimination against Arab citizens also undercuts Israel when it trumpets its democratic credentials beyond its borders.

For the anti-Netanyahu opposition, led by the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the options for assembling a governing coalition are all uncomfortable.

He could try forming a minority government of fewer than 61 seats in which one or both of the Arab parties would be left outside the coalition but would cooperate to some degree, opposing no-confidence votes in Parliament. Or he could agree to a unity government, if Mr. Netanyahu or some of his allies were to accept the opposition’s terms to share power.

Mr. Eisenkot could also accept a new round of elections in hopes of a better result, though many in the opposition fear this would benefit Mr. Netanyahu, whose alliance netted only 53 seats in the balloting last week.

Rula Daood, another leader of Standing Together, said that by shying away from including Arab parties in a new government, Mr. Eisenkot was playing into Mr. Netanyahu’s hands. She accused the prime minister of seeking to delegitimize the Arab vote by claiming, without evidence, that Arab parties stole the election.

Zvi Hauser, a former center-right lawmaker, warned in the newspaper Israel Hayom that bringing the Arab parties into government could cause a catastrophe. Coalition members, he said, would hold “worldviews that disagree even on basic questions of national security.”

Mr. Hauser wrote that every vote on policies affecting Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, enforcement of housing rules in Arab communities or the demolition of the homes of those who attack Israelis could become “a test of coalition survival.”

Yossi Klein Halevi, an author and senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute in Jerusalem, said that he was crestfallen last week when Mr. Abbas, whom he admired, sidestepped a television interviewer’s challenge that he label Hamas a terrorist organization.

Mr. Halevi has denounced Mr. Netanyahu for dividing the Israeli mainstream into his coalition — which puts a priority on Israel’s Jewish nature — and an opposition that prioritizes Israel’s democratic values. But Mr. Halevi said he feared that if Mr. Eisenkot formed a government relying on the two Arab parties, it would destroy the possibility of repairing that rupture for a generation.

“We will be seen as preferring anti-Zionists to our fellow Jews,” he said. “And that will be seen very widely by Jews on the right, and even some in the center, as a betrayal of the most basic Jewish solidarity.”

Among Mr. Eisenkot’s allies, Yair Golan of the left-wing Democrats party has spoken most enthusiastically of Arab party support. In an interview, he said Israel needed to cure itself of the “psychosis” of treating Arab citizens as potential traitors or second-class citizens, arguing that the Arab public had overwhelmingly proved its loyalty and solidarity since Oct. 7.

“They are a part of us,” he said. “We are on the same team.”

Mr. Golan, a former deputy chief of staff in the Israeli military, also dismissed the idea that it was risky to national security to include Arab lawmakers in the cabinet, saying that they would be excluded from the smaller security cabinet where operational decisions are made.

Mr. Golan said he envisioned a government including Raam and relying on outside support from the Joint List. He compared this to the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in the 1990s, which led effectively with just 56 seats in Parliament and outside Arab backing.

Some Israelis say the election results have presented Israel with a golden opportunity. By making common cause with Arab lawmakers, they say, the opposition could finally establish a national commission of inquiry into the security failures that led up to the Oct. 7 attacks and adopt military conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, who have long been exempt.

“It’s the most delicious moment,” said Yosef Abramowitz, a Jewish renewable-energy entrepreneur who said he had voted for Raam.

“Everybody has to grow up — now,” he said. “The Arabs have to break free of the Palestinian narrative as their organizing thesis. And Israeli Jewish society has to say that a national commission of inquiry and a full military draft are more important than the mythology that all Arabs are terrorists and terror supporters.”

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Natan Odenheimer is a Times reporter in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Trump’s Immigration Dragnet Sweeps Up Ukrainian Truckers Who Fled War

The New York Times November 03, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

At least a dozen Ukrainian truck drivers were arrested this summer, according to a representative for Ukraine. Several remain in detention.

By Jazmine Ulloa

The 55-year-old Ukrainian truck driver was hauling a load of cars into Oklahoma when he stopped for a routine inspection at a desolate weigh station.

The driver, Mykhailo Shekhtman, had fled Ukraine’s war with Russia, settled in Georgia under a Biden-era humanitarian program to assist Ukrainians. But on that cold February evening, Oklahoma state troopers took him into custody, believing he was unlawfully present in the United States, according to a Homeland Security arrest report. It showed he had no criminal record.

“I asked, ‘Why are you arresting me? On what grounds are you arresting me?’” he recalled in an October interview from a detention facility outside of Oklahoma City.

Mr. Shekhtman is among the more than 330,000 Ukrainians who reside in the United States through Uniting for Ukraine and Temporary Protected Status, humanitarian forms of immigration protection that allowed people escaping the war to temporarily live and work legally in the country.

But the Trump administration regards the entrance of many Ukrainians and other migrants under the Biden administration as unlawful. Some Ukrainians are now living in legal and financial limbo after the federal government suspended the Uniting for Ukraine program and is now considering whether to let the largest deportation protection program, Temporary Protected Status, expire.

For Ukrainian truck drivers, the crosscurrents have been even greater because of a massive federal and state crackdown on noncitizens holding commercial driver’s licenses. Multiagency sweeps have intensified in states such as Indiana, Oklahoma and Texas, entangling hundreds of immigrant truck drivers who have been detained during traffic stops and what used to be routine inspections at weigh stations and highway checkpoints. At least a dozen Ukrainian truckers were detained in Oklahoma and Indiana this summer, according to a representative for Ukraine.

Some Ukrainian truck drivers have been deported to countries like Turkey, where they have no ties, according to interviews with truck drivers and immigration lawyers. Others have been sent back to Ukraine, a country grinding through its fifth year of war, where residents face military enlistment, occupation and relentless Russian bombardment. The Department of Homeland Security did not disclose the total number of Ukrainian truck drivers who have been arrested or deported.

Mr. Shekhtman, who has been detained since his February arrest, is awaiting a hearing on whether he will be granted bond. Through his attorney, he provided documents showing he has repeatedly reported receiving inadequate food and medical care, describing deteriorating eyesight and kidney pain.

“I feel like I’ve been cheated,” Mr. Shekhtman said from detention. “I was invited here to be protected from the war, and so on. I hoped I’d come to a democratic country, and that everything here would be fine.”

In a statement to the The New York Times, D. H. S. confirmed Mr. Shekhtman’s arrest, saying the Border Patrol had previously arrested him after he unlawfully entered the United States on April 21, 2024, before the Biden administration released him into the country. Mr. Shekhtman and his lawyer assert that he had been granted permission to enter the United States before he arrived as part of the Uniting for Ukraine program.

The agency said Mr. Shekhtman had been evaluated by specialists for vision and bladder problems and that he “continues to be monitored and receives treatment for his acute and chronic medical conditions.”

On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced the results of the latest operation in Tulsa, Okla., standing with state enforcement officials in front of a big rig adorned with images of the American flag and a bald eagle. Over several days, officers across 15 states had stopped more than 1,000 commercial trucks, arresting about 40 immigrant drivers, including some with serious criminal charges, he said. The drivers hailed from 19 countries, including Ukraine.

“These individuals came over, and they’re putting those that are driving on the road with them in jeopardy,” Mr. Mullin said.

Defending the administration’s crackdown, he also contended that allowing unauthorized immigrants to operate commercial trucks was reckless and dangerous to public safety, saying many do not speak English.

The plight of Ukrainian immigrants has exposed deep rifts in the Republican Party and prompted clashes between immigration opponents and a coalition of evangelical groups, businesses and local lawmakers who have pressured federal lawmakers to shield Ukrainians from deportation.

Representative William R. Keating, a Democrat of Massachusetts, and Representative Brian K. Fitzpatrick, a Republican of Pennsylvania, and Marcy Kaptur, a Democrat of Ohio, have sponsored bipartisan legislation that would create permanent pathways to legal residency for Ukrainians. Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican of Alaska, sponsored another bill in her chamber this year. Both bills, however, remain stalled.

The administration announced this month that Ukrainians could retain T. P. S. for now, but the program’s future remains precarious. “They pay taxes, their children are often in honor rolls in schools, they do their share,” said Anna Move, co-founder of the Leonid Foundation, which assists Ukrainian refugees. Yet without stability, she said, many are debating whether they must now go.

Enforcement against Ukrainian truck drivers has centered on the freight arteries running through the Great Plains and the Midwest. Karl Ahlgren, a licensed chaplain and diplomat representing Ukraine in Oklahoma, and Ukrainian community leaders have tracked more than a dozen Ukrainian truck drivers swept into immigration custody in Oklahoma and Indiana alone this summer.

At least five remain detained in Oklahoma, according to Mr. Ahlgren, who has visited them at Oklahoma detention centers. “These guys are the sole breadwinners for their families,” Mr. Ahlgren said.

Tim Tipton, commissioner of public safety in Oklahoma, called the enforcement operations critical to spotting human trafficking and preventing deadly crashes.

“This is a huge public safety issue in Oklahoma when it comes to somebody driving an 80,000-pound truck who has not been trained properly, can’t read or speak English,” he said.

The federal campaign against immigrant truck drivers began in earnest in April, when President Trump issued an executive order directing transportation agencies to enforce a long-dormant regulation requiring commercial drivers to read and speak proficient English.

Since then, federal officials have stopped issuing worker visas for commercial truck drivers, revoked the accreditation of thousands of truck driving schools and issued emergency rules to prohibit commercial driver’s licenses for asylum seekers, refugees and other immigrants with temporary legal status. The efforts escalated following two fatal crashes last year involving Sikh immigrant truck drivers that killed six people, leading to criminal charges against the drivers.

The pressure on Ukrainians in the United States is unfolding as Moscow has intensified its air assault in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

Mr. Shekhtman recalled enduring constant missile strikes back in his native Vinnytsia in central Ukraine. He said goodbye to several friends and relatives who went off to fight in the war and never came back. He was a professional truck driver in Ukraine, Mr. Shekhtman said.

In April 2024, he arrived in the United States and found a home near Savannah, Ga. Once he underwent criminal background checks and obtained his work permit, he passed a state driving test, acquiring a license that allowed him to drive a small truck and trailer to haul passenger vehicles. The pathway had been well worn by other Ukrainians drawn to the industry for its substantial pay and established networks of Ukrainian and immigrant drivers.

But throughout his 2024 election campaign, Mr. Trump argued that President Biden had let in too many immigrants and that too many were exploiting temporary humanitarian programs. Since taking office, he has rolled back some of those programs and sought to restrict others.

Mr. Shekhtman said that before his arrest, he had filed an application with U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to extend his U4U humanitarian parole for two more years and had received an appointment date to provide his biometric data. But, he said, he missed the appointment because he was held in detention.

Jazmine Ulloa is a national reporter covering immigration for The Times.

Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist

Wired November 03, 2026

For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.

Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”

At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.

Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”

While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.

Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote

Wired November 03, 2026

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.

Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.

Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.

Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.

“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag

Wired November 03, 2026

Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.

Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).

On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.

That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.

Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.

Roli’s Lumi keyboard.

Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.

Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.

“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”

The Roli Airwave.

“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”

Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.

While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.

“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”

The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.

Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix. me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.

Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.

He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.

“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”
