Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences

Wired November 01, 2026

This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.

“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”

The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.

Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”

It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.

Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.

“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.

Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.

“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.

Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.

TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”

Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.

“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look

Wired November 01, 2026

Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.

The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.

According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.

The process that shaped this system could repeat itself in our own. In about 5 billion years, the sun will exhaust its fuel and expand into a red giant. During this phase, it could engulf nearby bodies, like the closest planets. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf. Any rocky bodies that survive this transformation could break apart and form a debris disk around the dead star, like the one astronomers are now observing in J1328−1450.

But the white dwarf’s two debris rings hint at another possibility. Their structure appears to be shaped by bodies that astronomers have not yet been able to identify directly. The data suggest that, following the star’s transformation, at least two planetary objects may have survived among the remnants of that system.

Researchers believe these two bodies could be very different in size. The one closest to the white dwarf would measure just a few kilometers in diameter, while the more distant one could be as large as Pluto or even the moon. Their interaction with the surrounding material would explain the formation of the two rings, although it has not yet been confirmed that they exist as separate objects. An alternative possibility is that the structure originates from different parts of a single planet-like body, such as its crust and core.

The Best Chromebooks and Googlebooks

Wired November 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Chromebooks are dead. Long live Googlebooks. OK, that’s an exaggeration, but Chromebooks seem to be on their way out. Google has introduced a new line of laptops, Googlebooks, which certainly look like an evolution from Chrome OS. Google announced that standard Chromebooks will remain in the lineup for the foreseeable future, but it also stated some of the latest models will be eligible for an update to the new Googlebook operating system.

Five Googlebook models have been released so far, and I’ve been testing them for the past couple of weeks. Despite being some of the most premium laptops Google has ever had in its laptop ecosystem, that doesn’t mean you should rush out and buy one. First-generation products always come with their fair share of compromises, and that’s certainly true here. As someone who’s been testing Chromebooks for over a decade, here are my suggestions on which to buy—and which to skip.

For more recommendations, check out Best Laptops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best Android Tablets, and Best Android Phones.

Acer

Best Buy

Unlike my Windows or MacBook laptop recommendations, I’m starting with something on the cheaper end of the spectrum. Despite Google’s best efforts, I still believe most people looking for a Chromebook in 2026 choose price first. Chromebooks have always been pitched as a cheaper alternative to PCs and Macs, and that’s still their strongest attribute—even with the arrival of Googlebook. And that’s why the Acer Chromebook Plus 516 is at the top of my list.

It often sells for under $500, cheaper than any Windows laptop I’d recommend buying. One reason is the responsive, smooth-feeling touchpad. That goes a long way toward improving the day-to-day experience of using the laptop. I wasn’t annoyed every time I had to click-and-drag or select a bit of text.

The Chromebook Plus 516’s biggest weakness is definitely the screen, which is true of almost every cheap Chromebook I’ve tested. The colors are ugly and desaturated, giving everything a sickly green tint. It’s also not the sharpest, as it stretches 1920 x 1200 pixels across a large 16-inch screen. But for usability and performance, the Acer Chromebook Plus 516 is a great value, pairing an Intel Core i3 processor with 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. At $350 when it's on sale, it’s a steal.

The Asus Chromebook CX14 and CX15 can sometimes drop to as low as $130. Unlike the Acer above, these are not “Chromebook Plus” models, so they can be configured with less RAM and storage and even use lower-powered processors. That’s exactly what you get in the cheaper configurations of the CX14 and CX15. I definitely recommend the version with 8 GB of RAM, but regardless of what you choose, the CX14 and the larger CX15 are mildly attractive laptops for the price.

Asus

Best Buy

I appreciate the relatively thin bezels and chassis of the CX14 and CX15, as well as the larger touchpad and comfortable keyboard. The CX15 even comes in a striking blue color. The touchpad isn’t great, nor is the display. Like the Acer Chromebook Plus 516, it suffers from poor color reproduction and only goes up to 250 nits of brightness. Its webcam is only 720p, which makes video calls a bit rough. But that’s true of nearly all the competition (and there isn’t much).

Of the two models, I definitely prefer the CX14. It lacks the number pad and off-center touchpad of the CX15—two laptop features I’ve always found awkward to use. Look, no one’s going to love using a computer that costs less than $200, but if it’s what you can afford, the Asus Chromebook CX14 will at least get you by without too much frustration.

Whatever you do, don’t just peruse Amazon and buy your kid whatever ancient Chromebook is selling for $100. It’s worth the extra cash to get something with better battery life, a more modern look, and decent performance.

Googlebooks share a lot in common with Chromebooks. These devices run a custom version of Android (Googlebook OS) that looks and behaves more like Chrome OS than the phone variant you might be used to. Like Chromebooks, Googlebooks get the full version of the Chrome web browser, which can be updated separately from the operating system—something Chromebooks can’t do. Googlebooks can also run Google Play Android apps natively, meaning they perform faster—more like they do on an Android phone or tablet.

The best aspect of a Googlebook is the seamless integration with Android. As a Google Pixel user, I love how easy it is to send and receive texts or even directly control apps my phone—similar to what Macs can currently do with iPhones. The Gemini-based AI features feel like smaller stakes by comparison, though the AI-based context menu can be handy. But like so much day-one software, it’s full of bugs and small issues that will hopefully be resolved. The inclusion of a year of Google Gemini is the same deal that was offered to Chromebook Plus devices.

The specs are also a major difference between Googlebooks and Chromebooks. All of the available Googlebooks come with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, on par with high-end Windows laptops or the MacBook Air.

Acer

Best Buy

Price is the biggest hurdle with the Googlebook platform in this first iteration. That’s why the Acer Googlebook 14 feels like the best overall option right now, which comes in at the cheapest of the available options. It’s priced closest to higher-end Chromebooks like the Lenovo Chromebook 14 or Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514—two devices I like a lot. The OLED display on the Acer Googlebook 14 is far superior, though, with a 2880 x 1800 resolution and 120-Hz refresh rate. That display is sharper, brighter, faster, and more colorful than any Chromebook.

Dell

Google

Best Buy

My runner-up pick is the Dell XPS Googlebook. This laptop best exemplifies the idea of the Googlebook, emphasizing portability, battery life, and high-end design. In comparison, the HP Googlebook is slightly thinner, the Asus Googlebook is lighter and has more ports, and the Acer Googlebook is cheaper. But the XPS Googlebook is the only one with a smaller 13-inch screen, which really shrinks the device’s overall footprint. It uses the same chassis as the latest Dell XPS 13, refreshed this year. The XPS 13 is one of my all-time favorite laptops you can buy right now, so it’s no surprise I like this Googlebook, too. Like the Windows version, the XPS Googlebook doesn't include a headphone jack—something to consider.

Both the Acer and Dell Googlebooks use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite processor, rather than the Intel chip the HP and Asus use. Unfortunately, none of the Googlebooks offer battery life that can compete with what you get on the Windows side. That’s a disappointment, because we know how efficient those Snapdragon chips can be. Plus, an M5 chip in the MacBook Air still considerably outperforms devices, even in browser speed (as tested in Speedometer 3.1). On the other hand, Chromebooks have also been behind in battery life for the past few years.

As good as the hardware is, don't be surprised if you run into a fair number of bugs in the Googlebook software. On Intel models, some Chrome extensions just plain won't load. Meanwhile, performance on Android apps can feel a little slow and clunky. And then there's the compatibility issue of Android apps themselves. While they run much faster than on Chromebooks, that doesn't mean they're all properly optimized for keyboard and touchpad. Google finally updated some of its own apps to support keyboard and touchpad (like Google Docs), but you still can't normally select text with the touchpad in Microsoft Outlook. An app like Spotify, meanwhile, technically works fine, but is still built for touch and looks weird to use on a laptop. This situation will almost certainly be improved over time, but in most cases, I just reverted to the web apps in Chrome to avoid having to guess and check on how optimized these apps are. On the other hand, that defeats one of the big advantages of Googlebooks over Chromebooks.

I also really wish Google had let manufacturers start with either less memory or less storage. The main issue I have with these Googlebooks is the expensive starting prices—and to me, that’s the main reason they don’t get much interest. It leaves you not appreciating the extra performance—and instead, wondering why you can’t get one for cheaper. So far, Googlebooks don’t feel like a proper Windows or Mac alternative as a premium offering when it comes to performance, nor the economic option like the Chromebooks they are intended to supplant.

Acer

Best Buy

Speaking of cheaper, there’s one Chromebook I’d recommend that has the premium hardware of a Googlebook without the exorbitant price. That’s the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. It’s a compact, modern-feeling laptop at just 0.61 inches thick. The white chassis is pretty, too. The MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 processor is also important: a very efficient chip that delivers much longer battery life than your average Chromebook. The review unit I tested had a sharp display, which made the laptop feel premium. However, I can’t find that model for sale online right now, so only this more basic, lower-priced version is available. The touchpad and keyboard feel great; it comes with extra ports, 12 GB of RAM, and it can even handle up to three 4K monitors.

Google mentioned that some Chromebooks will be upgradeable to Googlebook OS at some point. Unfortunately, the company hasn’t yet revealed which models will be compatible (or when it will be available), but I imagine the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 would be a perfect candidate.

We’ve tested dozens and dozens of Chromebooks over the past years, reviewing every major release across the price spectrum. Many of these are no longer available to purchase. I stand by my picks above, but here are a few standouts from our testing that are still worth considering for the right person.

Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 for $999: For a while, this was my absolute favorite Chromebook. In many ways, nothing quite compares to it. It came out in 2025 and set a level of quality that had never existed in Chromebooks. The OLED screen is certainly part of the equation, as is the MediaTek Kompanion Ultra processor, which gives it really solid performance and battery life, just like the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Unfortunately, the price of the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 has risen substantially over the past few months, and discounts are incredibly rare. At $999, you’re better off getting a Googlebook.

Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 for $479: Chromebooks don’t tend to be lookers, but Asus breaks tradition with the Chromebook Plus CX34 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s wrapped in a gorgeous white shell that, while plastic, felt durable in my testing. I’ve reviewed many bland, gray Chromebooks, and I found myself reaching for the CX34 more because of its attractive design. The hardware is typical for a Chromebook Plus, and it felt responsive even when I had my usual complement of more than a dozen tabs and a handful of apps running. Unfortunately, this model doesn’t come with a backlit keyboard, and its 14-inch, 16:9 display feels cramped compared to other Chromebooks I’ve used with taller 16:10 screens. If you can look past those shortcomings, though, the CX34 is a solid little workhorse that stands out. —Daniel Thorp-Lancaster

What Specs Should You Look for in a Chromebook?

Chromebook prices can vary widely, from $150 to $999, so specs can differ.

Processor: For the best experience, you should avoid older Chromebooks with Intel Celeron processors. The Chromebook Plus specifications offer a good baseline to guarantee speedy performance, and I recommend going with at least an Intel Core i3, Core i5, or AMD Ryzen 3 7000 processor. Just watch out for overspending on configurations with Intel Core i7 processors unless you need the extra horsepower for multitasking, Android games, Linux apps, and dozens of Chrome tabs.

While Intel and AMD dominate the processor scene, you’ll occasionally find Chromebooks using ARM processors like the Qualcomm Snapdragon 7c Gen 2. These can be fine for very basic tasks, but they won’t fare as well under sustained, intense loads. That said, a new generation of ARM chips is on the way, like the MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 powering the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14.

RAM: Always opt for at least 8 GB of RAM if you can afford it. You won’t find 4 GB of RAM in anything but basic, super-budget Chromebooks, and it severely limits multitasking. If you want to avoid slowdowns, aim for 8 GB of RAM, though if your budget is under $300, that may be difficult.

Storage: Unlike a Mac or Windows PC, much of your Chromebook work will be stored on the web. This means you can typically get away with less storage, but I wouldn’t recommend going below 128 GB. If you can afford it, get at least 256 GB. You’ll get the best speed from an NVMe solid-state drive, so look for that on the spec sheet when you’re comparing models.

Screen: Most Chromebook displays you’ll find are IPS LCD panels, and that’s just fine. OLED displays are finally starting to appear on Chromebooks, but IPS LCD screens are more common and offer a good balance of brightness, contrast, and color accuracy. If you’re shopping in the extreme budget range, watch out for TN LCD panels, as they’re generally lower quality and offer worse viewing angles. For resolution, make 1920 x 1080 (or 1200p for a 16:10 aspect ratio) your standard. You’ll get crisp visuals on 13- and 14-inch screens, and it’s passable on 15 inches. Higher resolutions will look even better, but they are fairly uncommon in Chromebooks.

Ports: USB-C ports are now commonplace on Chromebooks, so there’s no excuse to buy one without them. Try to get one that charges over USB-C so you can recharge with a portable power bank when you’re on the go. A microSD card slot can also be beneficial if you want an easy way to expand storage on the fly. Some Chromebooks also support Thunderbolt 4 over their USB-C ports. That’s an excellent option if you plan to plug your Chromebook into high-end monitors, but it isn’t necessary for most people. Instead, you can get similar external monitor support (and spend a lot less) with an HDMI port or DisplayPort over USB-C support.

What Are Googlebooks?

For years, it had only been rumors and reports. Whispers of some kind of replacement or evolution of Chromebooks—perhaps one that might even merge Android and Chrome OS. Aluminium OS was the early code name. Such an operating system would benefit both Google and Android users, yet attempts to unify the two have not worked out so far (anyone remember the Pixel Slate?). But that’s exactly what Googlebook-based laptops are attempting to do, and as of October 2026, the first wave of Googlebooks has officially arrived.

The Googlebook OS is built entirely on Android, but it maintains the Linux kernel in order to provide the full desktop version of the Chrome web browser. This is what makes Googlebooks feel like Chromebooks, without many of the same limitations. You still can’t install traditional software like on Windows or Mac, but it can run Android apps natively. These first Googlebooks start at $899, so the company is clearly starting with high-end laptops. Cheaper Googlebooks, presumably, are to come.

Google has insisted that it won’t phase out Chromebooks right away and will support them for a long time. But it hasn't provided a timeline yet.

What Is Chromebook Plus?

Almost every Chromebook we recommend has “Chromebook Plus” in the name. Google launched this initiative in late 2023 with its hardware partners to offer a new category of Chromebooks designed for a better, more premium experience. To be deemed a Chromebook Plus, a laptop has to meet or exceed the following hardware requirements:

The result? A new baseline that guarantees a certain level of performance when you see the Chromebook Plus name. With the rise in remote work, Google is focused on ensuring Chromebook Plus laptops deliver a superior video-calling experience, with higher standards for webcams and AI-powered camera enhancements. It’s also gradually folding new AI features into ChromeOS that benefit from the better hardware. When you buy a new Chromebook Plus laptop, you currently get a free 12-month subscription to Google AI Pro, which gives you access to AI features like NotebookLM and Gemini, as well as 2 TB of cloud storage.

Regular Chromebooks haven’t disappeared, and you’ll still find super-budget Chromebook models without the “Plus” moniker. Chromebook Plus models start at $399 and range up to $800, though you’ll often find them on sale for less. Expect non-Plus Chromebooks focused on basic needs to keep hitting store shelves in the sub-$300 range. The first wave of Googlebooks have targeted the price and specs category above Chromebook Plus models, but it's worth noting that future Googlebooks may more directly intersect with Chromebook Plus territory.

How Long Do Chromebooks Get Updates?

In 2023, Google announced a new policy guaranteeing 10 years of automatic updates for any Chromebook released in 2021 or later. That’s probably far beyond the usual upgrade cycle for most people, but it keeps secondhand Chromebooks and school-issued devices secure and up to date for a long time. When a Chromebook gets its final automatic update, ChromeOS will notify you that it’s time to throw in the towel.

The 10-year automatic update timer starts from when a Chromebook is first released. You can check when your Chromebook is set to receive its final update at any time in the “Update schedule” section of its settings menu (Settings > About ChromeOS > Additional details > Update schedule). Google also keeps a handy running list of automatic update timelines for every Chromebook model on its support site.

What’s the Downside of a Chromebook?

There are lots of things you can't do on a Chromebook. You can download and organize files, but you can’t install traditional software like you can on a MacBook or Windows laptop. Everything you do must happen in a web browser. You can open Chrome windows and tabs to your heart’s content, but when you go to download the desktop version of Photoshop or Microsoft Word, you’re stuck. Proprietary school or work applications likely won’t work, and you certainly can’t play Steam games. However, you might be surprised by how much you can actually accomplish in a browser window these days.

Android apps can, however, fill in some of the gaps. With access to the Google Play Store, you can install Android games or use Android versions of some apps. This can help in a pinch, though I've often found that web-based versions of these apps work better on Chromebooks when they’re available.

Other downsides of Chromebooks come down to hardware. Most Chromebooks are made of plastic and use cheaper components. Like many budget laptops, manufacturers often compromise on touchpads and displays.

Lastly, you may run into compatibility issues with certain accessories. Standard peripherals such as mice, keyboards, and external storage shouldn’t give you issues, and even most printers are compatible. Niche peripherals designed for highly specific uses just won’t work. For example, I use a USB colorimeter to test display quality, but Chromebooks don’t support it.

Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims

Wired October 31, 2026

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest-value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured, citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open-weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

Volta’s creators included a 240-word prompt, including bullet points and a numbered list, as part of their instructions to any LLM analyzing the collected data. “You are a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment from a structured evidence bundle,” the Volta prompt says. It instructs the chatbot to produce an “executive summary” about the person, details of what they do, “what they’re worth,” and a summary of “their opsec.” It adds that the chatbot should “connect dots across fields,” for example, checking whether someone’s Wi-Fi password matches their last name. “Go deep, not wide,” the prompt says.

“The prompt is pretty carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious,” Fetterman says. “But they’re building in the expectation to potentially hit model refusals at first request. And so they plan for failover kind of cascading to more permissible models as they go down the chain. And there’s also the capability to still use the implant without the AI. The AI calls are kind of above and beyond, but the malware will still work without it.”

Some low-level cybercriminals and scammers have complained about AI slop filling up cybercrime forums, but security researchers are increasingly discovering other hackers using LLMs for coding tasks or analyzing troves of stolen information. Researchers at threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike, for example, recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups with varying sophistication—operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian—using AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail, and travel.

Cisco’s Fetterman says Volta contains some clues that it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than being developed for one specific actor’s campaigns. And while the malware at its core is still a traditional infostealer, the AI expansion foreshadows even more invasive and sinister activity in the future.

“If you’re able to identify your high-value targets faster, you probably have a better chance of using their credentials or authenticating using stolen tokens more often than maybe you would have if you had to do that triage yourself,” Fetterman says, referencing the fact that authentication tokens expire and passwords can be changed. “We’re seeing more advanced capabilities accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. It’s really interesting and disturbing.”

The Online Right’s Closing Campaign Argument: Fascist Anakin Skywalker Memes

Wired November 02, 2026

If you quit checking X months ago (or left back when it was still Twitter) and have found yourself wondering how much of a right-wing echo chamber it’s become, just try making sense of the following posts.

Yes, it seems that while the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) will remain shut down for the foreseeable future, MAGA conservatives are picking up the slack, using the last hours before the 2026 midterms to imagine themselves and Trump-aligned candidates as the disciples of a genocidal archvillain from a space opera.

According to Christian streamer Kangmin Lee, Anakin Skywalker represents the “archetypal disenfranchised chud,” radicalized when he realizes the “political order” he once believed in is “deeply corrupt, hypocritical, and wicked.” Right-wing Substack writer Max Mersault believes that the Anakin posts are “culturally significant” and that you couldn’t “engineer a better anti-progressive memetic virus in [a] lab if you tried.”

Elon Musk himself, after funneling nearly half a billion dollars to Republican candidates this cycle, shared a seemingly AI-generated image of Anakin on a throne, accompanied by his love interest Padmé Amidala, their children Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, and a bevy of imperial guards and stormtroopers, declaring: “This is what they stole from us.”

Who is “they”? What is “this”? To the MAGA faithful staring down a potential blue wave thanks to inflation, a pointless war in the Middle East, and the president’s historic unpopularity, such details hardly matter. The Anakin memes are all about advertising your fascist worldview, lust for corruptive power, and endless grievances about immigrants or “DEI.” These guys also don’t care that Anakin was groomed to be an evil lackey by a decrepit old wizard and slaughtered children on his orders, since that’s just the price of overthrowing democracy.

But even this may be giving them too much credit. After all, their Anakin trend was preceded by a craze for incel-adjacent “Malfoid” content—a fanfic twist on Harry Potter that introduces a gender-flipped, female version of antagonist Draco Malfoy as a romantic prospect for our main character—and for some reason felt that this slop, too, made good reactionary propaganda. The US Department of Education got in on the meme, later updating it with Anakin imagery.

Likewise signaling the administration’s confusing embrace of fantasy IP, Katie Miller, podcaster and wife of top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, on Sunday posted to X: “I have zero unregretted user seconds spent on Anakin postings.”

The GOP and the tech right aren’t exactly known for their cogent analysis of the stories they hold near and dear, and their identification with a murderous tyrant is no great surprise. What’s somewhat harder to explain is their apparent delusion about this message reaching and resonating with well-adjusted voters outside their esoteric social media feeds. The Anakin stuff, some of them insist, “is not a meme anymore,” constituting a “monumental zeitgeist victory.” Along with the Malfoid posts, they claim, it has reversed “a decade of cultural rot and damage in less than a week.”

Meanwhile, back in reality, this amounts to nothing more consequential than playing with action figures. Wanting to be Darth Vader is the dream of a 10-year-old forced to clean his room and eat his vegetables. Hayden Christensen, who played Anakin Skywalker in the prequels, told Variety in 2023 that depicting his journey to the dark side “humanized him” yet revealed that he was a “pathetic person” and “trapped in this life that perhaps he didn’t really want.”

You might reasonably speculate whether conservative influencers tied to a weakened Trump are in a similar position these days. Just don’t expect them to ever acknowledge this burst of mediated angst as the cringeworthy coping it actually is. However the electoral showdown plays out, they’ll have a new aspirational antihero soon enough—and this time, you won’t dare laugh at their very important posts.

A Right-Wing Think Tank Has a Plan to Prevent Democrats From Being Seated in Congress

Wired November 02, 2026

With polls indicating that the Democrats are poised to win big in the midterm elections, the Trump administration is already attempting to mount legal challenges in certain races and cast doubt on the results.

A post published last month by the Center for Renewing America, an influential right-wing think tank, suggests a more radical strategy, asserting that a number of Democrats could be prevented from holding office even if they win their elections.

The post, titled “Can Congress Seat a Member-Elect Who Vows to Destroy our Constitution?” argues that even winning candidates from what it believes to be a purported “Red-Green Alliance” between “neo-Marxist progressives and anti-Western Muslims” can and should be kept from being seated in Congress. The post, in effect, claims that Muslim and progressive candidates don’t have to be legally accepted into their elected positions.

“This is another attempt to contort and twist basic norms that have never been used this way for their own partisan purposes,” says Richard Pildes, a professor at New York University’s School of Law.

The CRA was founded by Russell Vought, one of the main architects of Project 2025 and now the director of the Office of Management and Budget. Vought faced criticism for his anti-Muslim comments—he once said that Muslims had a “deficient theology” and “do not know God”—when he was nominated for OMB director during the first Trump administration.

The Center for Renewing America (CRA) did not respond to a request for comment.

Though Vought has described himself and allies, including members of the CRA, as “radical constitutionalists,” he has taken several steps that have infringed on the powers of other branches of government to expand the power of the executive branch. Most notably, although Congress is tasked with allocating and approving funds for the operation of the federal government, Vought has impounded, refused, or delayed the disbursement of funds, including billions of dollars that Congress has approved. Last year, Vought put a freeze on $5 billion in foreign aid funding, which was followed up by clawing back more than $800 million this year, a move that may violate the Impoundment Control Act, Maine senator Susan Collins said in late September.

The recent CRA piece—authored by Benjamin Osborne, a Georgetown Law School graduate who is serving as the organization’s legal fellow—argues that the beliefs the organization has imputed to so-called Red-Green politicians are against the US Constitution. Osborne writes that “when someone elected to Congress has personally embraced the destruction of the constitutional order espoused by these groups, he or she cannot truthfully swear to support that order as a condition of taking office.”

According to another CRA publication from earlier this year written by the organization’s executive director, Wade Miller, the so-called Red-Green Alliance includes the “Squad,” the nickname for the group of four progressive women of color who all won seats in Congress in 2018: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, Ayanna Pressley, and Ilhan Omar. It also includes politicians like New York mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. These politicians, the publication claims, are purveyors of “ideology dedicated to destroying capitalism, Christianity, and the Western political tradition.” None of the politicians named in the piece have self-identified as Marxists, though some, including Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani, are Democratic Socialists.

Corey Brettschneider, a professor of politics and constitutional law at Brown University and host of the The Oath and the Office podcast, says that both posts are “engaged in an attack on the Constitution and then trying to use the law of that as an attack on opponents,” something he believes a court would quickly be able to identify and quash.

Trying to use a Muslim politician’s religion as a reason for them to be disqualified from holding office, says Brettschneider, would likely be even more difficult than taking aim at a certain political group. “The protections I'd say are even stronger against that maneuver because the Constitution is explicit in saying you can't have a religious test for office,” he says.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment on whether it was aware of the Renewing America piece or what, if any, steps it is taking to prepare for challenges to a possible win.

While any successful legal case based on the CRA's logic would be unlikely to hold up in court, Brettschneider says, “clearly what they're doing is floating it to see if it will stick.”

Christian Grose, a professor of political science at the University of Southern California, says the effectiveness of a strategy like the one outlined by the CRA would likely vary widely depending on the margins of a possible Democratic victory. If the Democrats win one or two seats in the Senate, he says, Republicans could try to dispute results in order to maintain control of the Senate. “But if Democrats win the Senate by something like four seats, I think we will be less likely to see those kinds of things,” he says. “The bigger the margin is on either side, the less likely this will be a viable strategy, and it becomes more preposterous the larger number of winning candidates that someone would try not to seat.”

For members of the House, the outcome could depend on whether Democrats can snag a majority. If Republicans maintain the majority, they could vote to refuse to seat incoming Democrats. In 1967, the House refused to seat Adam Clayton Powell Jr., a Democrat representative from Harlem and the first Black person from the state of New York to be elected to Congress, due to allegations that he was misappropriating funds.

Grose says that any legal case would risk going unresolved beyond the start of the new Congress in 2027, meaning that whether or not a senator whose win was challenged could be seated would likely be determined by a judge issuing an injunction. “It could become a Congress-versus-courts showdown,” he says.

Pildes is more direct: “This isn't going to happen.”

But just because the legal strategy may not work, it doesn’t mean the administration or Republicans wouldn’t make the attempt. Brettschneider noted the administration’s multiple attempts to charge former FBI director James Comey with various crimes, even if prosecutors are unlikely to secure a conviction. “We absolutely need to take it seriously because Trump has been dismantling the guardrails and the norms that are supposed to protect against this, or trying to influence the courts through appointments,” he says. “Even if they don't get away with it directly, threatening and shutting down opponents creates fear and makes people worry ‘they might come after me next.’”

Anti-Oligarchy Activists Plan to Dox Elon Musk and Hundreds of Billionaire-Linked Homes

Wired November 02, 2026

An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”

Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

Few have done more to expand doxing than the Department of Homeland Security itself, which simply broadened the term to include, effectively, any “videotaping” of law enforcement. Its aggressive stance on keeping officers’ faces hidden, and its refusal to identify those credibly accused of crimes, has all but ensured public campaigns to unmask its employees. Last week, hackers published the names and work contacts of more than 40,000 DHS employees and contractors, citing its practice of collecting data on the public while hiding who its officers are.

Pressed on whether its strategy amounted to doxing, the Capytistas members agree that it does, saying they have no qualms with describing their efforts that way. The group has even taken as its creed an adapted quote from the late folk singer and labor organizer Utah Phillips: “Democracy is not dying, it’s being killed,” they say, “and those who are killing it have names and addresses.”

Most of the Capytistas’ work involves digging up property records, court filings, and the LLCs and trusts that wealthy people use to buy real estate. The activists say they turn occasionally, but far less often, to physical surveillance, human infiltration, and advertising intelligence, the location and profile data bought and sold through online ad markets.

To remain profitable, one of the Capytistas argued, the businesses billionaires operate need to continuously collect people’s personal information, often nonconsensually, even as their owners and executives enjoy relatively private lives—entire fortunes built around “doxmaxxing.”

A copy of the Musk dossier seen by WIRED sorts its subjects into tiers and contains 32 home addresses tied to Musk and his executives. Musk is the “primary target.” Tesla’s board members and top executives—among them board chair Robyn Denholm and Kimbal Musk—are “secondary targets.” Each profile pairs a critical biography, drawn from court rulings, labor board decisions, and securities filings, with a home address. Investors such as Vanguard and BlackRock and nearly 40 suppliers are considered “tertiary targets,” listed only by corporate office, factory, or mine.

Tesla’s press office and investor relations team did not respond to requests for comment.

The Capytistas see Musk as effectively a gateway for normies who have yet to join its class war. Its file on him is among the smallest it has prepared, and he ranks among its “least important” targets, members say. But he was chosen first because no other person draws as much public anger, and the group hopes to harness that and release it upon others whose fortunes rely on forever wars, omnipresent surveillance, and carceral expansion.

Law enforcement records obtained by WIRED show how quickly that anger spread across the country last year. Within months of Musk’s arrival in Washington, attacks on Tesla vehicles and dealerships had hit at least nine states, according to a joint FBI-DHS bulletin released under public records law. Other documents show intelligence analysts warning cops across the country that calls to boycott Tesla and protest Musk were multiplying alongside the attacks. Hundreds of demonstrations were planned barely two months after Trump took office for the second time.

In Nevada, analysts were forced to issue formal first responder guides to fighting electric-vehicle battery fires, which they said can take up to 8,000 gallons of water to extinguish. “As a high-profile tech company tied to immense wealth and business culture, Tesla can potentially represent those grievances,” one bulletin said of vandals who had “expressed anti-corporate or anti-capitalist views.” Musk’s role at DOGE in particular, a Northern California agency wrote, had made Tesla dealerships “symbolically larger targets.”

The Capytistas say doxing gives them one thing above all: a sense among those targeted that someone is watching. Some, they hope, will simply fold under the sheer weight of that attention. For the rest, the group wants the public to make its displeasure well known, hoping for protests outside homes and on golf courses—confrontations with those who buy their way into government in the very places they go to escape all the outrage.

Privacy is the one thing that the group believes billionaires, and now trillionaires, value that activists can take away. “The Capytistas intend to level the playing field,” it says, “by giving oligarchs a taste of the invasions of privacy they commit, and monetize, every day.”

Tech executives’ homes have already become targets. In April, San Francisco police arrested a 20-year-old man they say threw an incendiary device at the home of OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, setting fire to an exterior gate. The man returned less than an hour later to threaten to burn down the company’s headquarters. No one was hurt.

In the interview with WIRED ahead of the release, one member pointed to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson in December 2024, arguing that what the group is doing is trying to prevent such bloodshed—a sentiment echoed in a statement released by the Capytistas on Monday: “While Elon Musk and the other individuals we target will undoubtedly try to frame our work as extreme and stochastic, what we’re doing is using radical accountability to build an off-ramp that might prevent the inevitable violent and tragic outcomes the oligarch class has been steering us toward.”

“In the end,” they said, “we may be doing them a favor.”

Review: Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro

Wired November 02, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

Wi-Fi 8 hasn't fully arrived, and we're even further out from Wi-Fi 8-compatible devices to come out in the real world. But I've already gotten a taste of the future of wireless connectivity.

I tried out Asus's first quad-band Wi-Fi 8 gaming router, ahead of the final certification of the latest Wi-Fi standard. The router is based on the latest draft spec of Wi-Fi 8, so it will be updated as the standard approaches final certification. The only way I could test the benefits of Wi-Fi 8 was to connect together two of these bad boys.

​After a couple of weeks of testing, there’s no denying the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro is an impressive bit of kit with many extras you don’t get from other manufacturers, including a year of NordVPN service. The firmware has also been surprisingly reliable for me, unlike first-generation Wi-Fi 7 Asus systems, which took several updates to reach stability. But most folks shouldn’t be thinking about Wi-Fi 8 yet, and this router costs $900, a hefty early adopter tax.

​The Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro is enormous, with eight adjustable but permanently affixed antennas. It’s around 14 inches square and 9 inches tall with the antennas and looks like a giant dead mecha spider. It doesn’t fit comfortably in any of the usual spots I have my router, and it makes absolutely no attempt to blend in. It does look cool, though, with a translucent window that shows off some internal components and a big Aura RGB ROG logo offering seven color lighting effects.

Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

There are advantages to all this real estate. The advanced thermal design, with multiple heatsinks and channels for airflow, allows the router to operate at top performance reliably over the long term without a noisy fan. It remained silent and cool to the touch throughout my month of testing. There’s also space for a generous array of ports, including a 10Gbps WAN/LAN, a 10 Gbps LAN, four 2.5Gbps (one WAN/LAN), one 1Gbps LAN, a USB 3.2 Gen1, and a USB 2.0 port. You can even use link aggregation on the two 10 Gbps ports (y’know, just in case you need a 20 Gbps conduit).

Inside, you’ll find Broadcom’s BCM 6718 Wi-Fi chip, featuring a 2.6GHz quad-core processor, 256 MB of Flash memory, and 2 GB of DDR4 RAM. This is a quad-band router, so you have the usual 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, alongside two 6 GHz bands. I don’t want to drown you in spec soup here, but these are all 4 x 4 with OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access), 4096-QAM, and maximum-width channels, so we’re talking theoretical top speeds of 1.3 Gbps for the 2.4 GHz band, 5.6 Gbps for the 5 GHz band, and 11.5 Gbps for each of the 6 GHz bands. If you need explanations of the jargon and why each of these specs matter, you’ll find them in my detailed guide to how to buy a router. Just know that this router is at the top of the game.

Of course, you never get maximum speeds in real life, but the speed of the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro does not disappoint. You can reasonably expect up to 3 Gbps in the same room, around 1 Gbps through a wall, and I was still able to pull 350 Mbps at the bottom of my thick-walled old home’s garden. Comparing my upgrade pick of the best Wi-Fi routers, the tri-band Wi-Fi 7 Asus RT-BE96U, the GT-BN98 Pro proved slightly faster at all distances and longer-range across the board on every band. It also has an extra 6 GHz band, perfect for wireless backhaul if you want to use AiMesh (Asus’s mesh networking functionality) to create a mesh with another Asus router.

Multi-Link Operation (MLO), enabling you to connect devices on multiple bands simultaneously, seems to be maturing since its buggy debut with Wi-Fi 7. It enabled close-range speeds close to 5 Gbps in my tests, but that's using a second Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro as a client (most Wi-Fi 8 devices, when they arrive, won't manage that).

Bear in mind that I can’t test the Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support yet, which cross-checks with licensed services in the area so your router can boost power for increased range and coverage on the 6 GHz band. It is available in the US and will be in the UK soon, but not every country allows it, and your mileage will vary depending on your local licensees.

Wi-Fi 8 isn’t primarily about higher speeds. It aims to improve stability and reliability with a raft of features that compensate for local interference and reduce latency for important tasks like gaming. The Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro boasts adaptive Quality of Experience and device optimization, automatically recognizing gaming devices and streams and giving them priority.

Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

With four gamers online in my home, from two gaming PCs, a MacBook, and a PS5, it was smooth and plain-sailing all the way. There’s a Game Boost mode that employs AI to ensure stable connectivity and low latency for gaming streams, GTNet optimizes your server connections and keeps ping and packet loss to a minimum, and there’s a mobile gaming mode. You are still at the mercy of your internet connection and online servers, but this is as much as you can do right now on the home side of things.

Asus is always among my top brands for routers and mesh systems, in no small part because the company eschews the subscription model and offers a ton of additional value through features and services that other manufacturers want to charge you a monthly fee for. That includes robust security software, in-depth parental controls, and VPN support (you can redeem a year of NordVPN service with this router). There’s also real-time traffic monitoring and a traffic analyzer.

The extras continue with USB for mobile network tethering, file sharing, or media streaming. You can set up as many networks as you want (IoT, Guest, Gaming), all with their own specific settings. Bands are split by default, but you can combine them and use band steering. You can also set up adaptive device or activity prioritization. The mobile app is as full-featured as they come, and you can dig even deeper via the web interface. Chances are good that, however you want to configure your network, you can do it with the Asus WRT6.0 firmware.

One of the most pleasant surprises with the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro is the stability. When I tested early Wi-Fi 7 routers from Asus, I ran into all kinds of weird issues and glitches, and it took a while for firmware updates to shake them out. This router competes out of the box, and the Wi-Fi 8 spec finalization, further firmware updates, and AFC rollout will improve it further.

Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

It’s obviously early days for Wi-Fi 8, and most folks don’t need to spend anything like this money on a router. You can find many cheaper alternatives in my best routers and best mesh systems guides. The only other Wi-Fi 8 router I’ve tested is the TP-Link Archer 8 Ultra, but it’s not available Stateside because TP-Link still hasn’t secured a Conditional Approval from the FCC to sell new systems in the US (Asus has). In any case, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro outperformed it in my tests.

You could save around $300 and go for the still excellent Asus RT-BE96U, or save $200 with my current pick for the best gaming router, the quad-band Wi-Fi 7 Asus ROG Rapture GT-BE98 Pro, which is almost identical. But, and I’m surprised to find myself saying this, if gaming is the thing in your home and you have the money, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro is worth buying—even now. It will give you slightly better performance today, and far better performance in the future as you upgrade to Wi-Fi 8 devices (especially if AFC is available to you).

Here’s How the Trump Administration Is Trying to Undermine the Election

Wired November 02, 2026

Polls are looking pretty bleak for Republicans—and the Trump administration’s various attempts to interfere with the elections haven’t been too successful either.

In recent weeks, the Department of Justice, helmed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, a proponent of conspiracy theories about widespread noncitizen voting in the 2020 election, has pulled out all the stops to sow doubt in voters’ minds about the security and validity of the electoral process.

To do this, the DOJ has spent the past year demanding unredacted voter rolls, issuing executive orders to wrest control of elections from states, raiding election offices, proposing new laws to disenfranchise millions of citizens, and claiming that noncitizens were voting en masse across the country. (Incidents of verified noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare, as multiple bipartisan investigations have shown.)

There have also been escalating threats by the DOJ against election officials. On Thursday, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states warning them that they would pursue criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days. Earlier that week, a federal judge had admonished the Trump administration for making similar threats around criminal prosecution against election officials in a different case.

“They're trying to create chaos and distrust in the system,” says Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at UCLA Law’s Safeguarding Democracy Project. “They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.”

“This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,” a spokesperson for the DOJ tells WIRED, pointing out that the previous administration’s Justice Department sued Alabama and Virginia ahead of the 2024 election, claiming the DOJ was at the time trying “to stop them from removing suspected noncitizens from their voter rolls.”

Experts say that while the DOJ’s current legal efforts, including escalating fights in Alaska and California over candidates and voter rolls, are faltering, they’re also designed to lay the groundwork to question the results of this week’s vote.

“We have to expect absolutely, if the election doesn't go the way the president wants, that we will see the administration’s attempt to sow doubts in the election and maybe even challenge those results, but I'm also not worried about it,” David Becker, a former DOJ lawyer and the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, tells WIRED.

“They have failed at everything they've tried to do. Our systems have held firm. Our institutions have held firm.”

Thirty-four federal district courts have ruled against President Trump since he took office in 2025, blocking access to voter rolls and preventing executive orders being implemented, according to analysis from the Brennan Center.

Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, thinks that a lot of the actions taken by the Trump administration are about a show of force and optics more than anything else. “What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing. They are trying to communicate that they're in charge, and I think it's not working,” says Levitt, now a law professor at Loyola Marymount University. “But it is really important to remember that the federal government isn't in charge of the election process. State and local officials are.”

WIRED has laid out the details of the DOJ’s legal efforts in California, Nevada, Washington, and Alaska below, which have all been met with disdain from local and state officials.

California is officially a hotbed of election controversy. In October, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking a court order against California to compel the state to sequester mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 voters, claiming that these voters were noncitizens. On Wednesday, a federal judge, in a strongly worded order, rejected the request.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” US District Judge David Carter wrote in his order filed late on Wednesday.

Almost immediately, the DOJ filed an appeal, and a federal court quickly denied it.

The judge pointed out that similar claims from the administration about noncitizens on voter rolls hadn’t held up to scrutiny, and he had “further questions of credibility” about how they arrived at that number in the first place.

Last week, a federal judge also ruled that the DOJ had to turn over its list of around 20,000 names to the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, so that the group could analyze the dataset. On Saturday, the group submitted a legal filing stating that an analysis of the list found that over 40 percent of the names weren’t even in the state’s current voter files. In response, the DOJ has suggested that the publication of their analysis violated the terms of the lists released to them and is urging a federal judge to consider whether contempt charges might be applicable here.

“The DOJ has clearly written rules that prevent it from engaging in any investigative activity close to an election—rules that private attorney Todd Blanche cited when representing his client, Donald Trump, in September 2024,” Becker says. “But the DOJ continues to violate its own policies.”

To cap it all off, the DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas to California’s local election officials last week, indicating that despite repeated court losses it has no intention of backing down.

In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit designed to block certification of the election result in Alaska’s US Senate race if Democrat candidate Mary Peltola wins.

The reason for the lawsuit is the presence of a spoiler candidate on the ballot with a name similar to the incumbent Republican candidate, Daniel Sullivan. The DOJ’s lawsuit was filed despite the Alaska Supreme Court ruling in the summer that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could remain on the ballot, as no laws had been broken.

A New York Times investigation last week alleged that Democrat-aligned operatives had been involved in getting a spoiler candidate on the ballot, though Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement in the effort to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot. Asked about whether the common practice of putting spoiler candidates on the ballot was illegal, Blanche said, “It certainly should be.” On Truth Social, Trump said Peltola “should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”

“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau last week. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”

On Thursday, Alaska governor Michael Dunleavy ordered an investigation to determine whether state criminal or civil charges could be pursued against Peltola. In an interview with NewsNation, Dunleavy said that he could not commit to certifying victory for Peltola if that investigation was still ongoing.

“Dunleavy’s threat to overrule the will of Alaskan voters exemplifies what Alaskans hate about partisan politics and shows why he’s the least popular governor in the country,” a Peltola campaign spokeswoman tells WIRED. “Mary won’t be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted—and she’s going to win this race by focusing on solutions to Sullivan’s price-hiking policies and putting Alaska first.”

On Friday, the DOJ held a press conference in Anchorage and said that, in addition to its lawsuit seeking to block the certification of the election result if Peltola wins, the department was also launching its own investigation to determine whether federal civil or criminal charges could be applicable in this case. “We are aware of … the sprawling conspiracy to prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate,” said Michael Heyman, US attorney for the District of Alaska.

On Sunday, a federal judge threw out the DOJ’s lawsuit, ruling that its request likely violated Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot. Hours later, the DOJ asked a federal appeals court to overturn the ruling.

In July, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that it had identified over 270,000 noncitizen voters in just four states: California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. But that bold assertion soon started to unravel.

DHS officials had also claimed that there were 15,903 noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls but later conceded in a meeting with Nevada officials that they didn’t have evidence. The number of suspected noncitizens on voter rolls then dropped down to 185, but there was no evidence to support that claim either.

“As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens,” Nevada’s deputy attorney general Greg Ott wrote in a letter to DHS. “You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise.”

“The department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross-referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED about the situation. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

Ott added in the letter that while Nevada takes allegations of noncitizen voting seriously, “it also has a strong interest in preventing the wrongful disenfranchisement of voters” and is “committed to preventing the chilling effect on the right to vote from taking actions based on unfounded and unverifiable allegations of noncitizen voting.”

Last week, the DOJ claimed that federal data appeared to show that 400 noncitizens were registered to vote in the state of Washington and demanded that officials isolate those ballots, describing them as “the tip of the iceberg.”

They received another withering letter in return: “The timing of your letter is profoundly disappointing,” wrote Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs. “If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was a month ago.” Hobbs added that the DOJ’s decision to publicly raise concerns so close to the election was “not a sign of good faith to ensure a free, fair, and accurate election.”

Hobbs added that the DOJ had failed to provide individualized proof that any of the people on the list were ineligible to vote and didn’t offer any information about how they arrived at the lists of names or what sources were used. “Given the Department of Justice’s recent acts of election interference in California, Alaska, and now in Washington, it would be particularly inappropriate for Washington to simply assume the Department’s unsupported allegations here are credible.”

While not a filing by the Justice Department, the Potter County Republican Party has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from certifying the vote unless all Texas ballots are counted by hand.

The GOP’s basis for demanding a manual audit includes purported threats from artificial intelligence’s ability to supposedly hack into virtually any voting machine undetected, a claim presented without evidence, and the presence of voting machine parts manufactured in China. Levitt, the former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, described the lawsuit as “nuts.”

“That would be the technical term,” Levitt said. “I wish that they had filed the thing in Comic Sans on the back of a Burger King place mat, because I think that would help people evaluate how serious it is.”
